In class discussions and guest speakers were also really effective tools in further learning and developing a perspective. I would strongly encourage anyone with an interest in tech, policy, or venture capital to take this class - but really, I think it would be valuable for anyone.

The strength of this class is the opportunity to learn from a a diverse set of panelists across sectors (government, VC, tech entrepreneurs). a great way to get a finger on the pulse of what?s happening today in the SF tech scene and how we got here.

Absolutely, the course may be titled 'How to Get Urban Innovation Right' but it really touches on the basics of private- public partnerships and the role of tech in society; both of which are relevant to everyone in the 21st century. I would highly recommend this class to any students interested in urban tech. You can learn urban tech from readings, guest speakers, discussions, etc.

Yes I would highly recommend this class and Molly. Molly is a passionate leader in the urban tech space. She is extremely prepared for every class and guides the conversation in such a way that everyone in the class feels comfortable and encouraged to share their viewpoints. Molly is an excellent teacher and has left me with lessons I will take into my career for decades. Everyone should take a class taught by Molly!

100% yes! Molly is the best professor I've had at Haas/UC Berkeley writ large. She brings in so much real-world experience and has a well-rounded perspective on tackling our biggest urban issues. As someone with no real familiarity in the subjects of tech and urbanization, I am now very comfortable addressing these issues & continuing on to be a student of cities.

Yes. I would strongly recommend this course to other students who are interested in working in tech, VC, start-ups, or government. The course touches on all these spaces and more, and is the most interdisciplinary class I've taken at Haas. It is valuable to learn from other grad students, and especially from all the many, many guest speakers! It allows for really interesting in-depth discussion and is one of the few places that has taken a more thoughtful, critical approach to business and the limits of business. It's also really insightful strategy.
10/10 absolutely yes
Yes

Absolutely! This was my favorite class this semester - as a non-Haas student, I was constantly going back to my peers in my program and raving about this class. It flipped the way I look at things and made me think more critically about the relationship between technology and cities. Molly really encourages personal growth in terms of professional skills and more dynamic thought processes.
Very highly recommend this course if you have any interest in startups, VCs, cities, and/or technological solutions to everyday problems

I would recommend this class if you are looking for a different perspective. This class is a combination of business and public policy, and the diverse backgrounds of the students give you more beyond MBA class. However, sometimes it is high level and there are lots of readings (if you follow), and the latter half of the class felt a bit loose. But loved this class in general.

This class was a light and interesting way to think about the multiple stakeholders involved in the entire tech ecosystem. You get a chance to listen to stakeholders in tech, VC, policy, labour, media and more purely in the context of tech applied to urban issues (namely housing, transportation, and gig economy). The group presentations are a good way to dive into new companies of interest that might not have been on your radar and the memos were nice to solidify learnings. Given the breadth of topics, it is difficult to get into each in too much depth.
for ppl who interested in learning new tech trend about the cities, this is not the right course to choose and its more about policis, ethics sort of stuff

Yes! This is a fantastic class that encourages critical thinking, challenges conventional attitudes toward VC, technology, and innovation, and provides excellent opportunities to build and expand your network

This was my dream class. after every single session I came away grateful I got the chance to be in it. Molly teaches the critical thinking skills we don't get elsewhere in business school. The guest speakers were EXCELLENT — felt like being in a private podcast. Molly is so generous with her students and we're lucky we get to learn from her. Heavy workload but it is 100% worth it.

The course is really interesting as it tries to solve the hard question on how tech can help city challenges, as often there is a clear answer, but some other times it is not that clear. That is what Molly shares with a lot of passion and knowledge on the topic, she brings great speakers and usually challenges them making discussions more engaging. This was my favorite course at Haas. The content is truly relevant, not only for people interested in cities or policy. It creates a much needed space to discuss around the interaction between startups, government, individuals, and more. We finally reflect on if we are answering the right questions, and who is better position to solve each issue. The scope of the class is very broad, but thats the beauty of it, going from childcare to housing affordability, we are finally discussing how this issues are being solved and what role each type of actor can have. Its those classes were everyone participates, and you get to hear very interesting perspectives from your peers, while at the same time getting frameworks from Molly and the great speakers that she brings.
Absolutely. I learned more than in any other class.

Overall, this class is a very interesting take into how large tech companies impact our day to day living. The readings are interesting, and so are some of the class discussions, but feels like it shouldn't be a full semester long class. All in all, one of the better courses I've taken at Haas and Molly is a great resource to have if you're interested in urban planning!
The class participation and student engagement was the best part of the class so please sign up if that is the type of course you want to be part of.

Yes! Great class to examine the effects of VCs and startups on cities. Interesting history, cases, and guest lecturers. Yes, This program enriches students with great context about urban innovation and I don't think there is any structured opportunity to learn the amount of concepts we learned in class
I would 100% recommend Molly and Tech and the City to anyone who is interested in how innovation can be

deployed to society. She knows a bunch of really interesting folks in the industry, brings a really practical lens to addressing complex urban problems, and facilitates great discussions within class. This may be the best class I've taken through 3 semesters at Haas
Definitely. Great class.

I would highly recommend taking Molly's courses. She is brilliant, thoughtful, and provocative. She has so much expertise and knowledge on urban technology. Be ready to engage in class discussions and learn about multiple perspectives.
Yes, Molly has an outstanding mastery of all things urban tech and has really insightful perspectives. She brings in a wide range of incredible speakers that are really interesting.

YES! If you are interested in technology, cities, VC, or policy - or even if you just want to have some interesting discussions - take this class. Molly is a phenomenal teacher, and the class is very well-structured and challenges you to think critically and systematically about many issues. It was one of the best electives I've taken!
I would recommend both this class and the professor to all students. This was one of the more engaging, enjoyable, and valuable classes I took at Haas, and that is a credit to Molly Turner.
Absolutely! Incredible class
Yes this class and Molly are amazing!!! Molly is such a great instructor I wish I could take more courses with her. Highlight of my time at Haas
Absolutely recommend - Great class, expands your mind and thinking, and is knowledge every future tech leader should have.

sections.goodFor: Students who want their worldview challenged, and those in real estate, urban policy or tech who want a critical humanities-style seminar plus a strong practitioner speaker network.
sections.notFor: Anyone wanting practical frameworks to build or launch urban tech; the description misleads. Not for people who want to coast or dislike heavy reading, cold calls and a critical/pessimistic lens.
sections.workloadNote: Strongly front-loaded: an immense reading load in the first half, much lighter by around October. Heavy prep for discussion and participation throughout; the professor grades assignments herself.
sections.gradingBasis: Participation in discussion with cold calling, plus written assignments graded by the professor rather than a reader. Weights not discussed.
sections.redFlags: Misleading description - critical humanities seminar, not innovation frameworks (3). Reading heavier up front than advertised (5). One reports abrasive cold-call responses early on; 2 call discussion curated/biased.
sections.quote: Be prepared for heavy reading, especially in the first month. This feels more like a graduate seminar in urban studies than a typical MBA elective.
comments: Yes! Not enough courses at business school are asking tough, probing questions about technology and innovation, making this is a rare opportunity.

This was by far the most interesting topic and course material I've gotten to take at Haas. The course is structured with a ton of intention bringing lots of really interesting readings, guest speakers, and discussions to the table. It definitely requires critical thinking and some work, but I think it was worth it!
Yes I would, it's a good amount of work but it is very engaging, covers a lot of material and is very very engaging and exciting.

Mostly yes - it was the best class I took this semester but some moments were frustrating. The workload is heavy at first, and the expectations are very high to read everything and participate which can be a little stressful. The course balances out later, and there are some genuinely great classes and insights. Very discussion heavy, but sometimes it can feel overly curated to the point where you don't feel like it's worth participating.
This is a lot of work and sometimes a little arduous but I did learn a lot

I'd recommend this course with significant caveats about expectations. I enrolled thinking this would focus on how to innovate in urban spaces using technology — essentially a course on doing tech-driven urban innovation right. That's not what this is. Instead, this course takes a critical, humanities-oriented lens examining the ethical implications and unintended consequences of urban innovation. It's much more about understanding what goes wrong and why, rather than learning frameworks for designing and implementing urban tech solutions.

If you're interested in real estate or urban planning with a focus on responsible development and social impact, this course offers genuine value. The speaker series brings in interesting practitioners from Molly's extensive network, and you'll be exposed to thoughtful critiques of how technology intersects with cities. If you're approaching this from a tech or product management perspective (as I was), there's still something to gain — particularly in developing a more nuanced understanding of stakeholder impacts and ethical considerations. However, don't expect a course on innovation strategy or emerging urban technologies.
Be prepared for heavy reading, especially in the first month. This feels more like a graduate seminar in urban studies than a typical MBA elective.

Molly is exceptionally knowledgeable and clearly well-connected in this space. She knows her material deeply and brings real-world credibility. Whether you find her perspective convincing will likely depend on how closely your views align with hers going in, but you'll definitely be intellectually challenged.

Bottom line: Take this course if you're genuinely curious about the critical perspective on urban innovation and comfortable with a humanities-heavy approach. Skip it if you're looking for practical frameworks on how to build or launch urban tech products.

I found this course to be incredibly valuable as an MBA student preparing to enter the tech space. It made me consider how to think more critically about potential tech solutions, and if they really are solutions. Molly is very up front about the workload of the class -- be prepared that the first half of the course will be very reading/homework heavy, to set the foundation for the remainder of the course. If that is something you can commit to doing well, then I highly recommend the course. The second half of the semester is much lighter workload, as well.

Unsure. If you asked me after the first 7 weeks of class, I would have said no, but if you asked me after just the last seven weeks, I would say yes. At the beginning of the semester, Molly was intense, and there was an IMMENSE amount of reading with a lot of cold calling. After cold calling people, her responses to many students was abrasive and abrupt. I usually love learning, but in this class, it was harder to find that joy because I felt stressed and anxious. I feel like there is a way to ask questions, invite conversation, motivate students, and have debate without digging into people. During the second half of the semester, there was a big change. She relaxed more, and we had less reading and more interesting guest speakers. I think she really took our mid-semester feedback to heart and made changes. Looking at the semester as a whole now, Molly was incredibly organized, and she clearly cares a lot. She graded all of the assignments, not the reader, which is a ton of work. I think feedback is a gift, and she absolutely took the time to give thoughtful and detailed feedback. I do deeply appreciate that.

This is one of the best classes I took at Haas. Molly expects a lot. Don't take this class if you want to slack off, not go to class, not pay attention, not do the reading, etc. There are plenty of classes here where you can do that. Take this class if you want to learn. Molly has a nuanced, deep perspective on how tech and policy interact. She will equip you with knowledge of the history of cities and how you should think about it today. She will impart incredibly insightful lessons from decades of real work in this space. She is the real deal. The guest speakers she brings in are fantastic and she asks great questions of them. There are far too many classes that are just fluff pieces for guest speakers. Molly asks them to have and defend interesting perspectives. Your own perspectives may be challenged in this class. That's a great thing. But you should be ready for that if you're going to take it.

If you're looking for a course on urbanism, the challenges cities face and different solutions implemented around the world, this is NOT your course. This course focuses more on a bit of urbanism history in the Bay Area and mostly on managing the public policies challenges for urban tech startups.
Yes!
I would!! I think it is tough class but sometimes we need that here.

Molly was an amazing professor and this was the best elective I have taken at Haas. I appreciate that she created an environment where everyone was really focused - it's rare to see a class where no one was on their devices, and I think the reason for that is because of how engaging both the content and the guest speakers were. Molly is really knowledgeable about the subject matter and does a great job of sharing her expertise with the class - she has worked in this space for a long time and it shows. This class truly changed my worldview and has made me take different actions in my personal life - notably, to get more involved with local news and politics! The one thing to note is that their is a lot of work early in the semester (heavy reading load) but by October that totally goes away, and the class becomes much more manageable.
Front heavy with lots of readings! So be ready, but guests were very interesting and engaging
Highly recommended but the students should understand that the workload is relatively heavy.
I would recommend this course with some caveats. The description sets the expectation of a more balanced,

discussion-driven class, but in practice the conversations can feel somewhat biased and there isn't always enough time for genuine, open debate among students. The workload is also heavier in the first half of the semester than the course description implies, and the large number of guest speakers — while interesting — sometimes compresses the time available for deeper class engagement. Students who enjoy hearing from practitioners will find value here, but those seeking more structured, student-led discussion should be aware of the trade-offs.
I would recommend. She is smart and structured and different from any other professor on campus. Truly learned a lot but you must be ready to work, pay attention and be open minded to her style
I would. I think Molly brings a unique perspective as a practitioner and the class provides an interesting POV that isn't common here at Haas

I would unequivocally recommend this course to anyone who wants to have their perspective challenged, and wants to come away with a unique set of viewpoints on the role of governments and venture capital in how start-ups can thrive. Any aspiring founders could really benefit from Molly's perspective!

Yes but do know there will be a lot of tough love from Molly. She really wants to expand your horizons and challenge your world views but you need to be ready for it. For me, it was a good way to learn new and different things because with business electives the incremental learnings arent that great
Yes. Very well designed class.
I would not. See previous comments. The course is to pessimistic

This course is a great option for students who are interested in developing a POV on urban problems and tech solutions in cities. It is a class that requires strong engagement in and outside of class, but Molly brings great guest speakers and is very intentional about the course design.

rows.title: International Business Development for MBAs, IP course

sections.goodFor: Students who want real international client consulting plus travel and cultural immersion, and who can tolerate not knowing their country, team or client when they sign up.
sections.notFor: Anyone needing to know the project/team/country in advance, unable to absorb heavy hours, or serving as team lead - leads report far more work, little recognition. Class only teaches go-to-market.
sections.workloadNote: Heavy: team consulting project running January-May plus assignments in the following fall semester, with 80+ hour weeks during two weeks of in-country work. Students dispute the 3-credit allocation.
sections.gradingBasis: Team consulting deliverables (blog post, final presentation) plus a fall presentation for the last credit; guidelines not enforced evenly.
sections.redFlags: Credit/workload mismatch (1 argues it should be 4 credits); assignment instructions confusing and constantly changing; guidelines unenforced, advantaging teams that ignore them; team leads carry far more work.
sections.quote: When you sign up for the course, you have no knowledge about what experience you are doing to get (country, team, client), so it is definitely a risk.
comments: Absolutely. Amazing opportunity to get consulting experience while traveling the world.
This is a truly transformative experience. A lot of work, a lot of hard work!! But you get to learn so much, experience so much, and explore so much! I highly recommend this course????
I would. This was a GREAT course!!

This course, as many people know, carries a lot of uncertainty. When you sign up for the course, you have no knowledge about what experience you are doing to get (country, team, client), so it is definitely a risk. But that said, I think the whole experience was worth it once you are able to go to your country, experience a new culture, and meet your client in person.

There were a few issues with this course throughout the semester that I hope are addressed: 1. The class time was not always relevant to all projects and it seemed not the best use of time for all teams. I think sharing a variety of resources that might or might not be applicable to projects would be rather, rather than providing only one framework or way to do things and assume that all teams can use this in their project. 2. Especially at the end, guidelines provided for some assignments were not followed by all teams. For example, we were told to keep the blog post at certain length, or the final presentation at 3 slides and these guidelines seemed almost "optional" and not really enforced by all teams, creating an unfair advantage for those teams who did follow the guidelines. 3. This class should be 4 credits if they still make us do assignments in the fall semester. I think it is ridiculous that we only get 2 credits in the spring for the amount of work we put in, including traveling in country and working 80+ hours for two weeks while in- country. All other applied innovation classes that have client-facing work are 3 credits. The fact that we also need to do a presentation in the fall to get the final 1 credit out of the 3 does not make sense at all, and this should be 1 credit IN ADDITION to the 3 credits we should already be earning for all our work from January to May. I hope this changes for future classes.
Yes if they are willing to work extra hours
Project, team, and country dependent. Super MBA experience and would recommend doing it. Team leads should
expect to do a lot more work with little recognition.

It's a great course with plenty of opportunity. Well-organized but not all projects are Go To Market strategy, and that is all the course focuses on. Instructors are very helpful, but instructions for assignments are confusing and change constantly
Yes, this was my all time favorite experience at Haas. The in country travel was a once in a lifetime experience, and I made lifelong friendships with my teammates.
Yes for the travel and consulting case experience!! Bang for your buck
Yes for those who are certain that they would like to go into PM. I wouldn't recommend it to those who are uncertain since it may not be as applicable.
Yes - good from workload perspective and very helpful for people preparing for interviews.

It depends. Class is very light for the 2 units assigned (the easiest 2 unit class I have taken), but at the same time the value is somewhat limited. I would recommend this to someone who doesn't really know anything about PM and looking to understand the role better, but if you have some experience / knowledge in the field then I only would take it if you need 2 easy units

Vince Law and Sam Ham make a great team! I really enjoyed both of them as facilitators, and they were always very well prepared for class. They have great work experiences that can be applied to their teachings as well. I would recommend this course more for students who don't have any PM or related experience designing or implementing software/systems. My favorite part of the course were the Thursdays where we were able to hear from alumni from different companies and sometimes roles -- they were very relevant to us and widened our perspectives on the scope of PM.

Yes! This course provides an excellent overview of the opportunities/challenges that Product Managers face, and methods for overcoming these barriers. Extremely practical course with real-world applications. Excellent! If you don't have any previous PM experience and never facilitated meetings/projects before, this is a great course for you.
Absolutely! This course is super helpful who anyone interested in the tech industry or looking to polishing their soft skills.
Yes, immensely valuable — great for understanding the world of PMs, Tech, and cross functional partnerships. Vince and Sam are fantastic teachers and having this time with them is precious.
As someone with no prior PM experience, I thought this was an interesting elective and would recommend it as a relatively low-lift class.
I would not recommend this course, because it doesn't lead to substantial learning. Many topics are covered in Power & Politics, Negotiations, Strategy, Product Management, etc.
This course may be insightful if your knowledge about PM working environment is very limited.

Yes. The courses taught by Vince are always well designed and structured and often leads to effective, useful and practical learning. The case Vince prepared for this course is very relevant and insightful for the learning objective of this course. Also, Vince prepare videos and readings that are very relevant and easy to digest. (So no 30-page academic research papers or 20-page HBS cases where you need to spend a long time to read in order to find the important information from). I can see that he truly values and respects the time of his students and want us to have a high ROI for the time we invest in the learning the course he teaches.

I would highly recommend this course to other students. This course is an engaging and fun way to understand some basics about the product management industry. I would not hesitate to take this course again.
Yes, it was good.
It was the most practical class so far at Haas, it felt more linked to what we will actually do at work than the rest of the classes.

My feelings are mixed on this class. Especially virtually, it was really hard for me to pay attention during the lecture part of the class. I thought the meta activities and stakeholder monopoly were great. Some of the speakers weren't great and I didn't get what the point. I had a hard time paying attention and think I would have to some degree in person too. I think this class could improve by being more hands on and less listening to other's experiences. I wouldn't recommend this course if you are trying to learn about how to be a PM. I found the subject matter too general to be helpful. It felt more like a class about soft skills needed to work in teams rather than a course to prepare you for PM.
If you plan/hope to be a PM, this class will give you some helpful tips and tricks to consider.
this is really worth itif you want to learn how to influence and lead teams of people effectively

There might be more worthwhile courses for deeper learning but I do think this class had some real-world tips that will be more directly applicable to things I will be doing in the future than other classes at Haas so it's a good course to balance with more technical classes.

Vince and Sam are really nice. The class seems designed to be low-effort rather than to provide substantial learning. If that's for you go for it, but don't expect to improve your team facilitation skills.
For those interested in product management, this course would be worthwhile. For those who aren't, it isn't. Also the professor will email you if you miss class, its a little weird.
Yes! I thought the course was a really helpful one if you're interested in going into PM. Sam and Vince are great! Yes, overall this is a great introduction to the function
Yes
Definitely! Vince and Sam are wonderful teachers with an enormous amount of shared experience in product

management. The concepts and methods learned in this course are all based on real-life situations and I now feel much more prepared to face difficult work dynamics in the tech industry. I highly recommend this course!

This is a pretty fluffy organizational dynamics course that is not a substitute for taking Product Management. This is probably a good course for someone 100% planning on going into big tech/PM but as someone in a different space I didn't get much out of it.

Professors are kind, and have a lot of experience. While I did learn some cool things, I don't think the learnings from lectures are anything super useful unless you have no background in the tech / PM space. Great class structure though, and lots of organic interactions take place. Also great to be a quarter class.

Yes, this course provides a lot of relevant content for aspiring PMs, particularly on the interpersonal skills aspects of the job rather than just the technical product development. Guest speakers are very relevant, and the case we use each week is low reading while high value in illustrating concepts. Overall, the course is relatively lighter lift while being very engaging. Vince and Sam are very helpful in bringing their own experiences to the course.

I would recommend this course someone looking for a relatively low-lift 2-unit course, or someone with absolutely no background/understanding of product management in the tech industry. You'll learn about PM/tech vocabulary and topics at a very high-level. If you've worked in tech or have PM experience, there's very little value add. Sam and Vince are great instructors who have substantial knowledge of the material and have been successful in their industry roles.
For someone without tech industry experience who is going into a PM or adjacent role there is some value in learning more about the environments which PMs operate in.
10/10 would recommend this class. I learned so much in 7 weeks and feel a lot more confident heading into my summer PM internship!

I would definitely recommend this course to anyone who is interested in applying for a PM role. The course content reinforces PM best practices and introduces students to a cohort of peers seeking similar roles. The instructors are super knowledgeable and are a great resource for career advice.
Easy class with tangible takeaways - would recommend!
Yes, only if they are interested in product related roles and want to work on soft skills. This course has a very niche focus and may not be for everyone.

This is a light lift class and would recommend taking this for learnings on the soft skills of being a PM. Vince and Sam bring in guest speakers every week and the course load was effective but not very heavy. Class discussion was interesting and there was a lot to be learned from peers.
Highly recommend - great real life experience, approachable in career advices, amenable to student feedback and cares about our careers as PMs
Yes, if you are interested in product management with no experience, this is a great intro into the "soft skills" of being a PM.

I would recommend this to a first year spring student before their summer internship and if they are pivoting to PM. Its a really manageable lift and the professors are both extremely thoughtful, knowledgeable and kind.
Yes if they are interested in PM
Yes, pre-training for stepping into a real PM job.
Yes. The course is useful. However, I took New Product Development Process with Vince last semester and some content is overlapped.

Definitely not. In fact, I have talked to several of my peers from this class and I have heard the same response. This is probably the most useless class I have taken here at Haas so far (as someone who is trying to transition into PM). You don't learn anything more than you probably already know. Plus, this class is such a drag. You go to class on Monday, sit there for 2 hours just to have a class discussion that is close to pointless. And all your peers are working on something else on their laptops. The only somewhat benefit I have gained is from the Wednesday sessions when some guest speakers are invited. There are definitely better classes at Haas that would be more worthwhile for your time and money. However, if you want a VERY low-lift class that you can work on other things, this might be the class for you. I think this course has a lot of potential, but some aspects like the assignment pacing need to be rethought (the interview time turnaround for the first assignment was tough and it felt like it took a while for the other assignments to hit. It was also challenging to see the relevance of the non-interview assignments). However, I think that it's good exposure to 'PM-y' language and thought processes, so it could be a good intro for people new to PM.
Yes, lots of soft skills learned and I feel more prepared heading into my first PM internship. Every week there were guest lectures and they brought in really valuable insights and advice.

If you know nothing about PM, this might be a helpful class to take. However, given that this is a spring course, most students interested in PM will already have a good understanding of what it takes to be an effective PM through coffee chats, speaker panels, etc. in the fall. If that's you, I would not recommend this class - the content covered is quite broad and general, and I don't feel like I learned a ton. But if you have zero baseline knowledge of PM, this would be an interesting class to get that exposure. That being said, Sam and Vince are great instructors who are very helpful and kind.
I don't think I know more about facilitating a team after taking the course than I knew before.
Yes. This course provides practical experience for students to become a product manager.

I really wanted to like this course and was so excited that Sam and Vince were teaching it. They are phenomenal teachers and have a wide range of experience but when I got to the first few classes, I slowly realized this class was a huge waste of my time. The content for the course needs to be totally revamped. We had a whole class where we talked about if design thinking was dead and so many more classes like this is where we should have learned how to facilitate and lead discussions as a PM. Being a PM is difficult and most people don't have a technical background and are going to work on somewhat technical projects. This class should be geared more toward leading discussions when you need to get engineers to do something they might not necessarily want to do and then give them candid feedback on this. Unless they revamp the course, don't waste your time taking this and instead take power and politics. yes. for someone who wnats to be a pm, i would highly recommend taking all classes that vince teaches
would be nice if the class had a field trip option on a wednesday. i liked the guest speakers.

Not really. If you're expecting an actual PM class that goes over how to manage/develop products, you'll be disappointed. This class is more on how to manage teams that you would work with as a PM and focused on soft skills and political structure of a PM. Useful, but any student with work experience working with people would find it repetitive.
Yes! its a light class with lots to learn about how to navigate corporate/start work environments and how to convince management.

I would not recommend this course. I have been a big fan of Vince so enrolled this class but it was quite disappointing. Simply listening to each person's experience in every class made me easily bored. The cases we covered in class were also too fictionalized and didn't really resonate with me. I think it would have been better to have individual business cases from HBR or something.
Yes to both, with my only caveat being that I couldn't help at times feeling that I wanted a bit more of the things that I mentioned in the " areas of improvement " section
Absolutely. Fantastic intersection of theory and practice and the instructors are a real value-add
Yes. Great class. Lots of great speakers. Applied knowledge.
Yes, very practical and hands on experience. It's real money.

Yes, as the experiential learnings achieved from adjusting the Investment Policy Statement and allocation ranges, making and acting upon pitches, and pursuing adjacent learning opportunities (advocacy case competitions etc.) gave a well–rounded learning experience more than worth the 4 credits required. Ideal class for applying prior learnings from FIA, Portfolio Construction and other prerequisites and FIN/SUST courses.
Definitely yes!! This class is a must for students interested in sustainable finance. It's a great way to have real life learning and practice of managing a portfolio and learning about ESG
You get out what you put in – this can be a great opportunity if you're willing to take the lead as a student
Excellent course to learn how to manage a portfolio of assets with a focus on both financial and impact metrics. In short, there is nothing like managing an actual $4+ MM fund as an MBA student!
100%. Incredible course and instructor team
I'd recommend this course to anyone that is interested in learning more about impact investing! The hands–on approach makes it so that you learn an incredible amount about how a fund is managed.
I would still recommend this class because its a good opportunity to invest in the public markets with a sustainability focus in mind.

sections.goodFor: Students curious how AI both harms and helps sustainability - circularity, waste, water, energy - who want a light, speaker-driven format with real industry examples.
sections.notFor: Students wanting sustained group discussion or a hands-on venture/pitch component: two ask for more discussion and less speaker time, and the speaker roster skews to one company.
sections.workloadNote: Light: only short assignments before each session. Sessions run roughly 10:00-3:30 rather than consuming a whole Sunday. First iteration of the course.
sections.gradingBasis: Short pre-session assignments; grading not otherwise discussed.
sections.redFlags: Speaker lineup skews heavily toward Google (2 of 10 note it, tied to a professor's background); 2 want more group discussion instead of speaker talks; first-time offering.

rows.title: Sustainable Capitalism in the Nordics
rows.disagree: Modest rating, but comments are uniformly enthusiastic

comments: Yes 100% recommend!! Even if you're knowledgeable about our broken system in the US, Robert presents arguments I'd never heard before. Also, it's obviously super fun to get to go to Copenhagen for class!
Yes! Great class, really fun trip

100% yes! This course was one of my favorite classes at Haas and easily one of the most rewarding experiences I've had at Haas and beyond. If you're interested in learning about sustainable systems, stakeholder capitalism, and alternative business structures, I highly recommend this class. If you're only vaguely interested in these systems but are seeking an opportunity to travel to Copenhagen, visit inspiring companies, eat well, and bond with your classmates in a more intimate setting, I highly recommend this class! The programming for our immersive week in Copenhagen ranged from small class discussion, engaging conversations with inspiring guest speakers and presenters, visiting a wide range of sustainable companies and organizations, and learning from the people and business leaders of the Nordics. It was the perfect amount of engagement and learning that allowed for your own self-exploration outside of class time. Cannot recommend enough!!
Yes, I will.
100% yes - this is worthwhile and subject matter you won't get anywhere else at Haas.

I took this course during my last semester at Haas and it was a great way to cap off the program. I enrolled in the course because I was curious about the Nordic business structure and wanted to experience it first hand. What I got out of this course was so much more. The Nordic model is a real life example of Haas's defining principles in action. The people are humble and their education system has created a society that is constantly seeking knowledge and unafraid to challenge convention. While Professor Strand has been teaching this class for years, it was the first time being offered at Haas and it should definitely become a permanent offering. 'Mr. Nordic', as the professor is often called, has developed relationships with people and companies who welcomed us into their offices and homes to share their culture, all in the hope for a better future for all. The only downside of this course is that it is expensive. On top of the 2-units, you also have to pay $500 to the affiliate school, plus airfare, lodging and many meals. Still well worth it but definitely a factor to consider when enrolling.

This class was my absolute favorite class at Haas. Not only is the professor a great teacher, but on our trip to Copenhagen we met with some of the most interesting business leaders I've ever gotten a chance to hear from. The course material itself is a great synthesis of much of what I loved learning about in Business school: strategy, macroeconomics, entrepreneurship, corporate structure, sustainability. There is quite a lot of public policy discussed in this course, but completely makes sense to study it in the context of the Nordic Capitalist model.
Take this class for the immersion week in Copenhagen. A book by the Prof. is the course material and the course could use supplemental reading to reinforce/expand/detail the concepts in the book.
This class made my full MBA experience complete.

It helped me clarify and questioned critical aspects of how I define myself as a leader, how do I drive purpose and employee my skills to make the world a better place. The idea of thinking systematically and in framework created a clarified discussion on sustainability as a wholistic building block and true construct of society. The visual of how a systems society operates really helps question the status quo to transform worlds.

I truly recommend this class to all of the MBA program. This class provides a sense of individual, community, society and world that aids to create true leaders that live and breath the 4 Haas Defining Leadership Principles. I would even petition for this class to be a fundamental program and serve as the We Lead retreat for all MBA programs. 1000% YES. This is a MUST-TAKE class for anyone, MBA or not. We in America are often blind to realities in other countries, and the Nordics give us an inspiring north star to aspire to. We learned exactly why the Nordics are the happiest countries in the world, with some of the best rankings in the world in various areas.

Robert Strand is a passionate and invigorating professor, major kudos to him to arranging everything that went into the course. A substantial amount of learning happened for me during this course. I also appreciate the comprehensive discussion: there are flaws to/arguments against the Nordic systems and we cover those areas to have a well-rounded understanding of all things Nordic.

Quoting SAS airlines: " When we travel, we influence our surroundings, and we are influenced by others. The experiences we bring back from our travels inspire us as individuals, but also our society. " This class fully embodies this quote and I am so glad I took this class.
Brb, off to become my version of a Mr. Nordic to my family and social circles.

This was one of the most impactful experiences I had while at Haas. Robert has done such a great job of cultivating connections in the Nordics and in Copenhagen specifically that the trip to Copenhagen was absolutely amazing. The talks and presentations by the various companies, leaders, and government officials in Copenhagen were eye opening. The course readings were largely from the professor's upcoming book that is the roadmap for the course subject matter, and it contains some really great ideas and observations that have changed the way I understand at capitalism, especially how it functions outside of the US. I would highly recommend this course, and suggest that courses like this become part of the required curriculum at Haas.
Absolutely. This is the best course at Berkeley Haas and will completely transform your view of business' role and responsibility within society at large.

If there is only one class you can take at Haas, I would recommend you take this class. I felt that I really got an education by taking this one course. Here are a list of things that I think you take away from this course 1. Learn a lot about sustainability, science based targets and how companies in the Nordics are making sustainability a competitive advantage. This knowledge would be super useful for anyone in any company.
2. Make a lot of connections in Denmark and other Nordic countries. I met a lot of people from the industry & government in Denmark which is already paying off dividends for me in the US.
3. Really understand what Democracy, freedom & capitalism mean and how the Nordics have figured out a model of capitalism that is not only good for businesses but also good for citizens.
4. A week in Copenhagen, which is an amazing city.
5. A certificate from the Copenhagen Business School.
I can keep going, but I think those are more than enough reasons to take this course.

I would, hesitantly. The course concept itself is great. But the semester materials and preparation were totally inadequate. At times it felt like Robert was trying to get students to edit his pdf book rather than give us good academic materials to read. I learned a lot from the people we spoke to in country, but not much from Robert. He would say the same things over and over again and not add much value. He would tell us to "step back" but would proceed to interrupt and talk over people incessantly. It was difficult to be around and witness. Yes, this class was exceptional. It isn't often that you get the opportunity to study a culture and during an immersion week not only experience this culture, but also visit businesses that are championing this culture. This class is holistic and will provide a new way of viewing the world. The immersion week was a perfect blend of on–site obligations and freedom explore Copenhagen.

Yes –– passionate and knowledgeable professor shared great learnings about the leading sustainability region in the world, in a unique class and one week experience not offered elsewhere (esp. with such access to top sustainability–driven companies and CEOs).

I would recommend this course to other students, especially students who are interested in learning more about sustainability, corporations tackling sustainability challenges, and want to experience what it is like to live in a Nordic country. The spring break travel portion is filled with a packed itinerary with lots of learnings. Every day we had 2 meetings with different high level executives at companies such as Ikea, Ramboll, Orsted, and Carlsberg to name a few. Absolutely – this is a super unique experience and a great chance for those interested in sustainability, social impact, and politics to consider how things can be done better!
Good class but professor is kind of quirky. Pretty repetitive readings but excellent trip to Copenhagen

This course is great if you want to explore Copenhagen and are able to join it with a group of friends. The trip itself is rather self–directed outside of the 5–6 hours of daily speakers –– which has its pros and cons. Strand has quite a lot of enthusiasm for the topic at hand. The business professionals and firms that you meet with are very impressive though.
Yes. It was a great counter balance to much of the stale pedagogy in Haas' curriculum. It was a very thought provoking class.

I would definitely recommend. I really enjoyed the class and appreciated the opportunity to think through these big picture issues in a class setting. These are the issues that business leaders need to consider in the real world. The class will only benefit MBA students. I wish more classes at Haas were offered like this one. It was a rare opportunity to consider the interaction of business and society. I'm sure this class is one that I will reflect on long after graduation.

I came to Haas to take this class and am glad I did. It was a great experience and has reshaped how I think about the interaction between business, society, and governments. It will change how I approach my career and the impact I try to have in that

Absolutely! This was one of the highlights of my time at Haas. Great learning opportunity about another part of the world. Intellectually stimulating, interesting, and engaging course content. The trip itself was incredible and I enjoyed the sessions leading up to it as well.

Absolutely yes! I was a bit skeptical coming into the course but the course exceeded my expectations by a mile. If you? re interested in learning how capitalism can work for all not just the shareholder, how public policies elevate the standard of living of everyone and how the Nordics are already way ahead of us in terms of sustainability and climate change, you?d love this course. The class visits were enriching. The entire week in Copenhagen wasn?t hectic and quite manageable. Robert is phenomenal guru on these topics so you?re learning from the best. I?d recommend learning from the locals as well when you?re in Copenhagen.
Yes, for the trip to Copenhagen alone and interactions with leadership at major Danish institutions.
Would recommend?the companies that we visited and the content that the speakers shared was valuable.

This course was an incredible capstone to my time at Haas and I would highly recommend it to anyone who is interested in learning about a different model of capitalism in which business has a strong role to play in helping to alleviate some of society's most wicked problems. While the content of the professor's book and the pre–Copenhagen lectures did feel redundant at times, it did enable us to come into the immersion week in Copenhagen well prepared for our discussions with the various Nordic leaders we met. I'm leaving this class feeling energized about the Nordic model and excited to share my learnings with friends and colleagues in the US. Yes, absolutely. For the academics out there it?s a great thought exercise on how to make our societal systems work better. For business leaders it?s great to understand alternative forms of business and leadership styles that can be replicated here in the US.
I would recommend both Robert and this course to anyone interested in sustainability, in going overseas for Spring Break or in meeting new MBA classmates! (15 FTMBA and 15 EWMBA students attend)
Yes, it was definitely interesting to see a different mentality when it comes to capitalistic structures. Yes 100% – this is one of my favourite classes I've taken at Haas.
Yes
YES! If you are interested in sustainability and want to lead responsibly as a business leader, take this class!
Yes, the subject is interesting and the professor really cares about this area of work. The execution of the class can be improved from weekly assignments to company visit preparation.
Yes, but only if you are ok with a professor who doesn't care that much about People.
Copenhagen is fun and the speakers were great.

Robert is clearly very passionate about the Nordics, and one of the things I really appreciated was how he forced us to be on time, and always reminded us to clean up after ourselves. This may sound small, but I felt like these reminders helped us show respect for our hosts and speakers (and is not always a given).
The quality of the speakers was overall very high, and I did learn a lot from the immersion experience.

Robert could show more care and regard for his students overall. Among all of my professors at Haas, I felt that Robert cared the least about the individual students. This felt apparent when he would ignore student emails (citing that he gets too many requests and has personal boundaries), and respond instead by inviting students to attend his talks on campus. I just felt this was tone deaf, as the professor for an immersive class- it just felt that he didn't really care for his students and their concerns on a personal level.
1. Responding to student concerns: I would recommend that Robert spends more time and energy responding to student concerns at the beginning

2. Connecting students within the class: I think Robert should SERIOUSLY CONSIDER spending time to introduce the class to one another and having name tags! would be helpful to do this before the last day of class.

3. Reducing the before class readings: it made a lot of the week of speaker content duplicative with our reading 4. Not interrupting speakers as much- it sometimes comes off as too dominant and disrupts the flow of the speakers presentation.

5. The zoom sessions were a waste of time. Either use that time more effectively (class introductions, logistics info, understanding real content), or not require the full sessions. The discussions were mostly a waste of time. Yes - take this class if you're interested in geopolitics in addition to business and sustainability! The immersion week is fun and a good learning experience. Note that there is weekly prep before spring break.

This course will give you lifetime opportunity to learn about a set of countries that operate on a different way than USA. The societal learnings, discoveries and findings are overwhelming and incredibly positive for ones mba experience.
I dare to say this was top 3 of the best classes I took.

Professor Strand is a professional professor. His commitment and passion are a fresh of breath air compared to some classes where topics and professors are specifics and based on the right or wrong way of doing things.

I 100% recommend students interested in sustainability, and particularly the renewable industry, to take this class. This is what we expect from an MBA program: meeting with top business leaders and companies and having engaging discussions on how to accelerate the climate transition.
This course was definitely my most practical experience in my MBA program.

I loved the course, certainly learned a lot about sustainability in the Nordics and how the government, business, and unions work together. The immersion course was great and the schedule was thoughtfully arranged. I do think that because Robert has done this course a lot, he seemed a little less engaged to get to know us. However, he lined up a pretty good panel of guests and visits.
Great course. Trip was well-worth the time and money. Immersive although content can lean very pro-Nordic without much critical analysis of the Nordic capitalist system.
The traveling part is definitely fun but there is so much that can be improved.
The course yes, the professor I'd recommend as a facilitator/connector.
Yes, the travel element to this course was extremely special and left a greater impression on us than companies visiting campus
Yes. It's a fun class with an interesting take on capitalism

This was one of my favorite courses at Berkeley. Being able to take any of the study abroad classes is always such a great experience, but especially when given the opportunity to challenge my own perspective and witness a different reality than my own. All the companies we visited were great, and the spacing felt reasonable while still being able to squeeze in some sight seeing.

Great class, would definitely recommend taking if you're able to bid on it. There is A LOT of reading and you're expected to do weekly write ups in addition to the final project. You'll have a decent amount of downtime outside of class hours to explore the city.

I highly recommend this course with Robert. It will be most worthwhile if you are eager to learn about sustainability and are willing to become a practitioner of different view points into American capitalism. It's an important class to see this broader view. Do not take if you just want to travel to Denmark, is my opinion. Discussions are important part of the class leading up to the immersion week and Robert is very passionate about this field. Also, he has many important connections in the Nordic region that you can leverage into the future, including partnerships with other schools and businesses.
Robert demonstrates extreme passion for sustainable capitalism and sets up the immersion week in an excellent way to learn how it manifests itself in Denmark.

I wish there had been more facilitation of having the class know each other better (introductions, name tags, group events) it was very split between FT and EW with no formal group dinners, etc even with professor. This class needs a GSI to help with logistics and details

Yes. The best part is the industry experts that the class has access to. Gives a different perspective on how company leadership thinks outside the u.s. The speakers are engaging and passionate people with wealth of knowledge. I would recommend both the course and instructor to a fellow student. The topics of discussion and immersive experience broadened my mind/view of the world. Additionally, Robert is an engaging professor who cares about the topic and students. Given Robert's deep knowledge, infectious enthusiasm, and innate instructing abilities, with a few small updates it could be a tremendously impactful and enlightening course.
I would recommend this class for anyone interested in an abroad learning experience. The trip is much better than the lectures leading up to it.

yes I will recommend for anyone to take it, it provides such insights and experiences for translating concepts into actions from government policies to corporate governance playing out in front of you
at the same time, one will wonder and reflect on the purpose and meaning of life deeply throughout the trip, especially when traveling solo
I would highly recommend this course for anyone who is interested in alternative models of capitalism.

Wonderful chance to have meaningful and heartfelt conversations with peers outside of class and in the context of different models of being. I wish the facilitation of in class conversations was stronger. Take this class if you want to network with corporations in the Nordics and challenge your perceived ideas of capitalism, but expect to do the majority of your learning over beers with friends after class vs. In presentations.

Yes, the sessions were more fulfilling than anticipated and I really appreciate all the work that went into it. Yes! Very worthwhile and unique experience. It definitely broadened my perspective on different ways of doing things. Highly recommend the class but wish Robert was more involved/ approachable. Robert's effort in putting together the preparation material and coming up with a great itinerary for the immersion week is commendable. His enthusiasm is through the roof. However, I felt he wasnt approachable or didn't make an effort to get to know the class. The class visits itself were so great. I learnt so much in this week. This is going to be my best class at Haas because of the immersion week and all the great speakers I met!!
Robert's passion is contagious. He thoroughly loves the Nordics and the subject he teaches and it shows. It's inspiring to be around someone with his energy level and enthusiasm.
Would recommend because it's a way to expand and learn about a subject matter that for me was fairly unknown

sections.goodFor: Students interested in sustainability or the limits of American capitalism who want immersive company/exec access via Strand's deep Denmark network; strong for newcomers.
sections.notFor: Students already deep in sustainability - several say they learned little new; casual learners; and anyone who wants spring break free, since the week is packed.
sections.workloadNote: Front-loaded: weekly readings and assignments in the ~6 weeks before the trip, then an intensive spring-break week of Copenhagen site visits with class time only Mon am and Fri pm.
sections.gradingBasis: Pre-trip readings and weekly assignments plus in-class engagement during the trip; no exam mentioned.
sections.redFlags: Recurring (4+): pre-trip readings one-sided, repetitive and pitching the Nordic model without bridging to US business reality; some in-country sessions boring or filler; two say Strand is 'a little all over the place.'
sections.quote: I think this course can be insightful, but you will be pitched repeatedly on the Nordic model. Unfortunately a lot of it seems divorced from the reality
comments: Go on this trip! You should use all of your bid points! Robert is a fantastic teacher and does an excellent job planning the trip! Only thing to know is to expect a good amount of reading in the 6 weeks leading up to the trip. Yes!!! Highly recommend this course and professor. Learned so much, had really deep conversations on systems and society, and had a lot of fun. Don't miss this class.
Potentially. If you're interested in sustainability, Copenhagen and the Nordics, you'll enjoy the week. Otherwise, it's a class during spring break, so.. it's up to you.

Yes, absolutely! I highly recommend this course. It provided valuable insights and references about Nordic capitalism, sustainability, and the different paths we can take toward a more sustainable world. Having the chance to see things in person and engage directly with senior leaders driving sustainability efforts in their organizations was truly remarkable. If you're curious to draw your own conclusions and expand your reflections on " Is there a Sustainable Capitalism in the Nordics? ", this course is a must.
Yes, it's so inspiring to see the different attitude here towards sustainability. The real-life applications are a testament to ingenuity and gives me hope for humanity.
Yes! Very different course with real world learnings.
I would recommend this class to someone who is very interested in sustainability and is looking to pursue a career in it or in Denmark. As a casual learner, it was a bit less effective for me.

I think this course can be insightful, but you will be pitched repeatedly on the Nordic model. Unfortunately a lot of it seems divorced from the reality of how business works in the United States and not a lot of work put in to bridge that gap.
Yes! Robert's energy is infectious. An amazing course and amazing professor.

Highly recommend. Great conceptual lessons regarding corporate form and sustainable capitalism, including considerations for how ti actually works. Also great engagement with specific companies that are very relevant to the field of sustainability broadly.

Depends! It was super fun to travel with your class mates, but you will have class all during spring break and will not get to see and explore as much as you might have otherwise. Prior to class there are weekly readings and assignments that are interesting, but are also one-sided and repetitive and can be annoying. The class in Denmark mixed. Half of the sessions were super interesting and cool (with senior company execs coming to talk to us), others were not informative, boring, and felt more like a waste of time. Overall it was well planned but the sessions could be more concise to leave more time to explore the city. Less applicable learnings then I would have hoped, so depends if you are already well-informed.
Yes! A great way to think creatively and explore a different culture.

This is a great class and a once-in-a-lifetime experience. I highly recommend it to anyone interested in this topic. Professor Robert has strong connections in this field — you'll meet many talented individuals and amazing companies throughout the course. At the same time, you'll get to experience the Nordics during Spring Break, which makes it even more memorable.
Yes I would recommend.
Understanding the way Nordics operates business in sustainable way helps me to reflect my experience so far and able to see pros and cons.
Yes, this course was one of the best experiences I had at Haas, from connecting with fellow students to immersing ourselves in the Copenhagen culture, it has been an amazing experience.
This is definitely the most valuable and interesting course I've ever had!

Absolutely yes. It is an important subject that I'm so glad that I took the class as I didn't know much about before the class. It is designed for students to really think deeply about the problem and also relevant to our career and life. It makes you think a lot about what type of companies and culture you want to be part of, and how you make an influence for the long term grow for your career.
I cannot recommend this class enough if you are interested in Sustainability. Hearing from practitioners in industry was invaluable and Robert is a the perfect person to teach this course
Yes! This course is one of my best learning experiences during the MBA program.
Absolutely — copying in previous response here:

This is easily one of the best courses at Haas. A crash course in sustainable capitalism, with a healthy mix of theory and practical applications. Loved most of the readings, and the quality of speakers and activities organized during the in- person week was stellar. Robert is an incredibly passionate human, and it shows in the network and relationships he has cultivated that make something like this possible.

I'd recommend this class to lift the veil of American capitalism from your eyes. It's a lot of fun, great readings, low lift, and the trip to Copenhagen is jam packed with cool case studies of Nordic companies. I'd recommend adding structure to it yourself because Robert, though knowledgeable and energetic, is a little all over the place. If you want exposure to Robert's fantastic network of knowledgable and experienced industry experts, and the company site visits. Our cohort of 44 folks (mix of EW and FT) went to Copenhagen Business School campus for class time only Monday morning and Friday afternoon. The rest of the time, site visits! Be efficient if you want to connect with the speakers - we typically had to get on the bus or move to the next location quickly. Also, dress warm and in layers (I am California born) and wear very comfortable shoes (cobblestone everywhere and or if you plan to bike). Lastly, make time to fika!

Yes, the immersive experience is extremely beneficial for learning and understanding more about capitalism in the European context which is a leader in sustainable business for both the planet and its people. The course work is not too difficult and all reading and preparation is completed before you go to Denmark so you can spend the week absorbing and learning.
Would highly recommend.

It's a fun class to take if you're interested in sustainability and learning about other companies and Danish culture. There were a lot of site visits, so a good variety of companies and exposure with notable guest speakers. At times the lecture portions were a little heavy so could be more engaging. However an overall good use of time for spring break! Definitely take this one, even if you are someone like me who is not very into sustainability. You will change your thought after this trip. Besides, learning from class is not as effective as in-person and immersive experience, so definitely worth to spend your spring break here!

I would strongly recommend this class. I learned more on the week long trip than probably a whole semester of sitting in a class. Almost like learning by doing as opposed to learning by sitting in a class.

I would recommend this course if the student has a strong foundation in sustainability and is able to quickly relate to the concepts that are discussed in class. Without a strong sense of'why'associated with this course, it would be hard to follow along or remain engaged in class. I noticed that the same few students engaged in class, and others appeared disinterested
Maybe- I think that professor strand should adopt more feedback for how to make this course better and then I would be more likely to recommend.

It was not a must take class. It's interesting and fun to go to Copenhagen, but if you are someone who is thinking about sustainability or the problems with capitalism I'm not sure how much more you will learn.

Yes I would. This course was one of the best courses I've taken at Berkeley. As someone who entered the class with almost no knowledge around sustainability I learned a lot in a really fun way. The business and university visits provide a very unique and authentic opportunity to hear directly from people working in this space.
Yes! Very well organized course content and travel logistics. Curated company visit is well thoughout and echos with the course reading

Yes. I would be impossible to take this class and not be impacted by the exposure to the Nordics. I think the awareness will make you a greater business leader, more than a spring break bender (as fun as that can be)
Definitely! Incredibly passionate and he has done this class for 18 years and built very strong relationships in Denmark that make the class very worth while.
Fun class to travel and see a new country. Great discussions too. Do some of the readings though so you a get a better idea of what's heading your way

If you're even remotely on the fence, take the class. If you haven't very familiar with the Nordics / Scandinavian culture, take the class. It's invaluable that we get exposed and immersed in other business environments with different business structures. This class does a good job at whetting the appetite into learning more. Robert also has gone through incredible lengths arranging connections to key businesses and foundations in Denmark and Sweden during our visit, and these are hard to reproduce on your own.

This was the best class I've taken at Haas. Robert is an amazing instructor with deep knowledge of the subject matter and cares so much about the course and students. I'd highly recommend this course to anyone who is considering whether you know a lot about sustainable capitalism or not.
Absolutely! Robert is great and this topic is so relevant now.

sections.goodFor: Students interested in sustainability, comparative capitalism, policy or the Nordic model who want an immersive international experience over spring break.
sections.notFor: Students without spring bandwidth for heavy prework, or expecting business-model/finance content - the week skews to environmental sustainability, policy and industry site visits.
sections.workloadNote: Front-loaded: dense pre-trip readings and extensive discussion posts before the Copenhagen immersion week, then long days of site visits; prework exceeds comparable 2-unit trek courses.
sections.gradingBasis: Pre-trip readings and discussion posts plus participation in immersion-week site visits; other components not described.
sections.redFlags: Pre-trip reading/discussion load heavy and partly felt like busy work (6+ comments); learning objectives unclear (2); organization could be better (2); class grew to ~60 and feels unwieldy; you arrange your own housing.
sections.quote: I would recommend this course only if you have the bandwidth in the spring to take on 12-20+ hours of preparation material, as it has a lot of prework.
comments: Yes! This course gave a incredibly valuable global perspective on the topic of capitalism. The site visits are worth a hundred readings and the actual experience of being in Copenhagen is wonderful and can be magical!

This was an amazing course and experience because it was located in Copenhagen!! The class work prior to the immersion week was a lot more than expected and felt like busy work. It was great being in Copenhagen and visiting many amazing companies; however, the days were long. The learning objectives and takeaways were unclear but it's a great experience to take an international class
I would recommend the class, but would caution against the density and quality of the class material leading up to the week in Copenhagen.
Yes
Yes, definitely, if you are interested in Sustainability and Corporate Governance; great opportunity to learn and have fun at the beautiful Copenhagen.
The course is generally fun, there's not a ton of free time within the schedule though so do your tourist stuff on the weekend before/after.

Yes and I would absolutely take this class again given the chance. If you have any interest in sustainability, the Nordics, Europe, or anything social science related or international affairs, take this class.
Great course, highly recommend! I feel I learned a lot and my views were productively challenged. A lot of concepts came full circle for me being able to interact with companies.
Yes - great use of a break!
Yes, absolutely! He did a great job of teaching us this material and had a lot of knowledge

I would recommend this class! It is a great perspective setting and lets students analyze, benchmark, and experience a part of the world that has a lot to offer the rest. Robert helps to reframe the thinking around what it means to be a capitalist and an American.
Yes, I'd highly recommend. It's rare to have this kind of opportunity - expect to work hard:-)

Yes I think this was one of the coolest trips I've been on at haas and gave me a great insight to how the Nordics have done so well, I think it's a character building journey perspective growth type of class, not a hard or purely soft skills class. I really enjoyed it

I would recommend this course only if you have the bandwidth in the spring to take on 12-20+ hours of preparation material, as it has a lot of prework. This is not typical for other SIB and GNAM courses, and would be something I caution evening weekend students to when they plan their spring semester around. Otherwise, it does cover Nordic culture and sustainable capitalism very well and has effective course material. The site visits in country are very relevant, and immersion environment is very conducive to learning the subject.

Absolutely recommend this course! The subject matter of capitalism is so vitally important to be critiquing as citizens and business school students. It offers a wonderful way to benchmark US and international metrics to get a comparative view of the progress we have made and still need to go.

Prof. Strand is passionate, knowledgeable and so friendly to study with. His energy is infectious and encouraging. He puts a LOT of effort into the course and the trip is really worthwhile, with the different site visits. You do have to find your own way for housing and logistics, so be prepared to do some work on those fronts, rather than just sign up and follow the pack. It's an adventure, so bring a good attitude because a lot is fit into a short period of time. 10/10, totally recommend and believe this material should be core reading for MBA students ~
Yes, I would recommend taking this class but beware there is a lot of upfront prep before the immersion week so be prepared to spend 8-10 hours a week on reading assignments.
I'd recommend this course because it was a great crash course into sustainable capitalism and the Nordics as a region. It is not a challenging course, but very informative.
I would. I had some preconceived notions of how it is to live and work in the Nordic countries, but travelling there helped me learn what life is really like over there.
It was very useful to listen to a variety of journalists, executives, and educators talk
about their systems and institutions.
Robert is great! Very high energy and passionate about the topic.
Yes I would, Robert is clearly excited about the topic and wishes to help others dive deeply into the subject matter. His instruction style would only be improved by better organization
Loved the immersive nature of the class. Helped with connecting concepts to applications.

I think this is a really cool option for spring break, and a great way to get to know other people better. If you're interested in energy or sustainability, you'll find the site visits super helpful. If you're interested in what makes our economic system challenging and how it could be better, this course will also just interest you academically. I had some very deep discussions with others in the class about the Nordic model -- where we can learn from it, where it fails.

I do think this class is a lot more work than I expected -- the pre readings are very heavy and the discussion posts are pretty extensive -- it's much more work than other similar 2 credit spring break courses like the Innovation Sprint in Amsterdam. I also wished that there was a little more free time to explore Copenhagen during the day.
Yes I highly recommend it. You will take away a lot from this course. The connections you'll make is also wonderful. I loved it overall.

Yes! It is definitely one of the best courses I took at Haas. The reading materials were insightful and made me reflect a lot. Also the experience in Copenhagen, visiting and interacting with to Danish companies were very unique and rich to me!
Highly recommend for every student to take this course!
Yes, absolutely! Unlike other treks, this is a class with 2 units.

personally, I learned so much about capitalism, politics, and systems, and developed my critical thinking through real- world practice. I don't think I could have learned and applied these ideas so quickly in any other setting. I would recommend this class to any student who is interested in learning about the the nordic society, and what mechanisms work well in supporting capitalism in a democracy.
Of course!!

If someone is heavily interested in the climate and sustainability topics this is a good class. Oftentimes, the discussions were heavily policy based, at others it was focused on finance and renewable energy. I think this can be a lot to absorb if you haven't taken another course in sustainability

I'd recommend for people who are interested in learning about Nordic culture and way of doing business. It's not the same as visiting Copenhagen as a tourist. You really get to know how things are done in the Nordics.
However, coming to the week of the class in person is very demanding and requires preparation.

Absolutely, feels like this is one of Haas's marquee classes. The pre-work before the trip is not difficult but it is time consuming, so be aware of that. The trip itself is fantastic but the class size has recently increased (from 45 to 60) and that size of a group feels unwieldy sometimes. But those are small complaints compared to the experiences students get from the country visit

Yes. I thought this was one of if not the most thought provoking courses I've taken. At times it is hard to figure out how practical the information is in a US context, but overall it's very beneficial even just as a thought experiment. Plus, having the opportunity to explore Copenhagen allows you to see the outcomes of the system.

I would recommend but with some caveats. The class can be very useful for MBA students but may or may not be the most useful for understanding sustainability through a business/business model lens. Hearing the title of the course on sustainability capitalism, I didn't realize how much would be focused on sustainability as a function and industry and not necessarily on the business and financial models that make them possible. The class also has significant reading requirements leading up the immersion week, that other SIB class have not required.

I would definitely recommend this course to every person, as everyone is a participant in the imperfect capitalist system in the U.S., and we can all work to make it more equitable and sustainable for people and the planet. There is a decent amount of prework, which enables thoughtful discussion throughout the course. You will meet incredible folks across industries and the public and private sectors. The in country time is the best complement to the prework, and Denmark is an incredible country. It is helpful to see how change can be brought on at all levels, from internal carbon pricing to investing in the energy transition and alternative ownership structures and the power of a unionized workforce.
