I suppose it could be a little helpful for someone who is not an MBA student or is completely new to the U.S. financial system, but for anyone who grew up here and has paid attention at all to personal finance, it was useless. The content is way too broad and not nearly deep enough – we spent a whole week talking about saving, and that should have only been 20 minutes max. The class has potential, but it needs to go a lot deeper and be way more quantitative than what it is. Additionally, it should be split into two levels – one more introductory version for new US citizens and non–MBA students, and one for people who have experience on these topics but want to learn more. There should be more financial modeling and more info on things like stock options and less info on basic topics like saving. It is also WAY too much work for a two credit class. It should not have a midterm, or it should at least be an open book midterm since in the real world, you would always consult the internet when making these kinds of decisions.

Veselina has wonderful energy and is very generous to her class with her time and resources. I would recommend her as a finance mentor, but ensure you know the fundamentals beforehand as the class moves quickly.
Yes I would recommend to anyone who is unfamiliar with finance concepts.
I would recommend the course and instructor to a fellow student because the course contains valuable information that is applicable across roles and industries.
Yes - incredibly caring engaging and helpful.
Yes

I would say that Prof. Dinova was one of the more disorganized professors within the core, and her lecture style tended to be pretty scattered. Additionally, I felt that the concepts that we did / did not cover did not always align to what I would consider the financial concepts that should be covered in a "core" finance class.

Veselina is a great instructor who cares deeply about each student individually. Her class grew a lot on me and I found it deeply interesting to better understand how finance concepts are embedded into real world applications. Yes, I would recommend this professor and course! It was very interesting, and the professor was very engaging and caring.

While Intro to Finance is a core curriculum course, I did not see any advantages. Veselina is a great person and truly cares about her students, but the course is very unstructured and badly organized. I didn't learn a lot; it was not focused on application, and it was not a good investment of my time.

This is a very good class and Veselina is a great lecturer who makes a lot of effort to connect and know everyone. Watch the videos before class, they are so helpful. And print out the summary docs and revise. Class is mainly for general discussions which may help with your overall understanding but if you don?t watch the videos before hand, you will be very lost. Good program. I would recommend it.

I didn't really get much out of the class - lectures were long, indirect, and hard to follow. Though there usually was a lot of discussion, I didn't feel like I learned new content/skills from this class (i have no finance background either) I would definitely recommend this instructor to fellow students. Professor Dinova understands students' expectations of our academic experience and exceeds them. She is a talented connector and is one of the few professors who unquestionably cares about each individual student's professional and personal livelihood.
I would recommend. Vaselina is very energetic and her prep materiais are great. Classes can be messy, but prep materiais are well organized and complete.

No, I wouldn?t recommend this course or instructor to any student. I would recommend Vaselina as a good person to talk about other topics, or come to office hours with specific doubts, however at least from this class experience, I don? t think it is worth the time.
Absolutely! Veselina is a delight and makes learning fun. It?s a good introductory course to Finance.
The worst experience at Haas. Not worth tuition money.
Yes I would recommend!
Absolutely, this was a great course and I think Veselina is a must have professor while at Berkeley Haas. Yes to Veselina, no to the course

I would! Once you understand that she teaches the Quant portion through pre recorded videos and the conceptual portion in class, the class teaches you both the hard skill of basic finance and why its useful.
Yes
Yes of course

I would take Veselina's class as an elective to dive deeper into finance concepts once I had a solid understanding, but am less likely to recommend her for an introductory class if you do not have a finance background.

Yes, I would recommend Veselina to a fellow student. She cares deeply about her students and teaching effectively. I would encourage the student to study all her class materials in detail for maximum learning and would indicate to the student that they should not rely on the in-class portion to teach them what they need to know.
Yes, specially if want to learn without much pressure on grades and performance.
It's was a good course, and I learned a lot without much grades pressure.
Veselina cares about her students'post-Haas success, and will clearly put time and energy into developing skills and connections with students, if they seek them out
I would recommend this course to learn about finance fundamentals. Sometimes was a little difficult to follow and pay attention but she has great energy and really cares about her students.
Yes, I'd recommend Veselina to classmates because she is very invested in the Haas community and wants to help you succeed.
Yes
Yes definitely. I'd highly recommend anyone who wants to get into finance or has experience in Finance to take it. Yes!
Yes if you are prepared to learn a lot of finance in a little time she makes the course concepts relevant. I would recommend her if this person has a basis in finance already
yes, its a good class and I think that a good start for finance for people that have not see nthis in the past. its core so I/they do not really have a choice
Yes
I would recommend this class as its foundational to finance careers or any post-MBA class.

I don't think I would recommend her. I think she genuinely tried but even for "office hours", she said to find her on campus instead of having a specific office. How am I supposed to just find her on campus? I feel like small things like that made it difficult
Yes. It is an essential course for business and contains a ton of concepts that are essential to any business career. No matter what you are doing you should understand this material.
I would recommend anyone with even modest financial expertise waive this class, as it is too simplistic for anyone but people completely new to finance.

I would recommend Veselina! She is organized, caring, and incredibly knowledgeable. I appreciate all of the summary notes, preparation videos, and follow-up emails she crafted to enhance our learning. She deeply cares about her students, and I feel thankful to know her!

I would highly recommend this class for all people interested in learning the foundational concepts of finance. It is designed to be applicable and understand the viewpoint of corporations as they think about investing in new initiatives. It teaches important skills for managers to have.
Absolutely, amazing course and professor.

It was a great experience for me. Although I have a finance background, I had never calculated some of these concepts on my own before. Going through the process step-by-step was helpful in deepening my understanding of their true meaning and practical application. It provided a valuable opportunity to reinforce my knowledge and gain a clearer, more hands-on grasp of the material. By doing the calculations myself, I was able to connect theory with real-world application, which strengthened my comprehension and gave me more confidence in my ability to work with these concepts in the future.

I would recommend the course, I got a comprehensive overview of what finance entails. I would encourage Veselina to incorporate more slides/structure into her lectures, and then I think I would get even more out of it.
Yes, I would. Her approach is different and direct, but effective. You can tell she cares about her students.
I wouldn't recommend at all.
The concepts we learned are all free available in the web with a better instruction.
There was no value add at all of being in class.
yes
No -- neither for this course nor for any other.
No
yes, Loves what she does
I think Veselina is a great elective finance teacher, she just moves too quickly for an intro class
Unsure. Content is incredibly important but needs a more engaging professor and method of teaching.
Unfortunately no. Finance is a great tool to understand the world, but this class failed to impart any useful knowledge that you can use in real world.

I would not recommend Vaselina Dinova for Intro to Finance. She is a great person, but not a great lecturer. I was often let more confused about a topic from the class, and had to learn almost all of the material outside of lecture Well designed course work. I would recommend.
Yes. Course provide a cursory overview of finance and finance concepts
No. The class is not engaging and hard to follow
Given that it is required, sure.
Yes! Veselina is passionate, very available outside of class, and makes finance fun and simplified.
Unfortunately not recommend. The engagement level can be much higher with another instructor
I would recommend it because it's a good foundation in finance
Absolutely not.
YES! The knowledge is quite industry relevant:).
I think finance is an important supplement to the core! This isn't my area of interest, but I'm happy I took it. Yes
I would recommend it to someone who wants to spend time to dig into the basics of finances because the professor provides a lot of extra video courses
Yes - good baseline finance
No and no. This course was very disappointing as someone who wants to learn finance skills and pivot into finance. I feel like I need to do much more work to self learn than I should.

Maybe...it was an interesting course on climate and held a lot of potential, but I felt that it was a bit unorganized, perhaps because this was the first time it was offered so the kinks just need to be worked out. Kate Gordon is amazing professor but I was not impressed with Libby Schaaf, but the class was worth taking just for Kate alone.
Yes - interesting content! Could improve structure of assignments and discussions.
Incredible gathering of all the students interested in the space. I learned a lot from other students & a ton from the speakers

I would recommend if you are interested in California's green initiatives. I feel like the class is very California focused. I would recommend both lecturers but not this class until there was a major overhaul to the curriculum to be broadly applicable to those interested in facilitating a more rapid climate transition.
Yes, but with caveats. Not a class to "learn" from climate change. It is more a class to discuss current/past sustainability efforts

I would recommend this course with reservations. If you are looking for a course where you can have interesting discussion with your classmates about select aspects of policy, infrastructure, and finance as they relate to climate, I would recommend this course. If you are looking for a course that has a comprehensive throughline that teaches you about how to leverage policy to affect climate change, this class might not be for you.
100%. It serves as a fantastic survey of how climate, politics, and finance intersect and is taught by one of Berkeley's biggest climate experts, Kate Gordon, and a great speaker in Libby Schaff.

This class is great for understanding how public and private actors approach climate. Guest speakers are great and the professors know a ton and have a lot of great experiences to share. Assumes intermediate level understanding of climate so do not recommend to "newbies."

The course felt way too specific to California and the intricacies of various California laws. While the content was really interesting and so were the guest speakers it often felt like the things that we were learning just wouldn't be relevant overtime as we expand our careers beyond California. I would have loved more time spent on public and private partnerships.

This was a great class to take from experts in the field of enacting sustainability measures. I'd recommend this for folks who have a background in sustainability and want to learn about how policy measures can make a difference in solving for climate change.
I will recommend the course and the professors. The course mostly focuses in California but professors bring a great set of speakers and multiple lessons learned from their past work experience

This is a good class to learn more about politics of financing infrastructure projects in California. Most of the classes were focused on specific state policies and how them impact the development of projects (both promoting or stifling them).

I would definitely recommend this course. I learned a ton about areas I didn't realize were so interesting – how local governments finance climate resilience projects, how climate lobbying works, and so much about the state of California's approach to infrastructure, air quality, and more. I took it at the same time as Business Models for Social Impact, and there were some cool parallels to be drawn. Kate Gordon is a POWERHOUSE. Recommend!
Yes!

I would highly recommend this course. I think it is fantastic if you are new to the climate space or well informed. I also appreciated the focus on multilevel actions - from global policies to municipal action.

Yes, thank you so much for teaching this class. I think it brought together all types of students who were interested in the climate space and gave us an opportunity to talk about the non-science aspects of climate change. I really enjoyed the readings, and Kate was such an engaging professor and an amazing person to know in the climate space.
I do not recommend, the course was chaotic and too focused on California

Yes of course. All the climate fellow should take this course and this is valuable resource for them best understanding.. Yes, I've recommended the class to lots of 1st year students who are interested in climate or just curious to learn about it. This is my first climate class, and I feel so rewarding and thinking about masking a impact in my career This class is a worthwhile foray into climate action because--unlike many sustainability focused courses at Berkeley-- the policy focus imbues it with a sense of pragmatism. Taught by real practitioners, it was a worthwhile elective. Easy lift and great guest speakers if it fits in your schedule. Not very applicable learnings though.
Yes definitely! You will learn about the capital stacks, policy initiatives and international/local implications about climate mitigation/adaptation from two great teachers.

Highly recommend. Kate Gordon provides a insightful and incisive overview of the broad policy and finance landscape; insights into specific frameworks, approaches, and policy/finance tools; and concrete examples of what has
worked/not worked in real life, and Libby Schaaf sheds light on what this means at the local level
Yes! Great class with great professors
Yes! A great overview of climate topics

sections.goodFor: Students new to climate wanting a broad policy/systems primer, and those who want access to an extraordinary slate of guest speakers and the Berkeley climate community.
sections.notFor: Anyone drawn by the 'Finance & Infrastructure' in the title - it isn't emphasized; students who took several climate classes find it repetitive and law school options better.
sections.workloadNote: A very reasonable/light workload with some preparation; the real demand is speaking up in class, which several say is harder than in typical MBA courses.
sections.gradingBasis: Class participation and discussion emphasized; one student says assignments needed to be clearer.
sections.redFlags: Two say the title oversells finance/infrastructure; three say scope is too broad with no clear focus, sequence or takeaway; one flags unclear assignments and that Kate was notably more prepared and engaging than Libby.
sections.quote: If you really care about climate policy, yes. Not so much if you're attracted to the "Finance and Infrastructure" parts of the title, which are not emphasized.
comments: Absolutely worthwhile class to link together material that isnt otherwise inherently connected and through this class and the guest speakers we found a way to make remarkably intuitive connections to understand the ultimate goal of how to behave in a climate adapting world.

If you really care about climate policy, yes. Not so much if you're attracted to the "Finance and Infrastructure" parts of the title, which are not emphasized. Interesting class to get a feel for what a Public Policy degree feels like. Very theoretical, and fun class discussions. The real insights come from all the climate-interested people enrolled in the class rather than the profs themselves.

Maybe - if you have deep knowledge of the space and want to go deeper, but you have to be able to really make the experience into what you need it to be because it's a little all over the place as currently designed.

Yes, I would recommend this course to individuals interested in understanding the relevance of climate change and systems change. We dive into hairy problems and have an open dialogue where many viewpoints are welcomed. Great speakers who are experts in their fields.
YES - this class provides a holistic understanding of the challenges and solutions around climate change.

The course is more suitable for students who have much experience in climate and are planning to pursue a career in this path. Sutdents who just want to learn sth in Climate may find the course a bit dry...

I would absolutely recommend this class, especially as a person who had very little knowledge about approaching climate change from a policy and organizational lens. This class takes a broad approach which is great for people who are seeking to broaden their aperture in the climate space.

I would recommend this course to another student. It is a really engaging class grounded in real-world examples. Both professors are very engaged and willing to meet with students to gain a deeper understanding of course content. This course provides a high level overview of many different climate topics and Isa good primer for the space. What you get out of the course is what you put in to it, and it could be just that you got to hear from a lot of really cool people about really cool stuff, or that you took personal initiative to deep dive into one area of the course and came away with a really good understanding of that topic.

This is a good class for getting a foundation in climate infrastructure and considerations. The topics covered in class were helpful for understanding the landscape of government interventions and financing instruments. Kate was a more engaging and prepared lecturer than Libby, but Libby often had an interesting perspective given her role as former Mayor Oakland. The two were a good balance, but a few improvements to the class like clearer assignments would have improved the overall course experience.
most phenomenal course I took at Haas. Be prepared to work a little, and spend extra energy speaking up in class as this is more challenging than typical MBA courses.

Totally recommend - for people who want to learn about climate, it's a great place to hear about the most topical discussions going on at the global, federal and state level. For students with more experience in climate, it's a relatively laid-back class where you can come, have good conversations, hear from and meet amazing speakers and connect with the broader Berkeley climate community.

Yes, I would. Great professors with cool experiences. Fantastic guest speakers. Very reasonable workload. Just super broad topic lacking a clear focus, sequence, and takeaway... Climate, infra, politics, and finance is sort of everything... bites off too much.

I would definitely recommend this course! Kate and Libby bring in an extraordinary slate of speakers and have great experience to share with students. If you're interested in the subject matter, I think it's a must-take.

Yes. It's a good politics and sustainability course. However, I think I'd take a law school climate class over this if I had already taken several climate classes (my case), as some of the information from this class was repetitive from other classes. If you haven't taken many climate classes, you definitely would take this if you're interested in the political side. Note that it focused a lot on CA and the US, but good to have the basis/ model and know how to expand that out to other regions or countries. The law school climate classes just give you a better marginal benefit per credit hour than this class with less duplicative information if you've already taken many business school climate classes. Yes - interesting to see policy and business views come together.

Yes — this course is one of the few that truly connects climate policy, financing, and infrastructure in a way that feels both practical and immediately relevant to real-world challenges. Kate Gordon and Libby Schaaf create an engaging environment that blends policy insight with lived experience, making the class valuable for anyone interested in the intersection of climate and decision-making.

rows.title: Design, Evaluate, and Scale Development Technologies

comments: Not really. Not without significant work to adapt the course better, especially as it works towards MBAs. There are cool projects it would be fun to get involved with, but all of the busywork and assignments and lectures were repetitive with things we already know from our core, and made it too difficult to even invest in the projects. Fun to meet M. Dev Eng folks at least.

Maybe. I have mixed feelings about the course. I have a prior interest in international development, so a lot of the "intro to development" (plus stats and study design) material felt like repetition. I would have liked the class to be focused almost entirely on the project work. (The profs are new [this year?] to teaching the course and are very interested in feedback on the course, so it may see some changes in the future.) As to the project work, it was messy and imperfect like all consulting project courses are, and which project you end up on (and your team) will determine a lot. Weekly reading responses felt like busy work, even if the readings were sometimes interesting case studies. On the plus side, I did feel that my project was a useful glimpse into a development context, and given my interest in that, that may have made the course worthwhile. I also met a non-Haas student with whom I'm now working on a Big Ideas application, so that was great. (The class was about 15 Haasies, 40 Master's in Development Engineering students [a mix of really interesting/cool people and young inexperienced people who BS a lot], and a few randos.)
I would recommend this course for students who are interested in learning about situational contexts of developing countries and working on solutions to prominent problems in varying areas.

The class is truly unique in giving MBAs a chance to work in real development issues (I worked on water and electricity access in rural sub Saharan Africa) also great chance to work with engineers and other disciplines as an MBA. It could definitely be better structured but I would take it again if I could go back a semester.
Definitely wouldn't recommend it. Very high level, we didn't learn much theory.

sections.goodFor: Students who need the AI certificate or want conceptual grounding in how AI works and how it may reshape labor markets; Toby Stuart's sessions are singled out as the strongest.
sections.notFor: Anyone wanting hands-on AI skills - students never used an LLM in class despite the course being billed as strategic for non-technical people; also too foundational for anyone technical.
sections.workloadNote: Half-semester with four rotating professors: pre-class questions due Sunday nights (often opened too late to answer), in-class printed quizzes, and assignments students say added little value.
sections.gradingBasis: Printed in-class quizzes, pre-class questions and assignments; weights not discussed. Quizzes called poorly prepared and irrelevant.
sections.redFlags: First offering was 'a hot mess': 4 rotating professors with no handoff, misaligned start date (professor missed the first class), typo-ridden quizzes with too few printouts, stale bCourses, no GSI support.
sections.quote: not all the professors were equally good (Toby Stuart was great; Jonathan Kolstad was good; and Anastasia Fedyk was not as great
comments: This class had a few interesting lectures but overall was a pretty chaotic overview of AI and the future of work. The technical foundations and future of work sessions were interesting but the class is very dependent on the professors and how many sessions you have with each of them. Hopefully it will continue to improve as the AI Certificate improves over the semesters.
Course is poorly designed. I dont feel i have learned anything. Very theoretical, not hands-on. Until the PO designs a better course, wouldnt take it.

No. This class was billed as a strategic class for non-technical people to learn more about how to leverage AI in workflows, and we didn't once use AI/an LLM of our choosing in class. I expected to become more more AI-literate as a result of this class, and I am coming away from it having no new skills other than knowing a few hypotheses of how AI may (or may not) impact the labor market.

The way it was this year, not really. I'm sure the fact that it was the first time this course was offered played a role but it was a complete mess. Start date was misaligned between students and professors (we all showed up to the first class, professor didn't show up and then emailed us saying the class actually started a week later), quizzes covered topics that were a bit irrelevant in my opinion and were very poorly prepared (typos, faulty structure, not enough print outs for everyone, etc), assignments didn't add much value, and content overall was too theoretical and not very practical. Hopefully all of this (and other problems we had) improve drastically for next year.

While the topic is important, the course needs A LOT of work. Having four different instructors for the course was a recipe for administrative disaster. I think this course will improve next year, so I would still take it, but I want to note that it may be too foundational for AI experts. Toby Stuart who hopefully remains one of the lecturers for the course is a great industry leader and makes you think.
I would not recommend, better off taking an LLM course. I am not sure what they were trying to do making us take this course.

Yes. This class should be a core class, right after Data and Decisions. It is crucial for today's market that every MBA students masterizes these concepts and is able to "talk AI" and understand the technology in a proper way Interesting course to get exposure to the nuts and bolts of AI and how it will affect workplaces and society from several different perceptives.
Yes, The course is useful and brings clarity about AI in the business world

I would recommend this class because I still got unique insights into what's happening in the space and readings I would not go looking for own my own, but not all the professors were equally good (Toby Stuart was great; Jonathan Kolstad was good; and Anastasia Fedyk was not as great; we haven't had the fourth professor at the time of this submission so can't speak to them) but the learning experience fluctuated a lot depending on who was teaching. If Toby is teaching his own class on this subject, I would probably just take that.

No, but I think this class can only get better (hopefully it will). Some general comments about how to improve the class (it didn't feel appropriate to write it down only for one faculty): stop relying on the "this is the first time we teach the class so things will go wrong" and actively try to prevent that from happening (Question the status quo, anyone?); if you ask us to answer the pre class questions before 11 pm, make sure to open them with enough time to answer (most of the times I would try to answer them on Saturday (closed), Sunday 11am (closed), Sunday 5pm (still closed), and then by 9pm it was open but it closed at 11pm), and several times they didn't even open the questions so you would be checking all the time until finally giving up; communicate with other faculty on a regular basis (e.g., it happened twice that the printed quizzes were not enough for the students); and in general, the class should be called AI foundations and not Business AI foundations, as there was little to no connection to the business side (eg., it explained how AI works when translating words into 0s and 1s, then doing some calculations for the error, distance, etc when it could have been explained much simpler and why this is relevant); if the class will continue to have this technical focus, then there is plenty of overlap with the Intro to coding class
It was ok- I hope they update it to be reflective of the feedback in terms of balancing how much time was spent on the content the students found most interesting
If you need the AI certificate sure. I'd like to see an iteration of this class with less professors. 4 in one half semester was way too much.

I think this course could be good but this year was not well coordinated and prepare given it was the first edition. Also, is important it is taught from a business/ corporate lenses, not so focus on research and academia but rather what kind of problems, challenges and decisions we are gonna have to face in the corporate world (even if we don't have a technical role) and what do we need to make them efficiently. I would think of the course as a guide for a student who is put in charge of defining the AI strategy of a company, what kind of tools they implement and how these are integrated, what factors to take into account, how do you train employees, what workflows should be redefined, etc. I would recommend this class because I learned a lot about how businesses are currently thinking about AI and what AI strategy should look like.

This course will give you a strong and broad understanding of AI fundamentals from the theory perspective, which is great. There is little content on its application, though, nor really content on policy/ how to handle it/ etc. There is also no hands-on learning with AI. So if you take this class, be well aware that what you get out is theory and understanding (which is a helpful thing, no doubt), not practical application.

Hopefully, from an organization perspective, this class will improve because it was a hot mess this semester. There were 4 professors who each taught a few weeks of class separately. This was great from a knowledge and perspective breadth POV. However, they never seemed to actually talk to each other or have a handover when switching to then next professor, which made the class disjointed as they didn't seem to know what was covered, where we were at, when quizes where, if past deck material was actually posted, etc.. Furthermore, they didn't seem to manage or update bCourses regularly, causing confusion, and there was no real GSI in tow to help keep up with this either. First year course with a number of different professors so it tended to be disaggregated. Solid material and deep dive into AI.

sections.goodFor: Students who need it for the AI Certificate; two comments single out Toby Stuart's sessions as thought-provoking and worthwhile within an otherwise criticized course.
sections.notFor: Almost everyone else per these comments: too technical for non-technical students, too shallow for technical ones, and the business applications students expected are largely absent.
sections.workloadNote: Not discussed in hours; the graded work students cite is quizzes, which several say tested concepts not covered in class and rewarded memorizing slides.
sections.gradingBasis: Quizzes (called very difficult and slide-memorization based); attendance appears not to count.
sections.redFlags: Four rotating instructors made it disjointed (5+); title/description misleading - little business content (4+); quizzes covered untaught material (3); required for the AI Certificate and costly in bid points.
sections.quote: If Toby Stuart is teaching it yes. He was great. Really thought provoking and worthwhile discussion. Otherwise maybe not.
comments: As it stands right now, I cannot. I hope this becomes the class it should be (and a part of core), but clearly it was hastily put together and expectations the faculty had for the class were very different than what we had as students. If we want a technical AI class, we can go to a different school - we are here for a business class and this was not it. Additionally, the first two quizzes were mostly on concepts that were not even discussed (at least in detail) in class. No, not at all. And this is the only class at Haas where I'd say that.

The name "Business AI Foundations" is a misnomer. We never really got into the practical business applications of AI in any meaningful way. The course covered AI at a surface level from a technical perspective, but I didn't leave with any greater practical knowledge of how to actually use it. I think I got more value messing around on my computer during lectures than I did from the lectures themselves. Three of the four instructors I'd be interested in taking again, just in different classes.

So I'm left wondering what the point was. If this had been called just "AI Foundations," it was too surface level to earn the title. The business portion felt almost entirely absent. And the fact that it's required for the AI Certificate and costs a real chunk of points makes that worse, not better. The curriculum needs to change and the instructor team needs to be managed pretty dramatically before this is worth taking. Knowing what I know now, I wouldn't take it.

You have to take this for the certificate but if you don't need the certificate, you can probably get a similar amount of value out of just talking to other students, keeping up with the news, and taking Data Mining

Yes, this is an important class. Four instructors in such a short period was not idea. But in the future, one or two professors would be idea. Overall, this is an important class and i encourage everyone to take it to understand the AI impact and landscape in business.
Not as it currently stands - I recognize that the administration is revising the course to be more pertinent to stuent desires and to what the market is asking for, however.
The course give insights into the world of AI in bits and pieces, but it failed to bring it together, particularly difficult to see its business alignment.

This course has potential, but it's disappointing in its current form. The course spent a lot of time on technical topics that were too complex for non-technical people to understand, and not complex enough to add value for technical people. The rotating professors seemed cool in theory but made the class feel disjointed. If the curriculum was overhauled and focused more on practical business applications of AI and problems that businesses are encountering, it would be much more worth it.

If this course were more refined, I would recommend it - but in its current state, I would not. There is a lot of potential, and I believe the professors could be excellent, but the class needs stronger continuity across instructors, content, and the evolution of each lecture, as well as clearer connections to real-world business applications. The learning objectives were often unclear, and the quizzes did not meaningfully reinforce learning... they felt more like memorization of lecture slides than true understanding. As a result, I'm leaving the course unsure of what I actually learned. Given how rapidly AI is evolving, this is an incredibly important moment to offer a course like this at Haas, and it feels like the class didn't fully harness that opportunity.
For a Business AI Foundations class: Zsolt - Lean Yes, Thomas - No, Abhishek - Strong Yes, Toby - Maybe
no, but honestly this class is new, and I'm trying to give it the benefit of the doubt.
- You can't have this many professors in a course, especially because it doesn't seem like they had a lot of communication on how the class w as going
- What is the purpose of this class? That needs to be more clearly outlined
- Maybe include takeaways in each class so we can understand what we're supposed to take from all of this.

Interesting content, but definitely they are still figuring the structure out. I think with time it will be a really good class. Yes, I'd recommend it but it needs improvement. The overall course felt a bit disorganized.
Yes

All of the instructors were great except for Thomas Lee. He clearly knows a lot on the topic but struggles to communicate key concepts. He often reverts to highly pedantic and confrontational lines of questioning with students. This course needs some work. While the technical aspects of AI are interesting and important foundational knowledge, this course was too technical without linking that knowledge to business decisions. The quizzes were very difficult even if you did attend classes, while class attendance did not seem to be valued at all in the grading scheme. For people without a technical background, being successful in this class seemed out of reach. The last two classes were by far the best.
No. No one should take this class.

If Toby Stuart is teaching it yes. He was great. Really thought provoking and worthwhile discussion. Otherwise maybe not. Parts of the class were super technical and other parts just felt random? Feel like we need things to be more hands on and less theoretical

No, this class lacks practical applications of AI, and AI in business. This note is cross-professor and about the design and content of the class. Unfortunately, the added value from the class is currently very limited.
I don't know that I would take the course again in its current format. It felt very disjointed across professors and did not quite meet my learning goals for the course.

rows.title: Leader as Coach
rows.disagree: Modest rating, but comments are uniformly enthusiastic

comments: I highly recommend this course! Not only did I learn effective coaching communication skills, but I also gained valuable knowledge on empathetic communication for my role as a manager. These practical skills will undoubtedly help me excel in my career.
Great class! Very interactive and worthwhile. Highly recommend
I would recommend because I don't think many other classes like this exist at Haas

Yes. The course was extremely worthwhile. It's the only weekend course I'd recommend: there's very little lecture, and it's mostly practice based, so most of the time you're coaching, being coached, or observing. It's a great way to develop the skill of coaching, and feel confident bringing it into other areas of your life - both professional and personal.
Really enjoyed this class! Even though the schedule isn't ideal, the information and practice is invaluable across multiple aspects of life and I'm glad I invested the time to take the class.
Yes

This course was easily one of the most valuable courses I have taken at Haas. The teaching is fantastic, the learnings are applicable to all careers, and it puts you in a place to succeed in the future.
It was brilliant, I highly recommend it

This class will improve you not just as a leader, but also all the relationships in your life (partner, parents, friends, colleagues, and more)! Coaching is about helping others live more fulfilling lives. If you want to learn how to do that, take this class! You also gain skills that will serve you beyond coaching. People will feel more connected to you because this class teaches you to really listen and respond with empathy.

I would recommend this course to anyone that wants to help those in need in their lives. People work through issues all the time, this courses teaches to empower the coachee to help them help themselves, which is a highly applicable skill to have. Trust me, people would love to have a friend/colleague like you around if you can do this properly and consistently.
yes. i think it's a very good class for people to think another way to inspire others.
Yes. Coaching is an important skill to leaders today

sections.goodFor: Aspiring leaders and managers who want concrete, usable coaching tools (TGROW, playback and tracking, removing yourself from the equation) and repeated live practice.
sections.notFor: No one flagged a bad fit; the only caution is that it is not a light experiential elective - the days are dense and the workload is real.
sections.workloadNote: One student flags a pretty significant workload with days packed with activities and exercises. Highly experiential, with many low-stakes chances to practice coaching. No hours stated.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear; experiential exercises and coaching practice are the described work. No exams or papers mentioned.
sections.redFlags: One of 16 notes the workload is pretty significant and the days are packed with activities. Otherwise no recurring complaints.
sections.quote: Yes, this is a great intro to coaching. Just be aware the workload is pretty significant and the days are packed with activities and exercises
comments: Yes! This was a great class that pushed me to become a much better coach for my peers.
One of the best classes at Haas! Highly highly recommended!

Yes, it is one of the best and most applicable classes at Haas. It's a shame that more people don't take it! You really learn about the roles of a leader and how to use coaching techniques in life and at work. I believe people have a wrong impression of what coaching entails.
Yes, I will because I feel that every aspiring leader should be able to understand coaching to first coach themselves, if possible, and to lead their own teams.
Yes, I would definitely recommend this course! It's a fun way to learn how to coach. The class is very experiential. I learned a lot and enjoyed it!
Yes! This class is so practical that you can deploy it in your life and make life better!
Yes, Definitely. I would recommend this course to a fellow student.
The course teaches some effective tools for a leader to be a good coach for their fellow members.
Yes, this is a great intro to coaching. Just be aware the workload is pretty significant and the days are packed with activities and exercises

Leadership isn't coaching, and coaching isn't feedback. Much of what we think of as "coaching" really isn't. If either of those sentences didn't make sense, take this class-- your people will thank you.
Yes!
A Great soft skills course. Super applicable and down to earth, great instructors. Very hands on, which for me was very refreshing, in the best way. Highly recommend!
If you want to understand the fundamental principles of coaching and how to hold space for people, then this is the right class to take.
Yes, this is the best soft skill session I've taken during my MBA
Yes. Current office culture is somewhat unhealthy, and this course makes better future managers.

I thoroughly enjoyed this course - it was probably my favorite "soft skills" class that we had and I think skills are important and can definitely be applied in the real world, instead of just being theoretical

Yes, coaching is an essential part to being a leader and we are not typically taught how to be good coaches. Many of the tools we learn in class, such as the TGROW framework, playback and tracking, and ensuring that you remove yourself from the equation are important tools that we could apply to many other situations in our professional and personal lives. Additionally, there are lots of low-stakes opportunities to practice coaching. Highly recommend this course!

comments: No. Lectures and discussions weren't very strong. The material wasn't very worthwhile to learn. I did learn about a lot of companies and what they did, which was interesting.
I do not recommend as the environment is hostile and not conducive for learning. Professor is not nice person and comments are condescending.

This course was helpful as someone who had 0 background in business or strategy

Strongly not recommended. Worst core class.

Professor Cailin Slattery is an amazing professor and has a wonderful energy she brings to the class. I like how she included strategy cases, guest speakers, etc. to make the course engaging and fun. I definitely recommend her! I would recommend, it's good to know why you're making a decision and put a framework around it even if in retrospect some cases seem obvious
Only if not previous experience (working or studying) in strategy topics. If not, it is redundant Yes absolutely - she is engaging and excellently curates and interesting and fun classroom.

Yes, it's interesting although could be improved

It's a required course. I would recommend Cailin, she's a good professor.
Yes I would, this class was really powerful in helping me develop my active listening and be aware of the emotions and physical sensations I am experiencing in the moment.
Absolutely. One of the best courses I've taken at Haas

No. I would not recommend this course AT ALL. This class was bizarre with numerous references to BTS as an example of embodied leadership. That did NOT resonate with the class. Part of the course curriculum was to watch a video of the instructor performing a BTS dance cover. The BTS fan base is teenage kids so for the instructor to be this into it did not feel appropriate. The use of emotion from the instructor felt manufactured and disingenuous. The exercises in class were not effective on Zoom and dragged on and on.

I personally would recommend it to anyone who is open to actually examining and putting in the time to explore their own real identity, stress, anxiety, and goals in life. I am not exaggerating when I say that this course helped me rediscover what I believe to be my purpose and the meaning in life. I didn't come in thinking that would happen, but near the end session, I felt a wall inside me just fall down and realized how implicitly self-centered I had been throughout my whole life and what events informed that, and I realized I could make a conscious change to not let myself be defined by comparison & productivity. However I think this class comes down to how much you are able to put in (time commitment wise) and how open you let yourself be to evolving and changing. Every single person had different insights and takeaways and changes I think. So while I know this class is extremely polarizing, I found it valuable and perhaps the most memorable class I took at Haas because it caused me to re-conceptualize my own identity, self, priorities, anxieties, and how I see the world. For me, that's more valuable than a power & politics class that tells you how to win in the world / manipulate people in a nutshell haha. Because I feel like in my own happiness I have a framework to transcend a mentality where " i will only be happy if I have material success. " And that is freeing. On the other hand, this class is a lot of what can feel like busywork and journaling/writing, as well as reading, so it's not a commitment that can be made lightly. There's a lot of pre-work and post-work, and so it's not a 3-day seminar you can just show up, get insights, and leave. It requires substantial work on your own side, but setting aside that time for reflection helped me mostly (though I think it's maybe still a bit on the heavy side).
Absolutely, this is one of the few classes where you learn an applicable skill.
Course is probably one of the best at Haas in terms of a course that will actually teach you something and lead to professional growth.

This was the most transformative class I've taken at Haas. There is very distinctly a pre-ISEL period in my life as well as a post-ISEL period in my life. If you are open to the process and want to better self-regulate your emotions (as well as handle and take care of the emotions of people around you) I recommend this class. There is so much to be said about effective leadership coming from leaders that know how to self-regulate AND recognize the emotional experience of the people around them.

There is no other class like this at Haas. Take it if you want to spend 30+ hours thinking about yourself and how you interact with the rest of the world. Erica has woven together disparate practices into a cohesive whole. I found it useful and enlightening.
Yes, I recommend ISEL to all fellow Haasies.

ISEL teaches a holistic system of how to relate internally to oneself and externally to others (and vice versa). I believe it's crucial (absolutely critical) to learn such skills especially since as top MBAs we are ascending into managerial roles at elite firms in our capitalistic society.

Now, many students have not had positive experiences in ISEL. I respect that, and I went into the class knowing those experiences are real, legitimate, and exist. Ultimately, in order to benefit from ISEL, it's important to go into it with an open mind, earnestly doing all the assignments, all the practices, and all the readings.

ISEL is not perfect. It has some minor flaws; particularly in how it presents itself as being tied to the GSB "touchy feely" class, which sets up an unmet expectation; a minority few of the methods Erica employ feel too unrelated to the course content; the all virtual format my cohort experienced can be difficult for some — but some prefer it, but its also unrealistic given that we don't conduct our lives entirely virtually (for now...); many of the assignments deal with intersectional identity, but we didn't cover enough of that in fishbowl T-groups; I think the "crash-course weekend" might be too tiring to have lasting learnings for some people.
I would absolutely recommend this class for anyone looking to deepen their interpersonal skills and learn the tools for being a more empathetic and emotionally intelligent leader.
yes! i am glad i chose to spend some time at haas working on softer skills and feel honored to have done so with Erica, who clearly cares about this subject and her students an extraordinary amount.

Yes; The course is a good new perspective on other courses around leadership in the Haas curriculum. This is one of the only ones I know that talks about regulating your emotions (not controlling or avoiding them) and how that might benefit you and your connections to others. Erica and the co-learners are so passionate and they really seem to enjoy this work. It is a long class and lot of commitment but it is worth the investment.

This course is a great capstone of interpersonal leadership courses at Haas. The professors are incredibly nice and supportive. The three days of solid class on the weekend was long, but nicely broken up with breaks, stretching, and meditation. There is quite a lot of written work to do both before and after (6 total assignments that may take most of a day each), but maybe that is expected given it is a two unit class.
highly recommended if you are sensitive to other people's comments on you. you will be able to build up your capacity to deal with interpersonal issues and better connections with people around you

I would highly recommend the instructor and course to fellow students, as I truly believe this is one of the most transformative classes at Haas. Through this class, I reflected and reexamined my past experiences interacting with people in my personal life or at the workplace, and now have a better strategy in place to handle conflicts, and surging emotions. This class has given me the tools to be in touch with my true self and express myself in the world with authenticity and humility.

I would NOT recommend this course in its current design and fashion. The workload is IMMENSE, with very LITTLE learnings, and a very rigid instructor who created distance with students. There is a HUGE potential for this course in the curriculum and the team and instructor put a lot of work in building its content. But its force is becoming its weakness - it is too rigid, too structured, too dictated, and is the only course that Haas still offers online fully (which is a shame for the focus is on building connection and students do value in-person teaching). This online model may be more adapted for EMBA and EWMBA students.
No.
The class pre-work is insane...and so the workload during the class
I feel that this class could have been done in two Fridays maximum

No. It is a horribly executed class that taught me nothing. When thing started to get intersting, Erica would interrupt to add her two cents. The continous references to the k-pop boy band were completely unecessary and irrelevant. This class should also not be done in three days but a few hours a week for 5 to 6 weeks.

I would recommend this course, but I would caution student that this course is more about learning about oneself and one's subconscious reactions (and self regulation strategies) and less on application of how to apply the learnings in a business or professional environment.
I highly recommend this class. I learnt more than I expected to learn and grew so much with this class.
Definitely yes, wholeheartedly!
No other course will empower you with the same level of awareness and "tools" you need for a happier relationship with others and yourself, and a sense of freedom.

If you, like me, came to business school to develop soft skills, learn how to connect with others, and understand yourself, then this class is for you. Erica formerly taught Touchy Feely at the GSB and has adapted it to account for one's social background and to create deeper connection with students from all backgrounds. However, be warned that the course readings and engagement requirements far surpass that of an average Haas class (core included). Even though English is my first language, I struggled to understand the readings and assignments. The zoom nature of the course was also emotionally draining. However, I am leaving the course feeling empowered to become a better person, friend, sibling, and coworker.

Those who aren't sure they can handle the intense course workload should look at Jennifer and Rajiv's two-day Building Trust Based Relationships Course. The courses overlap with each other, although Trust Based Relationships doesn't go as deep due to the course's brevity.

I think I would not recommend this class, as is, to fellow students. The material is important: real connection and conversations, dignity, conflict, etc., are all critical pieces of developing as people and leaders, but this class was more work than learning and could be more impactful in a different format.
This is a good course to get better at communicating with people you care about under stress

This class is about self-reflection and building connections with people in different scenarios. Overall, the content is quite engaging, and I can see it being useful. However, the significant amount of pre-assignments and post- assignments and the time commitment of the whole weekend make me doubt my decision to choose this class. I think the content could be condensed into a one-credit course with substantial learning and much less workload. On the other hand, the instructor showed a lot of BTS content as examples of embodied leadership. But, I personally found it really hard to relate.

Do not take this class to take workload off the rest of your semester. The pre-work and post-work is ridiculously long. I came in interested to learn, but due to the length of the assignments, I ended up not being able to go deep in order to get it done within my schedule. The class was about as Berkeley as it could be. There were some good learnings but it felt like an hour of learning was extended into 4.

would highly prefer this class to be in person....zoom makes it hard to engage fully in the class. There are a lot of useful frameworks and exercises but hindered by the online format. Hopefully this changes.

To be honest, this ISEL cohort / class was a challenge (so many micro-aggressions and overall poor DEI competency from the teaching staff) however, they were genuinely open to feedback, I learned a lot of frameworks to talk through my own feelings, and according to my partner I'm already a better listener. I have asked that this be in-person again, but in the absence of that definitely take this at an Air BnB with friends.
I would because I learned a lot and I also feel a lot closer to my classmates and this was an opportunity for me to realize how amazing my classmates are.

I would not take the class if it is operated remotely. The format simply doesn't translate well to the virtual environment and 24 hours of virtual class over a 3 day period is a very tall order, despite instructor efforts to incorporate breaks. It is a good class to push yourself emotionally, but requires a ton of investment both from an emotional perspective as well as an time/effort perspective.

If you are super new to building interpersonal skills and embodied leadership, you might get something out of this course. The assignments are long and tedious, the class is long and not a super great use of time. I would want to see major shifts/changes in the course before being able to enthusiastically recommend the course, especially related to DEI.

This class has too much homework compared to the number of credits it is. The facilitation framework of the class needs to be updates to reflect more up-to-date best practices for DEI work. The class is significant emotional labor, especially for students from under-represented backgrounds.

I can not recommend this course in its current form. I had very high hopes but am very disappointed with what I experienced. The amount of pre- and post- work for this class is overwhelming, repetitive, and emotionally exhausting. The current format on Zoom is not conducive to such a heavy topic that is complex, emotionally intense, and has a great deal of nuance that you don't get through the screen. Most of my learning in this class was from classmates and unfortunately came at the expense of other students who were put in very uncomfortable situations. The teaching team is not as well-trained as they should be in DEI-related topics, including power, privilege, oppression, and marginalization.
Yes. I believe the future of work (in an AI world) would be about connecting more deeply with what makes me human. The course helped me discover that.
I would absolutely recommend this course and Erica. She is an incredible instructor and was willing to share and connect with us all.
yes, if your focus is on interpersonal skills building and having difficult conversation. This is not a typical leadership class.

Absolutely, this is the best soft skills class at Haas and broke down my negative associations with touchy/feely classes. Erica is one of the best, most aware professors at Haas and this course is essential for all future business leaders who want to elevate their ability to communicate clearly and even impacted my life well beyond my career into my family life and friendships. This course has had one of the biggest impacts on me out of all the courses I have taken in two years at Haas.
Yes
I highly recommend this class to my fellow classmates who needs some self discovery and struggle with inperson relationships.

Yes! This course made me much more aware of my personal biases, social context, and privilege and how these factors may leave an imprint on others. I have learned how to listen with greater empathy and connect to others amidst differences.

Excellent learning experience in a safe and encouraging environment setting. You will be able to learn different communication and interpersonal skills in first three days and then apply them to the real life scenario. Bluntly, I would not. However, I do think Erica and the co-learners have a wealth of untapped knowledge. Had this class been offered in person or include an office hour component, it would be EXTREMELY worthwhile as the topic is very real-world applicable and something that almost everyone struggles with in various ways.
Less structure will spur greater room for discovery, improvisation, Q&A, and as a result, learning.

highly recommend this class if you're interested in knowing how to self-regulate your behavior when you feel threatened and/or anxious, and how to recognize/describe/share your feelings to others. Human connects via emotions. It will teach you practices on how to address feelings like perfectionism, fear, comparison, self-doubt, and how to connect with other people deeply via feeling words.
Yes!

The readings for pre-HW 1 and 2 were very useful and interesting, definitely eye-opening and enriched my experience, thought very long (each took at least 6hrs). As for the class, the 1st day was extremely cringy and mechanical, it did not feel natural at all, but as time passed by, we kinda got used to each other and started becoming more comfortable with speaking to each other and sharing handles. The classes were too long and intensive, I think such a course would be better if taken over longer periods of time and not all in 1 weekend. On another note, the type of people in this class are the best, all of them are intentionally trying to work on interpersonal connections and emotions, they are emotionally available to be open and vulnerable.

Yes - this was one of my most amazing classes I've taken at Haas. I think that it provides such a depth of personal and interpersonal learning outside of any class. This is not a business class but more so a life class. I think that I learned more about being a leader and being a strong human than any other class at Haas. This class does require you to take it very seriously to get the most benefit out of it plus honoring the effort your fellow students put into it. I would not take this class if you are not committed to showing up. I would take this class if you are looking to learn more about how you can connect more deeply with other people.

I highly highly highly recommend this course. I think it should be mandatory. The amount of connection built among the group in such a short time is incredible, I've struggled with connection and belonging my whole life and this course created a safe place to feel "buoyed" and held by others. This is such an emotionally driven course and some precaution should be taken as there are likely things under the surface that will come up. This course is really counter- culture and goes against the social conditioning we've had our whole lives. We talk about deeply personal things, we focus on deep listening and ensuring everyone feels heard. I can't think of a better example of what Haas stands for than this course, because this is the course that most exemplifies "confidence without attitude". Before taking it, I was interested to get someone else's feedback and shocked to learn that "they couldn't recommend it" because of some things that came up in their course. I feel sad knowing that valuable lessons were not taken away from that experience, because I know Erica would have done her best to encourage connection instead of disconnection. I can't recommend this course enough, it really was a powerful experience. The downside is that it's a lot of effort, these things take a lot of work. The homework is challenging and reflective and you will feel tired throughout the days of the workshop. But it is so worth it.

Yes - this course requires significant energy, but the material is very interesting and fulfilling. I would recommend this course for anyone who wants to have a positive impact on their team (and anyone around them, really), and wants to learn how to advocate for themselves and resolve conflicts for the long-term with mutual understanding and appreciation.

I learned a lot from group practicing where I would never have had the opportunity to practice otherwise. But there're just too many assignments -- before, during, and after classes. Sometimes, I feel overwhelmed by the mental energy put in this class, especially the 2nd week where we had day-long classes for 3 days.

I would highly recommend this instructor and course because to be quite frank, I feel now that I have the tools to improve the relationships I have and to form strong connections with the people I have yet to meet! Erica really allows you to explore and examine the factors that have shaped your identity, and she provides data-driven research related to the emotions that we feel. It's a wonderful class to take, and I truly have learned so many things that I'll keep with me for the rest of my life.

I would 100% recommend this class. This class can really change how to interact with families, friends, and colleagues. I would recommend this course, but I think it could be slightly better in person. Zoom gives way to not paying attention.

Yes, it was really different from other Haas classes, much more philosophical.
avoid this class at all costs – it's super dull, not applicable at all, a lot of work and it's basically a philosophy class with nothing that can be applied in the real world. waste of time.

It's fun, not a lot of work, but can (at times) feel far from the application and that can be a bit boring.

I definitely would not recommend this class to a fellow student. Haas and the University offer other courses that are more value added for their education. The idea of the course seems interesting but the execution and overall quality is not worth the short and valuable time and expense of the students. A student would be better off purchasing the book "Work, Wisdom, & Happiness" and reading it themselves. They would mostly likely gain more insight, knowledge, and practical information than what was gained by taking the class. In fact, students within my class mentioned that they had read the book previously and found this to be the exact case. They were disappointed that the class did not deliver on their expectations since the book was considered to be interesting and useful. The course on the other hand was neither interesting or useful. I will tell everyone I know to avoid this class if possible. Absolutely. The ethical and philosophical concepts covered during this class are a great complement to the rest of the business courses taught in the school.
Really cool class, very different than other MBA classes but an opportunity to take the more philosophical view and explore what you want out of work and life.
Important topic but underdeveloped class; takeaways are less concrete than a typical business school class. Highly discussion-based, so your experience will depend on the engagement of your peers.
Yes
The class is very theoretical and more concerned with philosophy than practical applications.
Recognize that your life isn't about only achievements and remuneration.
I believe the topic is incredibly relevant and important. However, the class itself is not very engaging. It's a challenging class to conduct, and there is room for improvement.

I would not recommend this course, because it was not very helpful in terms of taking away toolkits or strategies that can actually help us in the workplace - rather, the lessons felt arbitrary and philosophical without any practical applications
Yes because it provides an opportunity to improve your speaking and allows you to understand areas you need to work on to improve your speaking abilities.

I would recommend this instructor to another student, however not the course. This course is simply not worth the time and extensive effort outside of the classroom for only 1 credit. This class should be more worth 3 credit hours towards our grade.

Doy is kindhearted, approachable, and understanding. I would recommend him, but think the Lead Comm course itself needs to be re-evaluated within the context of the core curriculum.
Stronly recommended though the workload is a little bit heavy while it is 1 credit

I would. I think Doy is a true delight, and clearly cares so much about his students. I always felt comforted when I would come to class. It's great to practice public speaking.
I think Doy has some amazing presenting skills, and students could learn a lot from him, but the class as it is structured now did not add a lot to my overall Fall A experience.
Not at all. Barely any content or structure
Yes - I grew a lot as a public speaker. I was better able to identify my strengths and weaknesses, and am more prepared to continue growing after this class.
Yes, the labs are really good
Absolutely will recommend. Very practical skills for the business world.

I wouldn't recommend either the instructor or the course to a fellow student. Overall, this class has taken up a significant portion of the time and energy I've spent on school and I think it's mainly due to how the assignments are structured. The assignments are the most poorly defined and ambiguous exercises I've had the displeasure of dealing with. We often didn't receive grading criteria until the day of, leaving some of us to scrambling to figure out how we can rework what we had to fit the rubric. There was one point where a couple of my colleagues rushed to make a presentation for their final assignment because, while the professor initially said it was up to us to use slides or not, he only let us know on the day of presentations that we were required to have a presentation aid. No big deal, just the final presentation.

During one of the earlier assignments, I tried to refer to the class decks to see if I could glean any more information from them and get a better idea of the assignment. Trying to find any coherent, clear meaning in one of Doy's decks is like trying to squeeze water from a stone. But thank you for telling me that a good story has a beginning, middle, and end. Not sure how I made it to business school without that.

The assignments also made no sense. There's no advancement of skill or something like graduating from one on one conversations to presenting to larger crowds. Some of them didn't even make sense as an exercise (decorative envelopes, anyone?). The most practical exercise for future business leaders seemed to be the class held on Zoom, but that too was muddied by the fact that the expectations and grading criteria were only divulged to students on the day of, so everyone was receiving awful feedback for executing a poorly defined assignment the way they knew how. I even heard of one group getting dinged for having too many presenters.

This was not the first or last case of expectations not being properly communicated in what's supposed to be a Leadership Communications class. There's no new age pedagogy or anything like that at play here, I think it's just a result of a complete lack of understanding on how to structure a course that doesn't feel like a complete waste of time, energy, and tuition dollars.

If this class sounds interesting to you, remember you will get out what you put in. There is one case a week and I recommend setting aside at least 5 hours throughout the week to work on it. I don't recommend this course to those who are just eager to learn, but don't have time to build relationships with Mr. Etter. This course is my worst experience in Haas for a couple of reasons:

1. Mr. Etter didn't teach on his class; instead, the class is for presentations by those who have attended his office hour. That means, the only way you can learn is to attend his office hour. But it doesn't work for those who have time conflicts or have time differences.
2. His classes were very hard to catch on, without too many visual clues and explanation of ideas.
3. Mr. Etter usually sent out takeaways by end of class, but it was very rough and hard to understand.

4. His classes were not recorded. If you missed any of the classes, then you would never have the chance to catch up. Finally, I've discussed with Mr. Etter about all those mentioned above, but unfortunately, he was very confident about his teaching style, and there's no way to change it. I'd like to inform the students who don't like those points I mentioned above to be careful about choosing this class.

I highly recommend this course. I learned so much by tackling difficult case work and during Professor Etters guided discussions.

100% recommend - great class to understand the business + art behind accounting and Prof Etter is fabulous! The best graduate course I have ever taken. The course was all case-based, resulting in significant learning and quality discussion in class. Professor Etter is phenomenal at guiding discussions and ensures that many diverse voices are heard. Instead of trying to get to the "right answer", he teaches that it is important to hear everyone's thoughts because many times in management there is no right answer. He is my favorite professor at Haas by a long shot!
I think it's practical and good for learning how to make slides as a manager in front of a board
If you are ready to do a lot of work, you will learn a lot (and have fun) in this class.
DO NOT JUDGE BY THE NAME. Highly applied class. A heavy lift but invaluable, particularly if you are planning to work in consulting, big tech, banking, private equity, big corporate.
Prof is an absolute character. Fasten your seatbelts and enjoy the eccentricity.

I would recommend this course. It is unlike any other course at Haas. In this class, the case method is used almost exclusively and it's a great change of pace. The course workload is definitely above average but the learning make it worthwhile.

Managerial accounting often has a negative connotation but know that Stephen is a CPA and a former PE partner and brings a lot of real-life experience based on his previous appointments on the Board. He knows where you should be focusing your attention on and brings a lot of life to a rather boring subject.
Yes - interesting topic, good challenge, great professor

Yes I would - I thought the class discussions, concepts, and case assignments were highly relevant for practical application. I would highly recommend course especially to those entering consulting/corporate strategy. Definitely recommend the class. The workload is on the heavier side, but devoting some time to the weekly cases makes for such great discussion in the class. Especially if you learn better by doing (rather than studying, memorizing, and taking a final), I definitely recommend this class.
Yes, great class for the quantitatively inclined and those interested in managing businesses.

Yes. Etter is a great guy, great lecturer, and great facilitator of lively discussion. He does not focus on the fundamentals, but more how you apply them and how you would make decisions. This was a great capstone to my b school career and got me thinking more in the mindset of a manager than an analyst.
Yes, I would recommend this course to anyone who wants a foundation on how to make managerial decisions based on accounting figures.
Take this class if you don't have better options - pick Corporate Finance over this class. Pick this class if you like to teach yourself topics and like a lot of cold calling and discussion in class.

Yes. It was a good deal of work - likely more than any other class I've taken during my second year - but if you spent the time and went to office hours, it truly made me feel more equipped to be a thoughtful business leader. Etter was also just a genuinely engaging and caring professor. He was among the best mentors and professors that I have had and am truly glad I took this class.
Yes. I strongly recommend managerial accounting. Best 2-unit elective no doubt about it.
Yes, I highly recommend this class for everyone
Yes, best class at Haas. Best prof at Haas.

I took this course to make up for learning finance and accounting remotely, and wanting to make up some of that knowledge with a practical class. I think Stephen Etter assumes we have some accounting experience (at least more than I had) so the cases ended up being very difficult, and it was unclear what the intended takeaways were supposed to be each week. That said, I appreciated the case-oriented teaching approach and practical angle to the class. It was at the very least good practice putting complex information into a presentation each week.

Yes. You learn the most in classes that challenge your thinking and make you work hard. This one does both but it's worth it. If you ever plan on being a manager and want to be the person making the difficult decisions, this class is a must.
Definitely - great course overall. Really enjoyed Professor Etter and his wealth of knowledge + humor

I would recommend this course if you have a decent amount of background on Finance/Accounting principles. For me personally, I will say that Core Finance did not prepare me sufficiently, and because of this, I felt like I had significant ground to make up in this course. This meant that I spent 5+ hours each week on each case. I will say that Etter was always available to answer questions via text, or jump on a quick zoom call to explain any areas that were causing me confusion. He is deeply passionate about this subject, and it shows in his commitment to ensuring that all students are able to walk away with a greater understanding of managerial accounting than when they walked in. He is a great professor, and I wish we had him in Core Finance!

It depends on what you want to learn. If you lack familiarity with how to use financial statements to make strategy and investment decisions, this is useful. Be warned that doing the cases well takes A LOT of time.
ABSOLUTELY YES. This is the opportunity to combine all the MBA learnings and practice them in realistic business settings.

If you are going to take one elective at Haas, then Managerial Accounting with Professor Etter is it...full stop. A kind, thoughtful, hilarious, and engaging man who is truly a joy to be taught by. Etter knows the material incredibly well and couples real-world teach with life lessons that I am better because of. He is quite personable, is always available outside of class, and has become someone I can count on for advice (and good wine). If only all professors at Haas could be like Etter...the MBA would be better because of it.
Yes. Challenging course, but you learn A TON!
Great course. Professor Etter prepared us well for the world we will encounter as managers of companies expected to make decisions with imperfect data. Highly recommend.
Yes!

Yes, Professor Etter is an industry expert with extensive experience and big picture lessons. The course, however, lacked the supplemental material, that some students may need, to explain the basic accounting principles required to understand and really benefit from the course.

Not worth the time. Etter's approach is to let students do the teaching, which is interesting sometimes. However, Etter relies on this tactic way too much, and does not actually lecture or teach the class much.
