There is an expectation that you should just know the material, so if you don't have the intuition going into a case, you are going to waste a lot of time chasing your tail and waiting for Etter to call on someone who knows what is going on. When that person is called on, you are just getting a students explanation of the concept, and Etter does not usually restate and rephrase into an easily digestible form for those of us actually trying to learn.

Professor Etter is very divisive. Some find his teaching style effective and some not. I personally did not find his teaching to be very effective. There is a lot of learning from doing the cases themselves – it is relevant material if you are new to accounting. It is a lot of work for a 2 unit class – you are doing a case every week; so if you are looking for an non demanding class, this is not it. Overall I feel pretty mixed about the class. Not a must, but also not an absolute no.
Absolutely! Heavy workload but totally worth it and very engaging class––even for someone not going into finance like me!
Yes
I would recommend this professor and course. It was challenging but the time spent was well worth it because I gained a lot of practical knowledge that I believe will be useful for me in the future.

This is a class worth taking in Haas. One of the few classes that are case based and I really enjoy this way of learning. I recommend this class 100%, even if you are not too interested in accounting. You will learn stuff here! This professor is divisive – very smart but his classes are a bit all over and he can come across as crass. 1–1 he's incredibly kind and understanding, working with you for hours to help you learn. However, his in–class attitude is not for everyone and swings a little "old white dude"
Maybe not
Yes. This was the most worthwhile course and the best decision making class at Haas

This capstone class serves as an ideal culmination of MBA studies, effectively consolidating the learnings from the program. This class is not recommended for those with a substantial background in accounting or finance. Highly recommend if you are interested in operational challenges like how to deal with costs of building a boat, how to manage restaurant decisions, etc. For someone like me who loves stuff like efficient payment of labor, how to do ROI on a project, etc, this course was invaluable. Amazing professor as well.

I would enthusiastically recommend this course to anyone at Haas. While there is a fair bit of learning managerial accounting techniques, the biggest lesson you will learn in this class is how to effectively present key issues to boards of directors in a way that optimizes decision making. The workload is relatively heavy, but worth it.

Great teacher! Handson learning through Accounting cases. You'll get from this class as much as you put in to it I'd recommend Steve, as there is a lot to learn from him. Not sure I would take this class again. It depends on your goals. Between Corporate Finance and this, I think Corporate Finance is more valuable for most MBAs. This one is more relevant for manufacturing decisions and operations.

The course is worthwhile for someone interested in PE or senior management. It comes at a cost, though. There is a lot of homework, and instruction in class almost always insufficiently prepares students to tackle the problem sets. I also felt like the professor could have spent more time explaining concepts and sharing more of his own experience in class.
Definitely take this course. Foundational to being a manager.
Yes, every student should take this course before graduating business school as a culmination of everything we learned and translating it into real–world problems and solutions.
This course is a great foundation for a variety of post–MBA roles and should be a core part of a business education

I would recommend taking the class simply because knowing Etter has been a pleasure. Going to his office hours was a must for me to actually understand how to approach the case and learn the material, but I feel like he appreciated me stopping by and we built a good rapport. I look forward to having him in my network and being able to consult him someday in the future

I'm not sure. It was much more work than I was expecting for a 2–unit course. There also isn't typically a "right" answer, which is difficult for a subject you'd expect to be more objective. Nevertheless, the value of this course is a professor with tons of experience who teaches you the need to defend your answer and/or be receptive to others' solution, which is truly a valuable career lesson.
Yes - highly recommend. This was a challenging course, but was a much more practical application of the information we learned in core.
Yes
Yes hands down

Professor Etter and the Managerial Accounting class are fantastic. This course does have a heavy workload, but you will learn a TON and the work is useful, not busy work. Etter is very engaging and makes the topics relevant and easy to understand.

This class is a must-take for all Haas students. Professor Etter is an awesome instructor who should not be missed. Additionally, the learnings of Managerial Accounting are the types of business concepts that can be applied to almost any company/role immediately following graduation. Highly, highly recommend.

Yes, I would recommend this course. To me, it was a class that most closely followed a work environment where ambiguity exists in large doses. He creates great discussions in class and people are accountable for completing the case to garner the best in-class discussions.
Very unique class and structure. Professor Etter is extremely dedicated to his students' learning and share great stories about his professional career

Yes - Etter brings a great energy to lectures (even after some health concerns this year) and class is enjoyable as well as learning tools you might use in an organization when evaluating or proposing projects
Highly recommend if you'd like a real understanding of how to engage board-level decision makers and board level decisions.
Definitely more work than other MBA classes through weekly course work, but well worth the time and the class bc of Etter

sections.goodFor: Consulting, finance, PE/VC or general management tracks who want boardroom-style practice presenting and defending financial analysis under pressure, and will self-teach.
sections.notFor: Anyone wanting structured teaching of managerial accounting, a manageable semester, or without a finance background; several say the class experience isn't worth the workload.
sections.workloadNote: Heavy weekly cases requiring prep and PowerPoint write-ups; called a lot of work for a 2-credit class. Mostly independent. Learning happens in the cases, not lecture.
sections.gradingBasis: Weekly case deliverables/slides, random-selection cold calls and in-class participation.
sections.redFlags: Recurring (6+): Etter interrupts and squashes discussion, cases never debriefed, no lectures on the principles so you self-teach; 2 allege unequal cold-call selection; 1 calls him unprofessional and inappropriate.
sections.quote: I didn't like Etter's teaching style at all – he basically just puts up students' case answer slides and makes them teach the solution, but then cuts them off
comments: If you want to be a consultant or in finance, yes. Otherwise is too much work!

No. The course syllabus looks good but the actual content is not worth it. Can we taught in 3 classes instead of a whole semester. The professor is clearly an expert in his industry but is not a good teacher. Was a bit disappointing. Some students also felt like he is very selective in who he picks for class participation and not everyone gets an equal opportunity.
No, not unless something changes about instructor or execution of the course.

I would recommend this course for anyone that plans on being in some kind of management role in the future. Although the bulk of the lessons are focused on cost accounting, the intent of the course is to prepare students for senior leadership roles and to make company-wide decisions.
I think this course is worthwhile to take if you're going into any sort of financial role

The cases in this course were really valuable. Though very time consuming, I learnt a lot from each one and it felt very applicable to the real world/business. One of the most practical classes I've taken at Haas! Etter is a great professor, very engaging speaker, and really cares about his students development and making sure that we're not just considered with getting the right answer, but with coming to a consensus as a group and really hashing things out. I'm very glad that I took this class! It's excellent practice for board room type of conversations, or in any professional setting. Great practice problem solving, thinking critically, and conveying well formed ideas verbally and in writing (PowerPoint slides). It was my most challenging class at Haas, but very well worth it.

It's more work than I expected – I probably wouldn't recommend taking this at the same time as another heavy workload case-based class like Corporate Finance (which is a much better class). I didn't like Etter's teaching style at all – he basically just puts up students' case answer slides and makes them teach the solution, but then cuts them off while they're speaking, so you don't really end up learning a ton in lecture... The cases themselves were worthwhile, but be ready to teach yourself.

Certainly, Prof. Etter's experience is incredibly valuable, and his teaching style was truly enriching. The cases provided insights I hadn't considered before, all of which are applicable to real-world business challenges. I believe this class — and learning from Prof. Etter — is highly beneficial for anyone pursuing a career in business management, private equity, venture capital, or investment banking.

I would recommend this course with reservations. This is a good course if you are looking for interesting in-class discussions and a fun professor. If you are looking for a rigorous treatment of managerial accounting then I am not sure this is the best course.

Prof. Etter keeps it interesting, but there's quite a bit of work, so you need to invest in the homework. Otherwise, it won't be very rewarding. This is not one of the course where you learn in the lecture. There's a lot of learning by doing. No, you basically self teach yourself the course material through the homework. I can't particularly recommend this class as my learnings were minimal.

For a student that anticipates finding themselves presenting financial or accounting data in business settings, this course will do a good job of preparing them for the pressure inherent in that. Learning was less in the slide content, and more in the practice of reading and analyzing the cases.
Yes but be prepared for large workload. Good functional development
I can't recommend this course in its current form, nor Stephen Etter.

The course work is incredibly arduous managerial accounting cases that revolve around concepts that will be foreign to anyone who is equipped with only core accounting. These cases are not supplemented with any lectures revolving around the potential principles you may exercise in the cases. The case discussions also do not yield any insight into how the case should have been approached, resolved, or cover what lessons were learned.
Largely the only class of my Haas career I truly regret taking.
Good class, pushes you to think outside the box. Be ready to speak up.
I was extremely disappointed with this class - many of us stopped going because we had a bad in-class experience and felt we weren't learning anything of value. Very disappointed.

[REDACTED IN THE PUBLIC BUILD] A student strongly advised against the course, called it a waste of time and a thoroughly unpleasant experience, and said the material is better covered in Pricing and Corporate Finance. They named it their biggest disappointment of the MBA. — Why: The original makes an unverified allegation about a named faculty member's professional conduct. The substantive course criticism is preserved; the personal allegation is not republished.
This was a wildly chaotic class... proceed at your own risk. You'll learn some things, but nothing is going to be handed to you on a silver platter
I would recommend the course but with regards to the instructor I would mention that you will need to come into the class ready to critically think as well as change the way in which you are taught.

Not really. Cases every week are quite a lot of work and the learnings get repetitive. While first few classes were really good, many things kept repeating and there wasn't enough structure to fully teach you the concepts.

This class is very much one in which you get out of it what you put into it. There are weekly cases which can be a lot of work depending on your overall course load, so this class might not be best for a heavy semester if you don't want to dedicate time to prepping. Etter likes to cold call via random selection, so it's obvious when someone didn't prep adequately.
This course is a lot of work, mostly independent rather than group focused and very challenging for those without a finance background.

I like Etter personally and have found him to be invested in students outside of the classroom, but I would not recommend this course. He did not manage the classroom well, frequently left key questions of the cases unexplored, and actively squashed classroom discussion through repeated interruptions. The course is a lot of work and the in- class discussion often felt like the juice wasn't worth the squeeze. I honestly was profoundly disappointed and I hope this course improves. Etter is a Haas institution and I think he has more to give, but he needs to reflect on what that is. Maybe - if you're fluent in finance or accounting, may seem like high level review.

Yes- it was confusing and challenging at times, but it was good extra finance practice and learned how to contribute non-financial perspectives to financial conversations. Workload is a little heavy for a 2 credit class
Yes. 100%, this will make you a much better manager -- like only 2-3 other courses do

sections.goodFor: Mainly students who need it for the AI Certificate requirement; a few single out Toby Stuart's and Abhishek's sessions as genuinely worthwhile.
sections.notFor: Anyone expecting practical business applications of AI, and non-technical students - several say success felt out of reach and they left unsure what they learned.
sections.workloadNote: Quizzes are the main out-of-class demand; students say the first two quizzes covered concepts never discussed in detail in class, and attendance appeared not to count.
sections.gradingBasis: Quizzes that students say test slide memorization and cover material never discussed in class; attendance appears not valued.
sections.redFlags: Four rotating instructors with no continuity (5+); too technical for non-technical students yet too shallow for technical ones; title misleading, business content nearly absent; quizzes on untaught material.
sections.quote: The name "Business AI Foundations" is a misnomer. We never really got into the practical business applications of AI in any meaningful way.
comments: As it stands right now, I cannot. I hope this becomes the class it should be (and a part of core), but clearly it was hastily put together and expectations the faculty had for the class were very different than what we had as students. If we want a technical AI class, we can go to a different school - we are here for a business class and this was not it. Additionally, the first two quizzes were mostly on concepts that were not even discussed (at least in detail) in class. No, not at all. And this is the only class at Haas where I'd say that.

The name "Business AI Foundations" is a misnomer. We never really got into the practical business applications of AI in any meaningful way. The course covered AI at a surface level from a technical perspective, but I didn't leave with any greater practical knowledge of how to actually use it. I think I got more value messing around on my computer during lectures than I did from the lectures themselves. Three of the four instructors I'd be interested in taking again, just in different classes.

So I'm left wondering what the point was. If this had been called just "AI Foundations," it was too surface level to earn the title. The business portion felt almost entirely absent. And the fact that it's required for the AI Certificate and costs a real chunk of points makes that worse, not better. The curriculum needs to change and the instructor team needs to be managed pretty dramatically before this is worth taking. Knowing what I know now, I wouldn't take it.

You have to take this for the certificate but if you don't need the certificate, you can probably get a similar amount of value out of just talking to other students, keeping up with the news, and taking Data Mining

Yes, this is an important class. Four instructors in such a short period was not idea. But in the future, one or two professors would be idea. Overall, this is an important class and i encourage everyone to take it to understand the AI impact and landscape in business.
Not as it currently stands - I recognize that the administration is revising the course to be more pertinent to stuent desires and to what the market is asking for, however.
The course give insights into the world of AI in bits and pieces, but it failed to bring it together, particularly difficult to see its business alignment.

This course has potential, but it's disappointing in its current form. The course spent a lot of time on technical topics that were too complex for non-technical people to understand, and not complex enough to add value for technical people. The rotating professors seemed cool in theory but made the class feel disjointed. If the curriculum was overhauled and focused more on practical business applications of AI and problems that businesses are encountering, it would be much more worth it.

If this course were more refined, I would recommend it - but in its current state, I would not. There is a lot of potential, and I believe the professors could be excellent, but the class needs stronger continuity across instructors, content, and the evolution of each lecture, as well as clearer connections to real-world business applications. The learning objectives were often unclear, and the quizzes did not meaningfully reinforce learning... they felt more like memorization of lecture slides than true understanding. As a result, I'm leaving the course unsure of what I actually learned. Given how rapidly AI is evolving, this is an incredibly important moment to offer a course like this at Haas, and it feels like the class didn't fully harness that opportunity.
For a Business AI Foundations class: Zsolt - Lean Yes, Thomas - No, Abhishek - Strong Yes, Toby - Maybe
no, but honestly this class is new, and I'm trying to give it the benefit of the doubt.
- You can't have this many professors in a course, especially because it doesn't seem like they had a lot of communication on how the class w as going
- What is the purpose of this class? That needs to be more clearly outlined
- Maybe include takeaways in each class so we can understand what we're supposed to take from all of this.

Interesting content, but definitely they are still figuring the structure out. I think with time it will be a really good class. Yes, I'd recommend it but it needs improvement. The overall course felt a bit disorganized.
Yes

All of the instructors were great except for Thomas Lee. He clearly knows a lot on the topic but struggles to communicate key concepts. He often reverts to highly pedantic and confrontational lines of questioning with students. This course needs some work. While the technical aspects of AI are interesting and important foundational knowledge, this course was too technical without linking that knowledge to business decisions. The quizzes were very difficult even if you did attend classes, while class attendance did not seem to be valued at all in the grading scheme. For people without a technical background, being successful in this class seemed out of reach. The last two classes were by far the best.
No. No one should take this class.

If Toby Stuart is teaching it yes. He was great. Really thought provoking and worthwhile discussion. Otherwise maybe not. Parts of the class were super technical and other parts just felt random? Feel like we need things to be more hands on and less theoretical

No, this class lacks practical applications of AI, and AI in business. This note is cross-professor and about the design and content of the class. Unfortunately, the added value from the class is currently very limited.
I don't know that I would take the course again in its current format. It felt very disjointed across professors and did not quite meet my learning goals for the course.

rows.title: Business Strategies for Emerging Markets: Management, Investment, and Opportunities

comments: Yes
Definitely. This is the quintessential grad school class

Heck yes. I think every first year MBA student should take the Emerging Markets course with Professor Levine. Most of the core curriculum was useless, and on a campus where we lack true international diversity (not in the American sense with the "d" word), the Emerging Markets class is a must. I have personally recommended Professor Levine's course to my peers, and the class has only enriched my MBA experience.

No I would not, the class did not result in any learning. Lectures seemed to be created minutes before class with very little structure. We often spent entire classes debating one minor detail. Grades were never released to us throughout the term so we had no idea where we stood in the course. He is very harsh in his criticism of your ideas and your work. Expect to work hard to meet every minor request he has for your final project.
I would NOT recommend taking this course.

No. David is an ineffective professor and it is very apparent that he does not care about the well-being or development of his students. He is extremely disorganized, generally negative in terms of feedback he provides on deliverables (which itself is limited at-best) as well as his overall teaching style and communication in-class.

sections.goodFor: Students who want real client consulting reps for a sustainability-focused company, and who value the guest speaker series; useful for the applied innovation credit.
sections.notFor: Students who need structure and faculty guidance: several call it deeply disorganized, with basic lectures, no framework enforcement, and no instructor intervention when a team goes bad.
sections.workloadNote: Semester-long live client consulting project is the bulk of the work, plus guest speakers and class-voted discussion topics; load swings entirely with your team.
sections.gradingBasis: Client consulting project deliverables; a framework is provided but students report few check-ins on whether teams follow it.
sections.redFlags: 5+ of 19: deep disorganization and 'spontaneous' planning, no guidance/check-ins on the consulting framework, experience entirely group-dependent, basic lectures; one questions the originality of the teaching material.
sections.quote: The course experience is highly dependent on the group project. There's a lack of guidance on the consulting framework and implementation of the framework from professors
comments: yes
I would recommend this course - the opportunity to work with a client on a real business challenge is really great. There is also a good mix of guest lecturers and class-voted discussion topics.
Absolutely... YES! I learned a lot and the experiential part of it was invaluable.
Yes, recommend this class for those looking to get into a consulting career. It provides solid foundation and familiarizes you with real work in the consulting realm.
The experience to work with a real company is really valuable.
yes- both are very personable and I would recommend that students get to know them personally as well.
Honestly no, it's a bit unorganized. Your experience is very dependent on who is in your group, and instructors aren't able to step in to adjust if thinks are truly back

The course experience is highly dependent on the group project. There's a lack of guidance on the consulting framework and implementation of the framework from professors (while the framework is given, it does not seem like projects have to align to it/not enough check-ins to ensure that teams are on track using the framework). The other half of the course are really great guest speakers that gives an overview of various sustainabiltiy topics throughout the semester, however there's a lack of structure on teacher-led content.
I don't know. If the course materials continue to be so unorganized then i wouldn't recommand to anyone. Yes

Take this course! Great way to link theory and practice - completing the consulting project throughout the semester with a real company and real clients made it feel very hands-on and valuable learning experience where we actually made an impact. One of the best courses I've taken as someone with a sustainability background who had grown tired of redundant theoretical sustainability classes - this one was actually worth it and I learned new things. Fine class if you need the applied innovation credit, but don't take it for fun. Despite good topics, deep disorganization and over-indexing on consultant nonsense made this feel like a waste of time. Very disappointing.
Absolutely
Yes, very interesting course and the instructors were awesome!!

I would not recommend it. The class seems very spontaneous, without proper planning, and the consulting projects have no guidance, and no hierarchy so it it so hard to actually do them adequately. I think this should be a speaker series. That part was nice. But the consulting project felt like I was doomed to fail from the start. So bad. I would not recommend this course. Some of the guest speakers were interesting, but the teachings didn't build on top of each other well and depth of content was severely lacking. Lectures were very basic and I don't think the format took advantage of the instructors' wealth of experience. I walked away without any clear value-add to my education or professional toolkit.

Highly recommend. This Strategic Business course blends core strategy frameworks with a live consulting project, amplified by relevant guest speakers and candid, actionable feedback, you'll leave with sharper problem-structuring, stronger storytelling, and client-ready deliverables.
I would recommend this class to a student who would be interested in hearing lots of interesting guest speakers, but caution them on some of the concerns I raised in the previous section.

[REDACTED IN THE PUBLIC BUILD] A student said the course is not worth the tuition and that comparable material is freely available elsewhere, and criticised the quality and originality of the teaching material. — Why: The original makes a specific unverified factual claim about how a named instructor prepares their material.

sections.goodFor: Students who need the AI certificate or want conceptual grounding in how AI works and how it may reshape labor markets; Toby Stuart's sessions are singled out as the strongest.
sections.notFor: Anyone wanting hands-on AI skills - students never used an LLM in class despite the course being billed as strategic for non-technical people; also too foundational for anyone technical.
sections.workloadNote: Half-semester with four rotating professors: pre-class questions due Sunday nights (often opened too late to answer), in-class printed quizzes, and assignments students say added little value.
sections.gradingBasis: Printed in-class quizzes, pre-class questions and assignments; weights not discussed. Quizzes called poorly prepared and irrelevant.
sections.redFlags: First offering was 'a hot mess': 4 rotating professors with no handoff, misaligned start date (professor missed the first class), typo-ridden quizzes with too few printouts, stale bCourses, no GSI support.
sections.quote: This class was billed as a strategic class for non-technical people to learn more about how to leverage AI in workflows, and we didn't once use AI/an LLM of our choosing in class.
comments: This class had a few interesting lectures but overall was a pretty chaotic overview of AI and the future of work. The technical foundations and future of work sessions were interesting but the class is very dependent on the professors and how many sessions you have with each of them. Hopefully it will continue to improve as the AI Certificate improves over the semesters.
Course is poorly designed. I dont feel i have learned anything. Very theoretical, not hands-on. Until the PO designs a better course, wouldnt take it.

No. This class was billed as a strategic class for non-technical people to learn more about how to leverage AI in workflows, and we didn't once use AI/an LLM of our choosing in class. I expected to become more more AI-literate as a result of this class, and I am coming away from it having no new skills other than knowing a few hypotheses of how AI may (or may not) impact the labor market.

The way it was this year, not really. I'm sure the fact that it was the first time this course was offered played a role but it was a complete mess. Start date was misaligned between students and professors (we all showed up to the first class, professor didn't show up and then emailed us saying the class actually started a week later), quizzes covered topics that were a bit irrelevant in my opinion and were very poorly prepared (typos, faulty structure, not enough print outs for everyone, etc), assignments didn't add much value, and content overall was too theoretical and not very practical. Hopefully all of this (and other problems we had) improve drastically for next year.

While the topic is important, the course needs A LOT of work. Having four different instructors for the course was a recipe for administrative disaster. I think this course will improve next year, so I would still take it, but I want to note that it may be too foundational for AI experts. Toby Stuart who hopefully remains one of the lecturers for the course is a great industry leader and makes you think.
I would not recommend, better off taking an LLM course. I am not sure what they were trying to do making us take this course.

Yes. This class should be a core class, right after Data and Decisions. It is crucial for today's market that every MBA students masterizes these concepts and is able to "talk AI" and understand the technology in a proper way Interesting course to get exposure to the nuts and bolts of AI and how it will affect workplaces and society from several different perceptives.
Yes, The course is useful and brings clarity about AI in the business world

I would recommend this class because I still got unique insights into what's happening in the space and readings I would not go looking for own my own, but not all the professors were equally good (Toby Stuart was great; Jonathan Kolstad was good; and Anastasia Fedyk was not as great; we haven't had the fourth professor at the time of this submission so can't speak to them) but the learning experience fluctuated a lot depending on who was teaching. If Toby is teaching his own class on this subject, I would probably just take that.

No, but I think this class can only get better (hopefully it will). Some general comments about how to improve the class (it didn't feel appropriate to write it down only for one faculty): stop relying on the "this is the first time we teach the class so things will go wrong" and actively try to prevent that from happening (Question the status quo, anyone?); if you ask us to answer the pre class questions before 11 pm, make sure to open them with enough time to answer (most of the times I would try to answer them on Saturday (closed), Sunday 11am (closed), Sunday 5pm (still closed), and then by 9pm it was open but it closed at 11pm), and several times they didn't even open the questions so you would be checking all the time until finally giving up; communicate with other faculty on a regular basis (e.g., it happened twice that the printed quizzes were not enough for the students); and in general, the class should be called AI foundations and not Business AI foundations, as there was little to no connection to the business side (eg., it explained how AI works when translating words into 0s and 1s, then doing some calculations for the error, distance, etc when it could have been explained much simpler and why this is relevant); if the class will continue to have this technical focus, then there is plenty of overlap with the Intro to coding class
It was ok- I hope they update it to be reflective of the feedback in terms of balancing how much time was spent on the content the students found most interesting
If you need the AI certificate sure. I'd like to see an iteration of this class with less professors. 4 in one half semester was way too much.

I think this course could be good but this year was not well coordinated and prepare given it was the first edition. Also, is important it is taught from a business/ corporate lenses, not so focus on research and academia but rather what kind of problems, challenges and decisions we are gonna have to face in the corporate world (even if we don't have a technical role) and what do we need to make them efficiently. I would think of the course as a guide for a student who is put in charge of defining the AI strategy of a company, what kind of tools they implement and how these are integrated, what factors to take into account, how do you train employees, what workflows should be redefined, etc. I would recommend this class because I learned a lot about how businesses are currently thinking about AI and what AI strategy should look like.

This course will give you a strong and broad understanding of AI fundamentals from the theory perspective, which is great. There is little content on its application, though, nor really content on policy/ how to handle it/ etc. There is also no hands-on learning with AI. So if you take this class, be well aware that what you get out is theory and understanding (which is a helpful thing, no doubt), not practical application.

Hopefully, from an organization perspective, this class will improve because it was a hot mess this semester. There were 4 professors who each taught a few weeks of class separately. This was great from a knowledge and perspective breadth POV. However, they never seemed to actually talk to each other or have a handover when switching to then next professor, which made the class disjointed as they didn't seem to know what was covered, where we were at, when quizes where, if past deck material was actually posted, etc.. Furthermore, they didn't seem to manage or update bCourses regularly, causing confusion, and there was no real GSI in tow to help keep up with this either. First year course with a number of different professors so it tended to be disaggregated. Solid material and deep dive into AI.

rows.title: Investment Banking Series
rows.ghostNote: One-unit, six-week speaker series on investment banking recruiting and careers. Same caveat as the VC series: small, low, variable prior.

sections.goodFor: Students with little or no accounting/finance background who want a low-lift, high-level view of incentives and how accounting shapes managerial behavior.
sections.notFor: Anyone with finance/accounting background or wanting hard FP&A/technical skills - several call it too simple, undergrad-level and not actionable post-MBA.
sections.workloadNote: Low lift - explicitly called a low-workload class; discussion-based lectures. Multiple say the weekly 2-hour session drags and pace is slow.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear
sections.redFlags: Recurring: content too basic and too theoretical for a graduate course (5+ comments), pace drags, and you do not learn hard accounting/FP&A skills despite the title. One asks for a full overhaul.
sections.quote: The class is too simple and won't give you an in-depth perspective on managerial accounting. Class content needs an overhaul to become useful
comments: Yes, this course pushed my thinking and understanding of the accounting structure within a company and encouraged me to really consider incentives and how they drive behaviors within the context of a firm.

If you are really interested in the accounting side of leadership - from the perspective of defining incentives - this could be a good class for you to take. However, knwo that it is almost all theory - you won't learn hard
accounting/FP&A principles in this class like you may in some others.

I think it's an interesting topic and provides some useful frameworks to assess how firms'accounting practices align (or don't) with what they preach. But the class is slow and at some points felt like a drag. If it is offered as a half semester class, I'd maybe recommend it but it always didn't feel like the best use of 2 hours every week.
Yes, it was a low lift class that gave a high level conceptional view of managerial finance and the types of incentives that drive decisions in that context.
I would recommend only if you are interested in working as a finance manager and/or your accounting knowledge is relatively basic.

The class teaches you important concepts around business. But the class drags and can be slow. Coming to the end of it, the slides are something important to keep in mind, as well as the frameworks, but the class was a little slow. Great professor, but the class needs to step up towards a graduate degree
I would not particularly recommend it. However, if you prefer a low workload and would rather not study internal accounting by reading the textbook on your own, it might be a suitable course for you.
The class is too simple and won't give you an in-depth perspective on managerial accounting. Class content needs an overhaul to become useful
Probably not unless you have next to no background in finance/accounting.
Yes, I would recommend Shawn and this course. It didn't require extensive accounting knowledge and was an
enjoyable, discussion based class with interactive lectures.
Would not recommend at this time- the way the course was taught felt too theoretical, and undergrad-level, learnings are not obviously actionable at the post-MBA level.

100% will. Not only the course is useful but also the way professor Kim teach is very well. Proper pace, clear goal, real- world application. And the professor's charisma would make you learn difficult knowledge in a very accessible way. Yes

Sure, the course covers complex concepts and insights into how managers approach decision-making. Is it always exciting? No, but you do learn how to become a more informed investor and a better consumer of the narratives that companies convey through their numbers.
If you're looking for a basic and high-level intro into the subject, then I definitely recommend it! But not if you expect to go deeper and take more out of it.

I would absolutely recommend this course and instructor. This intro to carbon footprinting and climate issues more broadly was extremely interesting and applicable. It's a course that would be valuable for everyone to take. Yes - highly recommend for anyone interested in learning the fundamentals of carbon accounting / footprinting and needing inspiration for how to bring impact to any sector
Yes, but not strongly. I would say he's okay but not amazing

The course is really interesting and very different from every other course I've taken at Haas. Chris Jones is great but somewhat disorganized, so flexibility is definitely key to getting a lot out of this course.
Yes. chris able to give us general overview about carbon innovation, carbon analysis etc. I look forward to learning more via group project.

I would recommend the class, if my suggestions were taken. Again, the professor knows SO MUCH about this topic. You really can't get more of an expert than him. But you don't really learn how to do Life Cycle Assessments or any sort of carbon reporting. You talk about it in theory, and he shows a lot of slides. I don't know if I have any hard takeaways from the course, except that I now know for certain that we are nowhere near achieving our sustainability goals.
I would recommend this if you have no background knowledge on carbon accounting and how companies are
approaching or thinking about this.
Probably not, I took it because it is one of the classes required for the sustainability certificate.

No. This class was poorly organized. Readings were heavy, research based, not case. Readings did not align with classroom discussion very well. Slides were all over the place - mostly graphs that we could have looked up on our own. No carbon accounting - explicitly said we could do it on our own time. Discussion based with little frameworks for actually making impact in our organizations.

I would not recommend this course as it is today. There was not a lot of substantial learning as most of the topics were surface level. It was not very focused on innovation and lectures were not informative. In its current state, the class felt like a very high-level overview of carbon emissions and scopes and many irrelevant tangents happened. I think this class could be improved and be worthwhile if it really focused more in depth on carbon footprint analysis methods/tools and applying those methodologies and how businesses could innovate to apply these concepts within the sphere of business. We just scratched the surface of that finally in the fourth class. If he started focusing on that earlier it would be more impactful.
Yes recommend good high level overview and raising critical aspects.
Absolutely, a great introduction to accounting for GHG and the corporate sustainability space

Yes, as a one unit course meeting twice I feel I had an opportunity to do some real learning, which I was not expecting. yes, he is very knowledgable, make sure you bring snacks to help with the long days.
Yes - this is the only course at Haas that gives students exposure to carbon accounting and relative frameworks. This is a good one-credit course.
Absolutely

Yes, Professor Jones did an incredible job highlighting the main framework to analyze carbon reporting and how companies can improve their reports and address other environmental issues. I'd recommend taking this class if you are interested in carbon reporting frameworks and are considering a career in claimte-related technologies. Yes, very engaging professor!
If you want a baseline understanding of GHG Protocol, what the Scopes of emissions mean, and what frameworks are already out there, take this class!

I didn't like the class, but given that it's only two Sundays it was ok. It was only an overview, and we didn't dive into any specific tools that we could use for carbon footprinting, which made it less valuable than I expected. If you don't have any knowledge of carbon footprinting this is a good intro, but if you have already researched this topic it will probably be a review.
Yes, the course is a good introduction and overview; however, if you are looking for a more in-depth look at carbon accounting, this is not the class.
Yes, if you're interested in ESG
Gives a very high level overview of ESG reports.
I would recommend to fellow students learning about the carbon accounting frameworks because it is interrelated with every industry
I wouldn't recommend this class as I think the main topic of the class was not covered in class and I would rather allocate these hours to learn about this topic on my own
Yes! I don't know of any other course on campus like this.
No. It doesn't teach anything concrete and is more of a AMA section
Yes, but it should be a 3 credit course for a stronger experience to build expertise
Absolutely, for a 1 credit it does pack all the concepts really well without overwhelming you.

I recommend this class because it equips you with essential knowledge in carbon accounting and ESG topics, empowering you to make informed decisions that align with sustainable practices. The insights gained are valuable for individuals and professionals aiming to contribute meaningfully to environmentally
I stronlgly recommend this course
Yes I'd recommend him

Cool practice of ESG public equity investing with really cool professors. You'll get to hear from very high profile guest speakers. It is public equities though, so make sure you are interested in that topic (versus other forms of sustainable investing).

Highly recommend this class if you are enthusiastic about the idea of being launched into the day-to-day of investment management. The coursework and decisions are very applied, but as a result some of the focus of the class might be less interesting to people who are not interested in the tactical elements of sustainable investing. The instructors (Anne Simpson & John Goldstein) are so knowledgeable and leaders in the field - it has been very fun to learn under their guidance.

This is an incredibly interactive class that will challenge your assumptions on what sustainable investing looks like. While it's challenging managing group work among 10-15 principals, I find this class very worthwhile.

No. I learned more in this clas in the little hour I spent working with a partner than I did the entire semester. I do not come fromthe ESG impact investing space and this course only allowed those who do to shine and elevate their opinions

I was really excited to take this course based on who was teaching it, but I honestly would not recommend the course. The course was very student run which was a little frustrating given the amount we pay for tuition. There were questions asked in class and the professors would often say, "why don't you research that and get back to the class." Yes, the professors are very well connected but it's clear that they have never taught a course before, which becomes frustrating when you're unsure of learning objectives and target deliverables. There are also a lot of varying levels of understanding in the class which made things difficult because overviews were never really provided to get people on the same page. There were a lot of guest speakers but I would have preferred more learning and less guest speakers. Absolutely--if you're interested in any aspect of ESG investing, public or private, there is no better source for the latest industry movements, dynamics, happenings, and strategies than in John and Anne. The course is being rebuilt, which comes with growing pains, but after this year it should be smooth in addition to being incredible.

The course is not a good option for students with little / no experience in the investment industry, even though allegedly it's not a pre-requisite. This greatly undermines the ability of students with different backgrounds to succeed in the course, creating an unfair environment.
Yes, especially people without any investment or ESG background.
SIF is a great class! Unparalleled access to industry leaders. You really get what you put in!

I have learned so much from John and Anne. They are at the forefront of sustainable investing and bring the nuance and complexity of the industry to life while also bringing an intense optimism for the possibilities within the space. They bring in fantastic guest speakers and make themselves available to us as resources often. It is a relatively unstructured course thus far, which is great if you have a lot of ideas or areas you want to explore. Future iterations of the class will likely be more structured in some ways, as this is the first time they are teaching it, but they are committed to helping us learn about what we want to learn about, which is great.

Yes! Great opportunity to practice making investments in a supportive setting. Super interesting guest speakers too! I would recommend this course to anyone with an interest in sustainable finance who is willing to be a self starter and to throw away all of their pre-conceptions about the investment industry. Its a great opportunity to challenge the status quo and explore innovative and exciting ideas, but does require a high amount of initiative from the students. The Instructor's are truly legends in the field and are very generous with their knowledge. However this course is quite unstructured and the learning outcomes were unclear. I became frustrated with the lack of process around decisions and clarity on how we were being graded.

I would say it depends on what your interests are. For me, this is new topics for me so it was hard for me to participate and feel engaged. Student's knowledge in this space is very broad so I think it's hard to tailor the course based on background.

Yes I would. It's a self-driven class, so the first few months of the class are really dedicated to building the class structure, so be aware of this. If you don't like ambiguity, then you may find yourself confused or lost at times - something to be aware of.
DO NOT TAKE THIS COURSE. I have never in my life experienced a course that did not have a syllabus and was

completely student run (when there were two paid professionals supposed to be running it). The fact that people in our class had to create a " syllabus " so we had any direction on what to do in the class was absolutely insane. Also, these students never got paid despite doing the job of a GSI. Furthermore, I've never been apart of the course where the professors showed up less frequently than the students, which is saying a lot considering I missed 3 classes this semester. The worst part about the professors not being in class was that we would never have a heads up, so we would show up to class and no one would be there to teach. There was never any teaching in the class. If you didn't know how to do something and emailed the professor they would never respond, so you were kind of out of luck. People who came from the finance background did all of the work for projects because I truly didn't even know how to. Professors did not respond to emails, even after many follow ups. Professors were also often times doing other work on their computer during class. I can't even believe they were being paid. Again, an insane course to even be offered. Don't take it.

If you are passionate about investment management and want to explore the intersection of sustainability and investing, than this is the class for you! If this is not your career path, I would stay away. This class is why I came to haas so I enjoyed it, but it was solely due to personal interest. The class did nothing to amplify this interest, and in fact made it hard to learn and enjoy.

This class has a lot of potential and likely changes year to year depending on the instructor and how they would like to manage the curriculum. This year, with two new professional faculty members, there was little learning to be had. It was entirely self-guided. I did learn about the specific stocks I pitched and it was nice to be part of a community focused on sustainable investing, but I would not recommend it in its current format.

I would not recommend this class at all. Despite having 3 faculty members leading the class, they did not actually instruct much and I find this a pity as I'm sure we could have learnt a lot from them. The class meets twice a week but the time is not well used: there is little time for team work, but also no real content that is being taught. Most of the classes require each team to give an update, one by one, about where they are in the process and what type of tools they are using (eg, are you tracking interviews on Excel vs. Word?), which becomes extremely repetitive and is not helpful. In addition, it felt like the entire class was designed for the final summit where the audience is a mix of investors and thought leaders in cleantech. I found it a pity that very little emphasis was being put on actually delivering something valuable for the entrepreneurs and startups we are actually working with and on making sure that students learnt, and instead it just felt like it was important to the faculty to save face in front of whoever was invited to the summit. Therefore, I felt that from beginning to end there was a huge misalignments in goals between the students, the entrepreneurs, and the faculty. From a project perspective, the class was way more "technical" than I expected (but unfortunately with nobody really teaching us any technical content), and there was surprisingly very little emphasis on go-to-market strategies and commercialization! That being said, I really liked that the teams were mixed, with students from many different programs, including PhD students. In addition, Bill and Sheeraz were always available, approachable and happy to help out, and I really appreciated their commitment to the class, their deep care for students and their receptivity to feedback!
this sucked - too much work, no guidance, lots of busy work type assignments, huge time committment and 0 payoff. only cool part is the startups themselves, and the other students in the class

Rewarding, especially if you haven't done consulting style before (less valuable if you have). The courseload is very heavy, so plan for this if you decide to take the class. Also, spend a lot of time selecting your company. Summit presentations were very rewarding
This class was a significant learning for my career and an engaging way to work with startups in delivering significant content. A class that you make your own!
Absolutely! By far, one of the best classes I have taken. An awesome learning experience and a fun community to engage with.
Yes. This is a great class. Really helped me develop, especially within the cleantech sphere.
Yes, this course taught me a lot about market research, interviewing, and giving effective presentations.

I would -- as a PhD student, this is one of a few opportunities to take a business class and diverge from the many technical courses we take. I think it was a good experience overall but is highly dependent on your team and the startup you'll eventually work with. I've had the good fortune of working with some incredible business students from whom I've learned a lot. The startup we worked with this year is also really responsive to our feedback and concerns. The instructors do a great job encouraging us to ask them for feedback or help whenever we need it, though I feel like I got more out of working with my team than the instructors' lectures.
I would highly recommend this course to fellow engineering students because it teaches engineers very different knowledge and motivates them to have their own startups.

Yes, if you could truly put the time in that this class deserves. This class is most valuable if everyone in the team in engaging and participating. There were different levels of dedication in the team and I think that dragged us down quite a bit.

I would definitely recommend this instructor and course to another student. I had a great time in this class and it was so useful to my education to have the real-life experience of consulting with a start-up and learning about how products are brought to market.

I have told students that if you have a passion for working in Cleantech you can get a lot of this class if you are willing to put a lot of work into it, however, if you are only casually interested then I would not take this course. Yes. It was a great opportunity to work with passionate entrepreneurs. High degree of freedom is the beauty of the class. You may set your own goal in this class and leverage the activities to achieve your goal. You can broaden your energy network in a very effective way with this class.
The final symposium presentation is a honorable chance to speak in front of energy professionals in the bay area and get your foot in to the community.

This is a LOT of work - but there is substantial value in deeply getting into a problem, working through it, building external connections, and potentially even finding jobs. Don't go in half-heartedly but if you're committed to cleantech it is the class to take.

If you are interested in clean or climate tech or energy, take this course. Your enjoyment of the class will highly depend on the technology you get and your team. I got an OK tech and an excellent team and the course was one of the best I've taken at Haas. If you end up on a team full of typical "haas apathy" (you know what I mean) then this class has the potential to be rough. Overall, this is an excellent learning experience and, for some of you, why you came to Haas, so take the class. It is a lot of work, but if you keep on top of it all semester, it's perfectly manageable. For all of those interested in how startups find their ideal market and design their go-to-market strategy this is a great course. It is a lot of work, so starting early by defining team dynamics and planning the semester with your team in the first week of class is ideal if you want to get the most out of this class.
Yes I would. I learned quite a lot from hands on research, which is the most impactful way of learning for me. The things I learned and connections I made are directly impactful to my future career.
Yes! I learned so much about early-stage climate tech start ups and the climate tech space in general. I am so happy that I took this course!
YES!

Students should have a very clear reason for what they intend to get out of the class, whether that is presentation skill development, deep exposure to a technology, GTM strategy experience, etc. and make sure it is worth the high workload required to do well in the course

Absolutely not. I was so excited about this class, and it was one of the main reasons that brought me to Haas in the first class. I'm very sad to say that this course was the single biggest regret of my Haas experience. It was poorly designed from the start.

This class hinges on having strong client partnerships. Several of the clients did not set their teams up for the success. They came in with different understandings of what they would get out of the course, indicating that the instructors did not prep or debrief them well. It's also very hard to teach uniformly to a class that is working with very different clients at very different stages. If you don't see a client you're SUPER excited about, please don't even think about this course.

The lecture materials were disjointed, and topics didn't flow well from one to another. The instructors attempted to give us group work time during class, but it was usually only in 20 minute blocks amidst other content. This was disruptive and we were unable to get much done in this time. Most of the content ends two thirds into the course, and the end is dedicated to the symposium presentation and report.

The instructors are just okay. Bill and Bill have been doing this forever, but it seems like their hearts just aren't in it anymore. Sheeraz was truly a fantastic instructor and is a great leader in this space.

Much of the course is spent conducting stakeholder interviews and doing market research. I believe that these concepts are better taught and better utilized in other courses and experiences at Haas. Due to the forced deliverables (symposium presentation and 75+ page report) and needlessly uniform teaching style, this class ate up more time than all of my other courses combined. It was a frustrating experience in which I look back and reflect that I have learned very little from it. I wish so badly that I could reset this semester and not take C2M. Please don't make the same mistake I did.

C2M is an incredible experience. Probably life changing. It gave me the opportunity to apply the learnings from my MBA to a real-life scenario. I would highly recommend this for anyone who wants to work in clean tech but I do agree with comments from previous years that it requires A LOT of work. I spent easily 5-6 credits worth of of time on it

No one should take this course until it is completely overhauled. Working with cleantech startups feels like the quintessential Haas project, and in many ways it is, however, there is little to no education being provided in this class. At their worst, AI courses are unpaid internships, and that's what this course is in its current form. Almost 2/3rds of total class time was dedicated to unstructured teamwork, which is unacceptable. If we could be properly taught about how to go about performing the final deliverables before they were due, this would be a decent class, but with so many years to get things right, it's hard to believe there will be any significant change.
Ultimately most of the course is experiential and I learned a lot through the process of the projects assigned and would recommend the course.
Yes, this course is one of the best classes I have taken at UC Berkeley. I learned a lot about the technology commercialization process through this course.

Overall if you are interested in the Cleantech startup space I think that this is a good primer for what it looks like. It puts you in a place where there is a lot of ambiguity and you need to just grind a lot to get to your ultimate goal. I think that most of that work has to happen at an individual and team level, and it is not easy, which can make it easy to complain about the instructors even if it does not necessarily have to do with them. Ultimately I think this is very valuable course and would recommend it.

C2M was a challenging but ultimately rewarding course to enroll in. I got to learn about a very interesting technology, dive into new markets and areas of knowledge, while working with a good team who were all bought in in their own ways. I think if you get the short end of the stick on the team perspective it can be a pretty miserable experience given the volume of work and relative lack of structure in the class.

I would highly recommend taking this class as it's a capstone class where we can practice aspects of finance, marketing, econ, data, sale and last but certainly not least, public speaking. I wish more Executive MBA (EMBA) would be aware of this class as it's a great opportunity to work directly with founders. EMBA also bring a different perspective as well as access to a more robust network that will come hand during the industry interviews.
If you want to learn about clean tech in an immersive experiential way, AND have plenty of time (i.e. few other time commitments) then it's a great experience
It depends. Your experience will depend heavely on the team you are assigned to and the entrepreneur you are assigned to.

Besides this, the class itself in terms of content was not particularly attractive to me. The content was not well structured and the feedback you get during the process of preparing the final presentation and paper are not necesarrily appropiate or helpfull.

On the other hand, you get a real consulting kind-off experience and learn a bit about how startups work. But for the most part, your are on your own with your team and the entrepreneur without too much detailed guidance.

This course is challenging not just because of the subject matter, the workload, or the deliverables, but because of the scattered instruction, poorly designed class meetings, and irrelevant interim deliverables.

Yes - beware that while this is 3 credits, expect to put in work akin to a 5 credit class. It really feels like a badge of honor to have for anyone looking to make their career in climate tech but certainly not a walk in the park and there are certainly easier applied innovation courses to take if you're not all in on climate tech.

For a fellow science-focused student I don't know if I would recommend it. This was a good overall experience, but the summit made me feel like most presentations could have been written a few weeks ago with minimal research. It becomes a game of giving the best "show" and not showcasing research. The final presentation that called TEM tea and had a planted question from a friend to start off the discussion made me feel sick to my stomach.

I cannot recommend this course in its current form. It is an ungodly amount of work which may or may not have any influence for the companies we work with. The professors do not maximize our class time or really teach us much valuable content. They do not provide enough guidance throughout the semester or add much value to the projects at all. This class has added a tremendous amount of stress to my life. I was warned that it would be stressful, but thought that if I approached the course proactively and diligently, I would be able to avoid the horror stories I had heard from past students. I was wrong. Given the current format, the stress is unavoidable.

I would only say that I hope this course changes. It has so much potential, but unfortunately falls short. A hard maybe. The course is well run and an intense learning experience. Students need to understand that this is at its core a marketing course. If students are going into other fields outside cleantech or marketing, this course may be less relevant. Weigh this against C2Ms significant time commitment. However, if going into cleantech, I feel like this course is a must take if for the network of C2M alum and sponsors alone. Learnings are largely based on the specific team and technology you will be working on so choose wisely!

Without significant upgrades, I would have a difficult time recommending this course to a fellow student. With that being said, it is an awesome opportunity to dive deep into a clean tech-focused market. I learned A TON about the market my team was focused on (critical minerals), but wish there had been far more teachings on Go-To-Market strategy, project scoping, and other project management skills.

I would absolutely recommend this course to a fellow student. I feel that I gained a lot of really valuable experience, and that it was very much worth the effort. I feel that I am a better-rounded student now.
If you are interested in Climate Tech, this is a course that you have to take.

Mixed feelings.... depends a lot on the expectations students have. Hopefully students get a very real understanding of the class before enrolling. Maybe having panels with alumni could be helpful before round 1 bidding.
Not sure; I have mixed feelings about the course. We worked very hard, but there was little guidance or class lectures that made me learn from them.

I would not. I think there are easier and more educational ways to fulfill this learning and the applied innovation requirement. I think that there was just not a lot of learnings in class and that the experiences vary so widely by the project that I would pick a different course for a sure thing. If you need a project, there are other classes. If you want to learn this stuff, right now it is better to chat with faculty rather than sit through this whole class and project. I would absolutely not recommend this course unless one of the startups is exactly the type of company you are interested in. You will learn very little from the instructors about cleantech, start ups, business strategy, etc. The priority of the course is not student learning but putting on a summit that connects the instructors and the broader cleantech community. The most direct learning you'll do is I guess around how to present a powerpoint at a summit - not exactly what I signed up for.
The course is very poorly organized. The uses of BCourses was so confusing and the expectations around assignments and final deliverables was constantly shifting at the last minute.

I was also pretty unimpressed by the quality of the startups. Furthermore, because the priority of this course is not actually student learning but the final summit which is basically a pitch competition you don't actually get authentic engagement from the startups. Instead the startups are more or less pitching to you the whole time because they want to win the money more than they are interested in your learning. Remember that the financial awards presented at the summit go to the start ups not to to you so they want your free labor to make them look is as good as possible! On top of that, it is a ton of work. The market report and summit presentation is a huge lift but you will not be learning new tools to execute on it. Instead, you are asked to bring whatever skills you already have to perform free labor. Yes, if the student is a non-Business School student and if is particularly interested in getting a sense of how climate technology and business intersects. I would definitely mention that even the class connects you and your team with a startup, there will be a lot of business knowledge that students are supposed to know beforehand. Probably not really hard to get those knowledge over the semester, but definitely something to keep in mind.
Yes if they're really interested in diving deeper into climate tech companies and working with start-up for commercialization. It is a lot of work so it depends on the students willingness to commit!

Definitely recommend IF you are interested in Cleantech. But it requires a lot of work outside of the class Working on this course absolutely destroyed my fall semester, and as much as I'd like to say I learned a lot about clean tech and go to market, I didn't really learn about either of those things. The course is basically one giant consulting interview with an added bonuses of working with 4-5 other people (at least 2 of whom probably don't actually care about this class) and a 70+ page paper on the end. Do market sizing on 20 markets, select some of them, interview random people so that there's an air of legitimacy to the whole thing, then send the final result over to a startup that might appreciate it or might literally never look at it.

No, I don't recommend it. Like many incoming students passionate about cleantech, I was really excited about this class but ultimately I regret taking it. Previous students tried to warn us but I chose not to heed their feedback and even bid all my points to take this class; after the first few weeks it became apparent I made the wrong decision. The class was not worthwhile at all, in fact it made my semester difficult. We did not get much lecture content or learn much and were expected to basically teach ourselves while at the same time do work for the clients on such short and immense time pressure. Essentially we were paying our tuition to do free consulting work, except it isn't free we're paying to work for these startups.

sections.goodFor: Students seriously committed to climate tech who want hands-on commercialization work with a real startup, a multidisciplinary team (MBAs, PhDs, law, policy), and the C2M network and credential; also valuable for technical and non-Haas students learning market research, TEA, and presentation skills.
sections.notFor: Anyone casually interested or expecting classroom teaching; recurring warnings that you largely teach yourself, that the experience hinges on your team and startup draw, and that the workload can swallow a semester; some felt an internship would teach more for less effort.
sections.workloadNote: Extremely heavy by consensus; one student cited at least 5 hours/week for 15 weeks, others said it consumed 5-6 credits worth of time, with a 70+ page market report and summit presentation dominating the back half of the semester.
sections.redFlags: Recurring (10+ comments): workload far exceeds the 3 credits; little direct instruction, with lectures described as disconnected from the actual project work; outcomes vary heavily by team and startup assignment; multiple students across terms felt the course prioritizes the public summit over student learning and described the projects as unpaid consulting for the startups.
sections.quote: This is a LOT of work - but there is substantial value in deeply getting into a problem, working through it, building external connections, and potentially even finding jobs.
comments: This is a great course! It teaches you a lot of things from working with startups to market discovery as well as exposes you to a lot of ideas in the climate tech space. Definitely one of the heavier lifts in terms of workload but was rewarding!

I would recommend this course to students if they want to understand the reality of startup market research. The course is quite scrappy and the research and conclusions are never developed in absolute confidence, but one of my key learning from the course is that it really is like that outside of the course too. Teams learn and grow and never stop learning and growing.

I'm not a Haas student, but I recommend C2M if you're interested in the cleantech space and have at least 5 hours/week to spend on this class for 15 weeks. You get how much you invest in the class. It was particularly rewarding to work with PhDs and grad students pursuing other fields of study, and a nice intro to network with folks in the space. Would absolutely recommend this course if you're interested in climate tech or deep tech / hard tech start-ups in general. The course was especially helpful for non-Haas students, as it included lots of business frameworks, practice building slides and presentations, working with clients, etc.

I would recommend this course to a fellow student if they are looking for a broad overview into connecting research/technology with business development. While the course content itself is not challenging, the workload and time commitment does become extensive especially as you approach the end of the semester. You will be able to learn a lot of new business concepts and understand what can make or break a technology, which as a someone from a research background don't necessarily get exposure to normally. The class structure can sometimes make it difficult to see how all the pieces fit together, but process ultimately gets the students to where they need to be. The class is very much designed to be "you get what you put into it".

I would but only if they're willing to put in the time. Overall, it was a lot of work with some assignments that felt silly or unnecessary but I do think I got a lot out of it as someone who has never worked in the hard sciences. If you're interested in commercialization work at all, this class is necessary.
Yes! Incredibly value learning opportunity. In addition to learning about startups, it also felt like a great presentation/public speaking skill buillder
I would recommend it cautiously, for several reasons.
1) The workload is heavy.
2) Lectures and class deliverables feel somewhat disconnected from the actual market research you end up doing, but the actual work is very interesting.

3) The climate tech curriculum is interesting, and could have more promise if the guest speakers come with a prepared presentation — I feel I got more value out of the guest lectures that had presentations this semester.
4) Rehearsals for summit and feedback from instructors during in-class working session is quite helpful.
Yes! I would definitely recommend this course to students. It was a lot of work but I learned so much about my start up and market and generally the process of climate tech commercialization.

It is a good class and a great way to learn more about a industry that you're interested in. I recommend being really thorough with the startup selection (before class starts), as that can make or break your experience (I got the one I wanted and really liked it). It is also a lot of work, be prepared to email (and cold email) many, many people that you're interested in talking to.

If you're interested in clean tech / climate tech, you must take this course for the learning, the network you build, and the credibility it gives you in the climate tech community (yes, really). Provides great hands-on introduction to a wide range of skill sets -- market research, techno-economic analysis, storytelling for business, customer research. It requires a ton of work, which you won't want to (or really be able to) put off until the end of the semester, but you'll have learned a lot by the end of it. Delivering this material in a compelling fashion as a classroom experience is a tall order for the instructors given the sheer breadth pf the course -- and the tension with the need to dive deep in your individual startup -- but the faculty puts a ton of effort into making it work and brings the very relevant experience and network to bear to do so.
Yes. Definitely recommended. Think of this class as Lean Launchpad 2.0 on steroids focusing on deep-tech and climate sectors. The most rigorous Applied Innovation class I have ever taken

It's a lot of work for little return. You must be *really really* into climate tech to enjoy this class. One nice thing about this class is the multi-disciplinary team you get to work on with PhD's, Law students, and Public Policy folks and you get to view problems from multiple angles.

Yes I will particularly because of the overall experience and impact. particularly for technical students I believe is a great opportunity to get to understand how startups work and even how exactly it may mean working in a founder of a a startup and the dynamics of the real world experience. I would however be very specific on the demands of the course and notify them of the extra requirements of time they may have to devote to the course in the beginning of the semester

Working alongside a real-world startup to understand their technology and find where it fits in the larger market was great, but the course did not really set you up for success. Class time was spent more on high-level theories and frameworks than actionable advice or insights, the group project dynamic of the deliverables made it more stressful and contentious than it needed to be, and at the end of the day I'm confident I would have learned more and worked less if I'd just done an internship at a climatetech start-up instead.

I'd highly recommend this course to students who are interested in or want to learn more about climate tech. The alumni and startup network, together with the industry expert guest speakers are valuable resources that brought this class to a next level. To me, this is more of a "program" than a "course", in the sense that there are amazing networking opportunities with guest speakers each class and happy hours to connect with past alumni. C2M is also a high profile program in the climate tech space and adds credentials to your experience if you want to work in the space in the future.
es, I would recommend it. For students with a technical background, it provides an excellent opportunity to explore potential business avenues.

I would recommend this class. I learned a lot about the business world that I would never have gotten a chance to engage with in other classes. I really appreciate how many people we got connected to and how many resources I was offered while taking this class. I am also extremely grateful for all the instructor's time and effort put into organizing multiple guest speakers, the MetLife Coaches, the Summit, etc... I have never taken a class with this much dedication put behind it. It is very energizing to see that much passion and energy behind a graduate class, not many classes in other departments are like this.
