This class was a great opportunity to put myself outside of my comfort zone and develop additional communication, analytical, and presentation skills. I have never spoken to a room that big before so the summit was a really knew and exciting experience. I also very much appreciate Berkeley offering a class with a values driven goal, if this was a class about a generic tech start up as opposed to a climate tech related one, I would not have been as engaged. The overall emphasis on supporting companies that are finding solutions to serious climate issues makes this class very motivating and the experience very rewarding. I am sure the skills I developed in this class will prove useful in the future. I found most assignments to be valuable and instructive, although I felt that some deadlines were arbitrary and unhelpful. The multiple business model canvas assignments did not really help our team. The assignment we struggled with the most was the TEA by far. I hade never made one before and I think we weren't properly prepared in this class to build a satisfactory TEA so I felt very unfulfilled by this assignment. To be clear, I think it is a great thing to learn how to do and excellent material for the class, but I would have appreciated more time spent on how to develop one and possibly multiple checkins and feedback sessions on this assignment as well. Without a complete TEA I felt that the some of the subsequent economic modeling we did on promising markets was inaccurate. The example TEAs provided were very helpful.
I would not waste my money.
No, because not much more learning compared to just watching youtube videos at home.

I would not recommend this class to a fellow student as the lack of organization and unresponsiveness of the teaching team makes it challenging to understand the intended learning outcomes of the course.

I recommend the course if they have some curiosity in crypto and want exposure. However, they will learn primarily from their own research and some expert students vice the teacher. The class is not a huge time commitment which makes it easily accessible to all parties.
No. For such an interesting subject I feel let down.

I'd recommend it to someone who is genuinely interested in learning about crypto. Otherwise, get ready to hear all about it. This is not your typical finance class. The class does not have your typical financial framework, but is very topical.

Heavily focused on crypto/blockchain. and a pretty low life class if you're interested. Do not recommend if you're interested in other parts of fintech (credit, loans, etc.) as the course does not really touch on them

No, I would not recommend this course solely for the reason that it felt more like a finance course than a fin tech course. The information presented was great, but it was less about exploring the technology and more about lending and banking systems.

No. There are better ways to learn about fintech, crypto, and blockchain outside Haas. If the faculty don't modify how this class is performed, it doesn't make sense to take the course for a person who is not an expert and wants to get immersed in the industry.

This class explores decentralized finance topics. It's very interesting, but it's one of those classes where you have people that are new to crypto next to people that know everything about it. So it is complex to go from basic financial services concepts to complicated payments/lending systems.

Yes, this course is a good primer on blockchain/fin tech in general. You definitely get out of this course what you put in, so you should be prepared to pay attention in class and actively try to participate (you will not be forced to). I would not recommend this course because it does not really discuss FinTech outside of cryptocurrencies and DeFi. I would not recommend this course / instructor unless you are very interested in FinTech. The material is good and the professor is very knowledgeable, but the course structure and teaching style didn't help me learn the topics well. Yes. This course is a great introductory class for those who want to learn more about payment system, crypto world and get enough to dig deeper. Prior to the class, I traded, invested in various crypto assets, but this class peeled the onion layer by layer, week after week on each of those assets and gave me insights in to the underlying fundamental of those (e.g Bitcoin, Etherium, Solana, etc.). The presence of folks who are working in Fintech in the class, helped accelerate my learnings as the discussion was very healthy and professor encouraged a lot of class participation. This class is not traditional finance, doesn't have any frame works. For folks looking for some hard content and rigor with assignments, this is not the class to take.
Yes
Yes, I would recommend this class. Its a low life and Professor Parlour is a very understanding and knowledgeable professor.

This class focuses a lot on blockchain, so if students do not have any interest here then maybe they should not take this course. But otherwise any interest in Fintech I would recommend taking this class.
If they have a strong desire to learn about fintech technologies, I think this would be a solid choice for an introduction into the space.

I would recommend this class to students who are looking for a class with low workload or are looking for a career in the FinTech industry. Not sure if I would recommend this class for students who just want to broaden their horizons. If you are interested in the future of the financial industry, I would take this class.

I think this is a very valuable topic to be discussed that's not known well enough. I wish there were more people who attended the class consistently to help enrich the discussion but I think overall, SF is such a FinTech hub and it's great that we can learn more about interesting topics within blockchain, Web3, and Crypto.
Really interesting class and very well taught

rows.title: Interpersonal Skills and Embodied Systems Leadership

comments: Yes, I recommend ISEL to all fellow Haasies.

ISEL teaches a holistic system of how to relate internally to oneself and externally to others (and vice versa). I believe it's crucial (absolutely critical) to learn such skills especially since as top MBAs we are ascending into managerial roles at elite firms in our capitalistic society.

Now, many students have not had positive experiences in ISEL. I respect that, and I went into the class knowing those experiences are real, legitimate, and exist. Ultimately, in order to benefit from ISEL, it's important to go into it with an open mind, earnestly doing all the assignments, all the practices, and all the readings.

ISEL is not perfect. It has some minor flaws; particularly in how it presents itself as being tied to the GSB "touchy feely" class, which sets up an unmet expectation; a minority few of the methods Erica employ feel too unrelated to the course content; the all virtual format my cohort experienced can be difficult for some — but some prefer it, but its also unrealistic given that we don't conduct our lives entirely virtually (for now...); many of the assignments deal with intersectional identity, but we didn't cover enough of that in fishbowl T-groups; I think the "crash-course weekend" might be too tiring to have lasting learnings for some people.

There is no other class like this at Haas. Take it if you want to spend 30+ hours thinking about yourself and how you interact with the rest of the world. Erica has woven together disparate practices into a cohesive whole. I found it useful and enlightening.

This was the most transformative class I've taken at Haas. There is very distinctly a pre-ISEL period in my life as well as a post-ISEL period in my life. If you are open to the process and want to better self-regulate your emotions (as well as handle and take care of the emotions of people around you) I recommend this class. There is so much to be said about effective leadership coming from leaders that know how to self-regulate AND recognize the emotional experience of the people around them.
Course is probably one of the best at Haas in terms of a course that will actually teach you something and lead to professional growth.
Absolutely, this is one of the few classes where you learn an applicable skill.

I personally would recommend it to anyone who is open to actually examining and putting in the time to explore their own real identity, stress, anxiety, and goals in life. I am not exaggerating when I say that this course helped me rediscover what I believe to be my purpose and the meaning in life. I didn't come in thinking that would happen, but near the end session, I felt a wall inside me just fall down and realized how implicitly self-centered I had been throughout my whole life and what events informed that, and I realized I could make a conscious change to not let myself be defined by comparison & productivity. However I think this class comes down to how much you are able to put in (time commitment wise) and how open you let yourself be to evolving and changing. Every single person had different insights and takeaways and changes I think. So while I know this class is extremely polarizing, I found it valuable and perhaps the most memorable class I took at Haas because it caused me to re-conceptualize my own identity, self, priorities, anxieties, and how I see the world. For me, that's more valuable than a power & politics class that tells you how to win in the world / manipulate people in a nutshell haha. Because I feel like in my own happiness I have a framework to transcend a mentality where " i will only be happy if I have material success. " And that is freeing. On the other hand, this class is a lot of what can feel like busywork and journaling/writing, as well as reading, so it's not a commitment that can be made lightly. There's a lot of pre-work and post-work, and so it's not a 3-day seminar you can just show up, get insights, and leave. It requires substantial work on your own side, but setting aside that time for reflection helped me mostly (though I think it's maybe still a bit on the heavy side).
Absolutely. One of the best courses I've taken at Haas

No. I would not recommend this course AT ALL. This class was bizarre with numerous references to BTS as an example of embodied leadership. That did NOT resonate with the class. Part of the course curriculum was to watch a video of the instructor performing a BTS dance cover. The BTS fan base is teenage kids so for the instructor to be this into it did not feel appropriate. The use of emotion from the instructor felt manufactured and disingenuous. The exercises in class were not effective on Zoom and dragged on and on.
Yes I would, this class was really powerful in helping me develop my active listening and be aware of the emotions and physical sensations I am experiencing in the moment.
I would absolutely recommend this class for anyone looking to deepen their interpersonal skills and learn the tools for being a more empathetic and emotionally intelligent leader.

Yes - this was one of my most amazing classes I've taken at Haas. I think that it provides such a depth of personal and interpersonal learning outside of any class. This is not a business class but more so a life class. I think that I learned more about being a leader and being a strong human than any other class at Haas. This class does require you to take it very seriously to get the most benefit out of it plus honoring the effort your fellow students put into it. I would not take this class if you are not committed to showing up. I would take this class if you are looking to learn more about how you can connect more deeply with other people.

I highly highly highly recommend this course. I think it should be mandatory. The amount of connection built among the group in such a short time is incredible, I've struggled with connection and belonging my whole life and this course created a safe place to feel "buoyed" and held by others. This is such an emotionally driven course and some precaution should be taken as there are likely things under the surface that will come up. This course is really counter- culture and goes against the social conditioning we've had our whole lives. We talk about deeply personal things, we focus on deep listening and ensuring everyone feels heard. I can't think of a better example of what Haas stands for than this course, because this is the course that most exemplifies "confidence without attitude". Before taking it, I was interested to get someone else's feedback and shocked to learn that "they couldn't recommend it" because of some things that came up in their course. I feel sad knowing that valuable lessons were not taken away from that experience, because I know Erica would have done her best to encourage connection instead of disconnection. I can't recommend this course enough, it really was a powerful experience. The downside is that it's a lot of effort, these things take a lot of work. The homework is challenging and reflective and you will feel tired throughout the days of the workshop. But it is so worth it.

Yes - this course requires significant energy, but the material is very interesting and fulfilling. I would recommend this course for anyone who wants to have a positive impact on their team (and anyone around them, really), and wants to learn how to advocate for themselves and resolve conflicts for the long-term with mutual understanding and appreciation.

I learned a lot from group practicing where I would never have had the opportunity to practice otherwise. But there're just too many assignments -- before, during, and after classes. Sometimes, I feel overwhelmed by the mental energy put in this class, especially the 2nd week where we had day-long classes for 3 days.

I would highly recommend this instructor and course because to be quite frank, I feel now that I have the tools to improve the relationships I have and to form strong connections with the people I have yet to meet! Erica really allows you to explore and examine the factors that have shaped your identity, and she provides data-driven research related to the emotions that we feel. It's a wonderful class to take, and I truly have learned so many things that I'll keep with me for the rest of my life.

I would 100% recommend this class. This class can really change how to interact with families, friends, and colleagues. I would recommend this course, but I think it could be slightly better in person. Zoom gives way to not paying attention.
Wonderful course and instructor, Erica is great!
Came into this class dealing with some past trauma and some recent trauma, thought this course was just about communication, that's it.

But this course ended up being a powerful experience in which I was granted the rare opportunity to interact with strangers and classmates in a highly structured setting, and also ask tough questions of others. Ended up learning a great deal about myself!

Definitely recommend. After taking the course, I felt I have taken the first step on the journey to love myself before I can love others. This course will ask you to look inside, stretch and be vulnerable so only attend the course if you are ready to do that. The home assignments are huge so be ready for that too.

I DO NOT recommend the course. It could be fit for a psychology program but definitely not an MBA. I signed up for it to build "interpersonal skills" but I have gotten none of that. While the instructor was immersed in the methods and was dedicated to giving students a good learning experience, the content seemed very light and the

exercises/practices felt like a waste of time. I found it very hard connecting what I did during the course to any helpful skill or competence relevant to my journey as a business leader or career person.
The course seems to be overly focused on neurobiology, feelings and emotions, which I personally did not find helpful for my journey in becoming a business leader.
Also, if it has to be taught, then it may be best taught in-person.
Yes. The experiential portion of the class (almost 95% of it) really got me rethink about the way I approach people and life.

I would definitely recommend this course to other students with the caveat that they have to be genuinely curious about the material and content. The course is truly transformative for those that make the commitment to immerse themselves in the course content.

Depending on what stage you are in your leadership or professional development, this class might resonate with you. I went through many practices that were useful and explored concepts I had not done before.
Having said that, I felt we could have package more grounded, concrete learnings in this 2 unit course compared to other similar courses.

Not at all! This course had very little to no substance and was a sheer waste of time. The course description was so different from the content that was taught. this can be described as a breathing, dancing, distressing spiritual class. If you are on the verge of an emotional breakdown, perhaps this class can serve as a therapy session for you. Most folks in the class were surprised by the content. The professor shares some of her childhood memories, her love for dancing and a rock band (BTS) that she adores over and over. I am beyond flabbergasted how Haas even approved this class. It is a total waste for time and money. The only useless class I have ever taken at Haas. It was like being held hostage for 4 days for no reason. Please do yourself a favor by not enrolling for this class.

Yes...she reverse engineers connections. Makes you think of negatives cycles, and defines emotions and how to deal with them. As someone who never took a course like this, and was from a quantitative background, probably the coolest course at Haas I've ever met. Businesses, politics are all about managing relationships and this teaches you about the very human fundamentals of connection from neuroscience and psychology.
Yes! Especially as a career switcher without a quant background.
Sydnee will do her best to help you succeed. She teaches hard topics, so if you can put in the work, she will be there to help you win.

Yes, this was a great into to statistics and was not too intense for students getting used to being students again. If you have to take a statistics class, Professor Caldwell is a good professor for it. She provides a lot of support and extra resources to benefit students.

Yes I would. If you are a "poet" like me, Sydnee can help you understand the material because she cares how everyone does, not just the people who "get" the material or who have taken the class before

She was also super responsive to questions on our D&D slack channel and in class, and frequently provided extra material (video content, Excel practice etc) to help. She also did a great job of tying it back to real world examples, e.g. from her work with Uber or Steve's work at eBay. Super practical, and wish there was more time to practice these skills which are super important in most business contexts these days. One thing I recommend: actually keep up with all of the material! It's an easy class to get behind in and due to the pace, catching up later is not a good strategy!
Yes, knowing statistics and specifically how they apply in a business context is incredibly valuable.
Yes, because data literacy is a necessity for leaders of the future.

I recommend this course if you're looking to have a better understanding of the corporate sustainability reporting landscape and what to look for when evaluating companies on their sustainability. Professor Stormer has such deep experience in this space and was very clear in her approach.

This course is not for you if you're looking for practical application of theory and frameworks. As the course is currently designed, you can expect to receive a very high level overview of sustainability reporting, but little insight into how corporations actually collect and aggregate data.

If you already have a good working knowledge of sustainability accounting frameworks (e.g. if you can explain to someone what the SASB, GRI, TCFD, and CDP are, how they're distinct but complementary to each other, and why they're critical in advancing prograss in corporate sustainability practices), then you probably won't learn a ton from this course. But if those acronyms are just alphabet soup to you, and you're intrigued about these rapidly evolving standards and how metrics which can be compared across companies and industries will be essential in facilitating the green economy transition, this class will take you from zero to well-informed in less than a month. I came in totally clueless, so felt like it was well worth it.

Yes,very valuable insight which you would never be able to just teach yourself. However there were many confusing points in the class due to lack of clarity from the professor. If you dont have investing background you will need to spend some extra time familiarizing yourself with terminology or being careful with the problem sets.
Yes, but students need to be prepared to spend more time research and network after the class to learn more about the actual VC business

You get as much out of this class as you put into it. If you put little into it, you'll get a basic overview of the business of venture capital (spoiler alert: it's still a lot of luck and n-of-1 wins); if you put a lot into it, I think you can develop a great network starting with the professors and learn an interesting baseline that will help you start a career in venture (or better understand some of the questions VCS ask if you're thinking about entrepreneurship). If you're trying to deeply understand VC/ what VCs are looking for, you probably won't get all the way there with this course, but it's a good introduction if you're exploring/ just getting started.

I would recommend this course to a fellow student if Sean and Keval take a larger role in future iterations. I would highly recommend this course to fellow Berkeley students, including those not interested in entrepreneurship or venture capital. I believe this course substantially improved my understanding of the industry and I have a greater appreciation for the opportunities in Berkeley and the entire Bay Area. This is easily a top 2 course I have taken at Haas so far.

Highly recommend for anyone interested in either a career in VC or entrepreneurship or investing. This class has resulted in substantial learning to peak inside into the world of venture capitalists. A great class to take after the entrepreneurship class.
Yes

Yes, I would recommend this course - more for students whoa re interested in VC not PE. We did not spend alot of time on PE business model and strategy. This is a great balance of theoretical and practical course for students who are exploring a career in VC.
This was a great class and gave me a good overview of what VC world would be like

This was a nice class to take and get deeper into the VC and startup ecosystem. It was not necessarily what I expected, but I enjoyed the class and I think it gave me a more realistic view of the industry and it's challenges. It was not a class that boasted that everyone should be in VC/PE, and did talk frankly about challenges in the industry and what the future could hold. I would recommend it if you don't have internship or work experience in VC.

Yes I would. This class is a comprehensive intro to VC and has extremely well prepared content and guest speakers. It teaches you not only the basic stuff such as term sheet and valuation, but also give you an overall picture about the entire VC industry and help you understand the dynamics. Instructors often hold partner's meeting in class to discuss about the pros and cons of a deal and your argument about it. Some of the guest speakers are very helpful as well - they are from different background and worked in different stages of VC firms.

I learned a lot since I have no prior experience in the VC industry. However, I believe it could have been a 2 unit course rather than a 3 unit course, and it could have been more concise. If you are at all interested in working in the VC industry, then I would recommend it as you will make important contacts and introductions in the industry. Yes, useful class if you aren't familiar with VC and if you want to learn more. Workload isn't too crazy for a 3-unit class. I would recommend this course. It took a few lectures to get into it, but the lectures, discussions, and guest speakers were very informative. The course is lighter on theory but the discussion and speakers are rich (both in bank account and educational value). It is a good way to bring together learnings from other classes and enjoy yourself while you learn.
Yes
Heartily recommend this course. One of the best courses at Haas.

Yes. The class has an amazing amount of breadth and is good at presenting what it's like to pursue a career in VC. The industry itself can be very ambiguous, so don't expect any black and white solutions or career paths, but it's very thought provoking.

Yes. The course is really good for anyone who is interested in learning about the VC field. The course covers all the aspects of the VC business. The combination of relevant cases and relevant speakers makes the whole experience really great. I highly recommend this course.
I would recommend this course if you are interested in learning about VC/PE, though I would not recommend this course if you are interested in learning how to get into VC/PE.
Absolutely! Gives a great insight and understanding on how VC evaluate opportunities and make the deal flow work from start to end. Any one focusing on entrepreneurship or VC should take this class.
For an overview kinda course, it suffices. But you don't learn a lot more, especially on the valuation side. Very good guest speakers though

Yes, I would absolutely recommend as this class is very informational and fun. Almost everyone, no matter you want to become a VC or not, should probably take this course because you will apply the knowledge from this class
somewhere in your career and investment.
Yes - a great foundational course for a typical opaque industry in order to learn enough to be able to teach yourself more complex topics

I came from a non-VC, non-financial background and I enjoyed the course. It gave me a summary of how investments and the VC world works which I think is helpful in B-school so that we can make the decisions if this is something we want to do long term or not. I also really appreciated all the guest speakers the instructors chose and brought in as they came from diverse backgrounds and provided very good context and supplement to class instruction. Overall, I would recommend this class.

Mixed feelings about this class- While they bring in cool speakers who are great VCs, the class itself has outdated cases from the 90s and early 2000s. Hence, it is not completely representative of today's VC market. I wish the class also focused on what it means to be a good VC- how do you ask proper diligence questions? Maybe they can bring in actual startups for us to ask live questions from the CEO
I would recommend this class if you want an intro to VC/PE. If you are already in this space, then this might not be a class for you. Either way, be prepared to do a lot of reading.

Recommend this class for anyone looking to get a foundational understanding of Venture Capital. The class is the best structured class I've taken at Haas given three faculty members. All three (Sean, Terry, Keval) are very knowledgeable and bring a different aspect to the course. Your venture team matters for most of the class so choose wisely. Yes. All 3 are fantastic and among the best I've had at Berkeley Haas.

Yes, especially if you want to pursue a career in VC. About Private Equity, understood as LBO, the class has nothing. Also, the class is very interesting if you want to be an entrepreneur because you meet several VC managing partners who explained us trends, targets and investment thesis that are very useful to raise money.

It's definitely a different vibe compared to other Haas classes (participation is 35% the final grade and case method is better in theory than in practice; also, VCs in general probably think a little too highly of themselves), but overall it was a worthwhile course. Fantastic lineup of guest speakers (Lauren Kolodny from Acrew, Byron Deeter from Bessemer, Paul Kwan from General Catalyst, to name a few), Sean/Keval/Terry have a ton of experience and great
insights/thoughts about the VC industry overall, and I did end up learning a lot about VC.

Would definitely recommend this course if you're interested to get a crash course and learn about venture capital. The workload was a little more than most classes, but I genuinely understood venture better through this class. The professors brought in PHENOMENAL speakers and have been personally helpful. I got a lot from the class but will caveat it doesn't necessarily prep or hone you to do a venture Associate / Sr Associate / Principal role - you'll still need to figure that out elsewhere

Absolutely. I'm a (hopeful) entrepreneur with a startup operator background and took this class to understand how the other-side of the investment table thinks. It delivered on that and was highly engaging every minute with some life lessons sprinkled in as well.
Yes would definitely recommend to students interested in venture capital.
Yes

I would recommend this course to you only if you are really passionate about VC or are very interested to understand the world of VC. This course is definitely has a high workload and is much more discussion oriented. If you think you will learn a lot around valuation, financing, more technical skills - then you will be disappointed. There is some elements of it but it is only touched upon. Overall great course if you are new/wanting to develop a deeper understanding of the VC space.
Very valuable course, highly recommended. It is 100% VC - do not expect PE.

It depends. If you want to break into VC or if you already work in VC, this is an extremely valuable class. For the rest, if you're just interested in VC but don't want to make a career out of it, I would not recommend this class. It gets pretty technical at times, some assignments are the very heavy lift and my general perception is that the instructors expect you to come up with extremely insightful comments, that are hard to make if you don't have previous experience in the space.

Participation is essential to this class. They keep track of participation and will cold-call people who haven't participated recently (which I did not appreciate, it felt like there were putting people on the spot too often and that the expectations were too high).
Overall, good class for people that are really into VC, not recommended otherwise.

Highly recommend, even if you don't have experience in this industry. Instructors are well prepared for case discussions and really try to get you to think and develop points of views. Speakers are insightful and a big part of the class experience.

Yes! This was the best course I took this semester. It was a really helpful, practical intro to VC and covered a wide range of very practical topics (e.g., term sheets, valuation, etc.). The professors were great and brought in a really amazing set of guest speakers from different VCs. Classes were engaging (attendance and participation expected) and the assignments were very well designed to consolidate learnings.

I would only recommend it to people who have worked in VC before - it seems like the entire class had already worked in VC, and the playing field was not level at all. There was no basic intro to the concept of PE and VC, and many of my peers felt lost in class.
Yes - great class and learned a lot.

sections.goodFor: Repeatedly called one of the best classes at Haas for anyone targeting VC or planning to raise from VCs as a founder; commenters praise the three-instructor team (each bringing a different angle) and a guest speaker lineup cited as worth the class by itself. Works for beginners and experienced VC folks alike, per multiple commenters.
sections.notFor: Despite the title there is essentially no private equity or LBO content, so skip it if PE is your goal. Several students without a finance or VC background felt lost, and those wanting deep technical valuation training or casual observers unwilling to carry the heavy, participation-driven load were disappointed.
sections.workloadNote: Heavier than a typical MBA elective: a case per class, substantial reading, and assignments several called hard, though most felt the work translated directly into learning.
sections.gradingBasis: Participation weighs heavily (one student cites 35% of the final grade), with case discussions, cold calling, problem sets, and a venture team component.
sections.redFlags: Recurring (5+ comments): no PE content despite the course name; recurring (4+ comments): assumes VC/finance background and newcomers can feel lost; a few (3): cold-calling and participation pressure felt excessive; isolated: outdated cases from the 90s/2000s, assignments disconnected from class.
sections.quote: Very valuable course, highly recommended. It is 100% VC - do not expect PE.
comments: I would ABSOLUTELY recommend this class to a fellow student. It is a lot of work, relative to other MBA classes, and Sean's teaching style is intense and may not be for everyone. I recommend this class to anyone interested in VC and even those who have already worked in VC. This class goes deep enough into the details to be practically useful to those going into VC. Sean is additionally one of the best and most engaging lecturers I have had at Haas.
Emphatically, yes

Very valuable class that teaches you a lot about venture capital. The assignments are hard and not necessarily tied to in class work so that is frustrating. But this is the most engaging high energy night class I've taken at Haas. Cold calling and lots of participation required.
Yes, only if they want to enter VC or raise funds from a VC.
Yes, this class was extremely worthwhile. If you want to learn about venture capital this class is a must. One of the best classes offered in the entire MBA program.

Absolutely! This class was really insightful for someone not coming from a VC background. The cases, lectures, and assignments were well structured and lead to meaningful learning. Sean/Keval et al are also fantastic professors to teach this. They bring decades of expertise and insights which adds value to this class. One of the big value adds to this class is the amount of guess lecturers and speakers - this made lectures dynamic and their insights provided alternative viewpoints and approaches.

I would definitely recommend this course to any aspiring Venture Capitalist / Entrepreneur as it teaches you the A-Z of Venture Capital. The guest speakers are incredible and the frameworks Sean teaches are invaluable - especially with regards to Term Sheets and Valuation!

Yes! Even if you aren't interested in a career in VC, the frameworks for evaluating investment opportunities are extensible. Workload is a little on the heavier side but all the assignments resulted in substantial learning No, if you don't have sufficient VCPE background. Sometimes, I found it hard to keep up with the pace of the lecture as lecturers dive right into calculations without providing basic foundations.

Would wholeheartedly recommend this instructor and course to anyone interested in VC. This class resulted in tangible learning outcomes that would not have been possible without taking the course, and the exposure to guest speakers, internship announcements, and related opportunities is unparalleled across Haas' course offerings. Definitely yes, if you are interested in VC, starting a startup or generally learn a lot about the VC and innovation ecosystem.
Yes, I highly recommend this class! It was my first elective, but the best class so far. It is very applicable to my day-to- day work.
With instructors' hands-on experience and extensive connections in the industry, the course is very engaging and can result in significant learning.
YES
Simply the best class at Haas.

EW295B provides a strong overview of how venture capital works, though you will need some prior knowledge of venture capital to truly get the most of out the class. The course moves quickly and covers a lot of content, and is filled with a a number of insights and speakers from across the industry. Highly recommend for those who want to pursue Entrepreneurship in particular, as it is useful primer for seeing fundraising from the other side of the table. Yes

I would definitely recommend this class. I leave having a much more foundational understanding of the VC industry that I did coming in. However, we do cover some very specific, though relevant, details of VC and a baseline knowledge of the industry would have helped. The beginning of the class felt just like so much content to understand and absorb rather than expanding on knowledge I already possessed.
Absolutely, this is the course to come to Haas MBA for. Exposure, knowledge and experience.

Such an amazing class! I can't believe how good this was. You should definitely take it regardless of your experience in VC (I have 4 years of direct experience and loved it as much as my friend that has no prior experience) if you are interested in the industry.

If you're looking to get into VC, this is definitely the course to do it. If you're in VC and want to learn more or get more external expertise, I would. New to VC myself, I learned a TON here, especially because of the guest speakers bringing in a macro and varied VC perspective. Sean and Keval are knowledgeable SMEs and enthusiastic about the topic. It is a good bit of work, but value adding.
Yes — I'm leaving with a solid understanding of VC and have a new roster of folks that I might be able to approach when I start something.
Strongly recommend! One of the best course in Haas.
Yes, for someone who comes from a purely operating background this was a great preview into the workings of the VC world
Best class I have taken at Haas. The outside speakers alone are worth the class but Sean and team are engaging and their polish made me excited to attend lecture.
Yes! I learned a lot in the class and this is one of the best classes at Haas.
Yes, if you're interested in venture capital, this is the class for you.
Yes I would, I consistently enjoyed going to class. Expect that this class is wide and not deep, but I did feel like I got a lot out of the class
yes, I think this is a good, starting class for those who want to learn VC from the scratch

Yes, this was a top 3 Haas course for me. Sean and Keval are so enthusiastic about VCPE and every class is buzzing with energy. Sean really cares about his students and wants them to learn and grow in their careers. The guest speakers come from a wide breadth of backgrounds (varying types of investment stages and industries, and plenty of female speakers) and allows students to connect with those working in the industry. I'd retake this class again in a heartbeat.

This is a fairly advanced course so you should only take it if you want to go into VC or be an entrepreneur who will work with VC's. Everything in the class is about how be a successful VC, run a VC firm, and make good investments. There is nothing on private equity or other areas of finance in general. So it's the perfect class for any wanna-be VC's and entrepreneurs.
Awesome class
Yes, course was a great way to learn and understand VC through course work and weekly guest speakers.

Yes, this was one of my favorite courses at Haas so far. I had no background in VC and learned a ton. Expectations are high (one case per class, occasional cold calling), but for me it was worth it. Sean is really engaged and clearly loves teaching. There are also a ton of great high-level guest speakers.

The professors were friendly and approachable. However, to be honest, this is the worst course that I've ever taken throughout undergrad, a Master's program, and now the MBA. The course objectives were poorly defined and going into the final exam, I have no idea what to expect. The way that R was incorporated into this 7-week course was completely haphazard, so the homeworks had basically zero learning benefit. The group project allowed for some creativity, but had limited learning benefit for me as well. I don't understand why there were two instructors for such a short course, either. The case studies were interesting to discuss, but apart from that, this course was highly disappointing. The instructors and program office need to completely re-evaluate this course on its own and within the context of the core curriculum, especially if Haas wants to market this course as a point of difference between us and the competitors.

Not really. Half of the class and great portion of the assignments are dedicated to things not core to the learning. Would not recommend this course. As someone who doesn't know how to code, I was interested in learning how to code, but found it difficult to navigate coding amongst other concepts introduced. I would prefer to either make this a semester long course or have the course be focused only on 1) concepts or 2) coding.

This class is trying to do too much in 1 semester. Split between 2 professors, spending half our time on R yet not tested on it, splitting class in half between causal and predictive questions, etc. It is clear that Haas still has not settled on an effective format for delivering these critical subjects to students.
Yes, data and ML concepts are highly important, especially for tech-oriented leaders.
Instructors are great, course needs some help. I believe this material belongs in the core, but with some major structural changes.
Yes if they improve the course structure and learning objectives.

No. As it is, the class is somewhat unclear and unfocused on the core objectives - are we supposed to learn how to code, or understand the broad principles of data analytics, or learn how to apply business analytics solutions to business problems. Right now, it seems like it is trying to do all 3 without a clear structure. This leaves students confused and disengaged.
The instructors are good but I do not recommend this course until it has a structural overhaul and deeper thought is given to the curriculum and course objectives

I'm not sure...I wonder if it would make more sense to do a 2-day coding workshop (perhaps in python or sql) and then the course on data analytics theory/strategy. Could also be interesting to know how to interpret data that we're presented with (i.e. identify where people may have gone wrong in their own setups)
Yes, but it needs to be changed (this is for Conrad, I do not think Jonathan was as good at explaining)

I would not recommend this class as it is. I could imagine an intro to Data Analytics class that was a beginner version of Intro to Coding for MBAs which I've heard is fantastic, or a more conceptual intro, but trying to go deep on both was totally impossible. Only a handful of people I spoke to felt that they were able to stay engaged in lab and really get anything out of those experiences. Jonathan and Conrad are both kind, well-meaning and helpful professors who were willing to answer questions after class. The content in lectures is useful and interesting but the labs were presented/framed in a way that was very difficult to learn from.
No, it did not result in substantial learning and only covered very basic knowledge rather than true application of the concepts / data analysis.

I would not recommend this course as is. They have still not figured out what the learning outcome for the course is, and it is poorly balanced with more work geared towards R programming than learning business applications of data analytics. Do yourself a favor and get good at CTRL+C, CTRL+V,CTRL+Enter.
I'll definitely recommend!
Yes on teacher - no on course. We need a full semester for this to stick (or a focus only on code)

Yes, but I think there needs to be a better link between R and the class content, it felt weird that we did so much R but it was mostly copying/pasting from lab and the point of the class was "not to learn R" - I think we need to explain the link and why we're doing R and the learning objectives more clearly
No. I feel like all of the content could be gained by an afternoon of youtube. I mean, there was literally a lab that recommend watching a youtube video to understand the course material.
Absolutely yes, partly because I value this subject.
Thank you Conrad! 100% would recommend.
No. I learned nothing, and it's so sad because I was excited to learn data analytics.
Yes for students with no data analytics background
yes
I would recommend Conrad as an instructor, but I'd recommend that Haas gets RID of this course as a core class. It was not applicable to my goals and was way too far out of my comfort zone.
yes this professor was good, but not the course
Yes
I think this class has potential but I would prefer to recommend a class that offers a high lever overview of data analysis tools rather than such a deep dive in one, less useful one.
Yes, I learned a lot about data analytics and how to approach real problems
Maybe. I think the course touches several concepts, applications, and softwares but has thus far not helped me build confidence to deeply understand any specific topic.
Interesting course to understand prediction and causal inference problems. A mix of theory and practice (through lab sessions and final project). Dynamic classes and cool topic!
Yes, Conrad was a great teacher!
Yes, interesting perspectives and application of data analytics.
Yes, I would definitely recommend Conrad as a professor.
Yes, passionate and clear.
Yes! Conrad May be the best professor I've had at Haas
I enjoyed Conrad as a professor - I think this class has room for improvement, but felt like I learned a lot that will be useful in understanding and interpreting data analysis in the future
I would recommend Conrad but I would not recommend this course. The R labs are useless and the Data content is too advanced to be a core course
Yes I would, I think if you are interest in this hard topic you can take full advantage of it.
Yes, Definetely

Yes a good class to take if you are interested in using data in a business context...and you probably will! Good learnings. Pacing is a bit fast. Wish we slowed down and covered fewer topics a bit more in depth.

For students semi-familiar with statistics (and retained enough knowledge from Data & Decisions) and have some familiarity with code, data & analytics is a good primer to machine learning and casual inference for practical applications. Jupyter notebooks are pretty common in practice, especially in smaller scale organizations, and it was good that people got exposure to this and R. There were some initial technical issues with the server labs and R isn't the most common language used in industry (not far behind), but I think it's a good introduction to the practical side of analytics.
I would absolutely recommend the course, as everyone needs to have a certain understanding of this.

I would recommend this class as it is right now to a student who has experience using R. I would recommend the non- lab version of this class to anyone, as I think the theoretical applications are very useful to future business endeavors. I would definitely recommend this class, but I would suggest that you need to put the work from the very beginning to be able to understand R software and its applications.
Remove the Lab/coding portion
I would definitely recommend - Conrad is very clear and easy to learn from.
Yeah I would
Yes
And I think this course would make more sense if data and decisions had gone better
I felt like we were learning five classes at once

The course as it is structured right now could use some improvements, because I think many students have given up on it and are fully reliant on their study teams. But it is absolutely a foundational course, especially as new AI technologies like ChatGPT immediately change the professional and educational landscape.
I would not. The course objectives were to learn how to interact with someone in the workplaces who codes/does data science work, and there should be better uses of our time to achieve that same goal
i think the concept is very relevant to real world situations but it was a lot of lecture materials
Would recommend the instructor, but not the course. I hope the program office makes changes to how this course is taught
Yes! The material is valuable for almost everyone's jobs.
Yes, I enjoyed the real-world examples related to analytics.
Yes. Great class to gain baseline knowledge of data analytics.

Absolutely not. Students should not have to waive out of this course - this course should just not exist. This course is entirely a waste of my time. This class had no reason to be a mandatory core class. Would require eliminating for ALL students in future years. This course could not decide if it was a coding class (we had R-labs, but were NEVER taught how to code and just wasted hours in a program where the script was already written and we just had to "run" it). No, unless required or if the format changes a lot
Very ambiguous course
Not recommend

No. There is no practical application or learning in this course. I don't think I have learned or improved in any material way.

If you have a strong coding (R) or analytics background, I'd recommend waiving this course. It gives a good overview of analytics techniques but I think that if you already have a background in this, your time might be better spent on an elective.

I would not. The course content and application were very disconnected and I unfortunately do not think I learnt much as part of the class. A complete overhaul for future cohorts is highly recommended.

Yes, I would recommend this course and instructor. It was very interesting to learn about causal models! I would not recommend this course. I would potentially recommend the instructor to a student who was interested in taking a small-sized data science elective.

I would not recommend this course as it is. I think the structure and content needs to be further refined. Conrad seems to be a great professor but a little bit slow-paced. The content of Data Analytics should be more advanced and application-focused.

I don't know. I can't promote or condemn any professor performance in this class. The class lacked intent... and I don't know if that blame lays on the professors or on the academic office.
Professor is knowledgeable and with some course changes I would recommend.

No. This is the one of the worst core classes at Haas and that's saying something.

The class - generally speaking, no. The content of this class is too redundant since we also have the AI requirement. It's a good workshop, just not worth my time given that I have already been exploring entrepreneurship, innovation, and design. It's a lot of what ifs and not a lot of action. And I honestly don't think it was worth the time that I put into it while I was simultaneously in other innovation classes. The concept and practice of design thinking should be core to MBAs but it shouldn't be a core class or should be offered right in the beginning when you get here.

In this class actually, I had an epiphany. DT talks about how to collect data and maybe that should come before Data & Decisions that talks about analyzing data. no, i would not. unfortunately, it felt like i was checking off boxes versus actually learning. i was really looking forward to this class and felt let down by the content, project restrictions, and do not think i learned anything substantive. i would have rather spent the time working on my own business and/or learning a new skill.
I would recommend this course and instructor to a fellow student who is looking to get into Project Manager because this course provides practical lessons for solving complex problems.

This class was an interesting overview of the design thinking process. It was helpful to try out the process by working with a team on a real project, but at the end of the semester I feel like the class could be taught in many fewer sessions.
Instructor yes, course no.
No. Felt like it was too vague of a course.

I love the topic of design thinking, but I would not recommend this class to anyone. If someone wanted a basic intro on design thinking, I would send them to the interactive design foundation website. No, I would not recommend Mariana. She brought a lot of enthusiasm to each class, but she was a poor instructor overall. She could strengthen her teaching and the course as a whole by learning more about design thinking. There were questions she answered that didn't necessarily put the user at the front and center, which is the primary principle of design thinking. She also responded to a student's question by saying that we as designers can tell the user what our opinions are around an idea or influence their thinking during co-creation - this is inaccurate and does not represent the design thinking mindset, which is all about going in with a beginner's mindset and asking the user what he/she/they think. As researchers, we are supposed to leave our opinions at the door. Marianna could also do better to explain concepts and exercises; she essentially leaned on GSIs to facilitate exercises (who also were not trained well and seemed to want us to operate in a cookie-cutter fashion, such as correcting our team with 'you need to write your themes starting with an 'I' sentence', to which you don't in a professional, real life setting).

Overall, this course was an incredible disappointment as someone who has done design thinking professionally and has taken a course in undergrad, because it was poorly structured and lacked any sort of substance. If design thinking is going to be taught in 5-6 classes that are 2 hours each, it needs expert facilitation and instruction, where students are told how they should be thinking, what they should be doing, and why they're doing it. Exercises should be realistic for the time frame - we shouldn't be trying to attempt a whole 'design thinking project' in this short amount of time, when students don't even understand what design thinking is, let alone how it's applied. This course barely helped students understand the purpose of design thinking, why it's important (how it became revolutionary) in the corporate and startup context, and how it has evolved into broader innovation/product teams. It's a shame the course was structured and taught the way it was because it shed such a negative light on such an important methodology and mindset for MBAs.
I think it could be condensed into a quicker class, like a 2 day workshop or something. I think the learning is helpful, but it doesn't need to be such a long drawn out process.

This was the most transformative class I've taken at Haas. There is very distinctly a pre-ISEL period in my life as well as a post-ISEL period in my life. If you are open to the process and want to better self-regulate your emotions (as well as handle and take care of the emotions of people around you) I recommend this class. There is so much to be said about effective leadership coming from leaders that know how to self-regulate AND recognize the emotional experience of the people around them.
Absolutely, this is one of the few classes where you learn an applicable skill.

I personally would recommend it to anyone who is open to actually examining and putting in the time to explore their own real identity, stress, anxiety, and goals in life. I am not exaggerating when I say that this course helped me rediscover what I believe to be my purpose and the meaning in life. I didn't come in thinking that would happen, but near the end session, I felt a wall inside me just fall down and realized how implicitly self-centered I had been throughout my whole life and what events informed that, and I realized I could make a conscious change to not let myself be defined by comparison & productivity. However I think this class comes down to how much you are able to put in (time commitment wise) and how open you let yourself be to evolving and changing. Every single person had different insights and takeaways and changes I think. So while I know this class is extremely polarizing, I found it valuable and perhaps the most memorable class I took at Haas because it caused me to re-conceptualize my own identity, self, priorities, anxieties, and how I see the world. For me, that's more valuable than a power & politics class that tells you how to win in the world / manipulate people in a nutshell haha. Because I feel like in my own happiness I have a framework to transcend a mentality where " i will only be happy if I have material success. " And that is freeing. On the other hand, this class is a lot of what can feel like busywork and journaling/writing, as well as reading, so it's not a commitment that can be made lightly. There's a lot of pre-work and post-work, and so it's not a 3-day seminar you can just show up, get insights, and leave. It requires substantial work on your own side, but setting aside that time for reflection helped me mostly (though I think it's maybe still a bit on the heavy side).

Yes, I recommend ISEL to all fellow Haasies.

ISEL teaches a holistic system of how to relate internally to oneself and externally to others (and vice versa). I believe it's crucial (absolutely critical) to learn such skills especially since as top MBAs we are ascending into managerial roles at elite firms in our capitalistic society.

Now, many students have not had positive experiences in ISEL. I respect that, and I went into the class knowing those experiences are real, legitimate, and exist. Ultimately, in order to benefit from ISEL, it's important to go into it with an open mind, earnestly doing all the assignments, all the practices, and all the readings.

ISEL is not perfect. It has some minor flaws; particularly in how it presents itself as being tied to the GSB "touchy feely" class, which sets up an unmet expectation; a minority few of the methods Erica employ feel too unrelated to the course content; the all virtual format my cohort experienced can be difficult for some — but some prefer it, but its also unrealistic given that we don't conduct our lives entirely virtually (for now...); many of the assignments deal with intersectional identity, but we didn't cover enough of that in fishbowl T-groups; I think the "crash-course weekend" might be too tiring to have lasting learnings for some people.
I would absolutely recommend this class for anyone looking to deepen their interpersonal skills and learn the tools for being a more empathetic and emotionally intelligent leader.

This course is a great capstone of interpersonal leadership courses at Haas. The professors are incredibly nice and supportive.
