Yes, if their background is not in economics. The content is relevant and gives a basis on which to build on for managerial decision making (and pricing)
Yes, would recommend - challenging but will learn a lot, not worth avoiding because it is hard
Yes
Yes - as said before one, he has a wealth of knowledge and can really learn a lot from him.
I would recommend the class overall.
Highly recommended
The course definitely, the instructor not so much!
No I would not.

Absolutely because the way the professor explains the importance of the topics is the most important takeaway I would recommend Professor Feldman, but would also recommend that you have foundational economics knowledge or are prepared to work quite diligently to understand the content. The class moves very quickly and covers a lot, but the office hours and other review materials are helpful. Sven comes off more tough than he is and I would recommend getting to know him better and you will have a much more lovely time in the class.
Demonstrated commitment to learning and improving
Yes, absolutely! I'd also encourage them to ask Prof. Feldmann for more material that pertains to his CSR expertise and how that relates to economics.
I think this class was important but it was very hard and the lecturing style means you have to put in a lot of work to this class in order to try and understand

Micro is a pretty challenging course, even with prior experience on the subject matter. However, I do feel like of all the economics classes I've taken since undergrad, I probably learned the most in this one — especially after the class got more on the same page with Prof. Feldmann after the midway point.

No. I am pretty upset that my hard earned tuition dollars are going towards classes like this one with professors who can't figure out how to convey complex concepts in an applicable way. Professor Feldmann teaches this class as if you've majored in Econ and are ready to get started on your Econ PhD. I can't say that I learned anything of substance, which is a shame because this class has the potential to be engaging and useful.
I wouldn't necessarily recommend - I thought the style of teaching made the course harder than the concepts themselves.
Would be hesitant, since I think there are easier ways to produce the same value
I would recommend the professor, only in the case the student will have enough time to do readings and pre work before class

I would recommend this course and instructor. While Professor Feldmann's teaching style does not resonate with everyone, I found him to be an extremely knowledgeable professor that cares deeply for students' understanding of the material.
I think this course is fundamental part of the Haas curriculum and Sven pushed us through difficult concepts successfully. Thanks Sven
Absolutely!
Yes, I think this course is a great introduction to economics for anyone who has not learned the concepts before Yes, great learning experience.

I think this course and its concepts are extremely critical for a business education and decision-making. Sven will challenge you and push you to develop a strong point of view and develop stronger intuition and skills around the subject. I strongly recommend this course.
Yes, this class provides quite basic theory that all business people should be equipped with.
N?A
Yes, but I would brace them for impact. This is probably the hardest Fall A core class.

Probably not, he clearly deeply understands the topic but is not great at making the concepts easy to understand and accessible to students without a quantitive background. I found a lot of it hard to follow, but when I looked up the content on my own and read other sources I found it easier to understand

If he continues to make changes like he has the second half of the course, and incorporates practices problems into his teachings, then yes. I greatly admire and respect him especially for how he listened to our feedback and then genuinely made changes in response.
It is one of the most important courses in business school. not sure how a business leader can thrive without knowing what we saw in this course
I would, referring to how the second half of the course went.
I don't know. I found the most interesting part of the course is making a decision tree and finding the optimal price. If you are not interested in this two parts, maybe you can waive it
Absolutely NOT!
Sven is miles away from the Haas core values. I cannot understand why is the academic team at Haas is keeping Sven even after people are clearly not happy with his teaching style.
If it were not for the GSI, no one would have understood anything.

Sven was incredibly understanding of our class when we came to him with issues and adapted his teaching style accordingly. Our class greatly appreciated this and recognize his commitment to our learning. This class does, in my opinion, over-index on algebra, especially for an MBA course. Most of the homework and exams revolves around our ability to set up and solve algebra problems. I'd enjoy this class much more if we focused on conceptual applications of economics rather than plugging and chugging through math problems.

Yes, this would equip anyone with more of an economical way of thinking, particularly in the context of thinking at the margin, realizing opportunity cost, and better understanding pricing mechanisms.
Yes, definitely.

I really like the experience this class provided and would recommend it. I wish there were more technical components. If the technologies were broken down into categories and there was technical instruction tailored to those categories, I would have learned much more. Technical learning was limited to personal research and interviews.

This class has the potential to be really great, however it currently isn't. The instructors seem to be holding onto the past and haven't adapted the class to the boom that the cleantech industry has experienced in the last few years. The course is disorganized (their bcourses needs a big update) and the technologies selected are not similar enough to have one set of content for the course (software vs deeptech & hardware at very different TRLs). There needs to be more cases, possibly bringing in entrepreneurs that have actually commercialized hardware/deeptech

cleantechnologies because there are quite a few now and that would help us structure our learning. The focus on "beachhead" markets seems difficult when some technologies are still at the lab-scale and others are already being sold to consumers. They might consider hiring a GSI to help them with this. There is too much focus on the presentation vs the market report because the presentation is public facing and helps fundraising, which feels a little misaligned.
Maybe. Your experience depends on a lot of factors: the startup you work with, your team, your ability to plan and organize in advance.

The course is A LOT of work. I was putting at least 10 hours every week into it, and sometimes it feels like it's just not worth it. This is also not a class where you will learn something--there are no lectures or cases and there are barely any reading--but it's more learning by doing. You learn a lot about the markets of your startup, and some of it might be replicable for a very early stage startup. I think you can have a good experience if everything aligns and you have luck, but you still have to be aware that this course is really a lot of work.

Maybe. I really enjoyed the class and found I learned a lot. That said, it's challenging (which could be good or bad depending on who you are), requires a decent amount of work, and can be hit-or-miss depending on the

company/founders you match with (and not everyone gets their first choice). I came into this class without any energy/cleantech background, more interested in the entrepreneurship aspect of the class (namely, finding a good beachhead market), and it ended up being a great fit for me. I don't think "I'm interested in cleantech" equals "I must take Cleantech to Market"; it's more about if you're interested in early-stage startups and finding a market for a new technology.

This class is very much focused on group work and whether your experience is good or bad is highly contingent on your team (including your ability to work together) and the company you've been assigned. The instructors are helpful for high-level discussions and guidance on business models, thinking about applications of tech, preparing for the symposium, etc.

You should not if you are not interested in the topics. You need to expect to manage team dynamics properly since there are both students who have strong interests (and commitment for the time) and less interests.
I do not take class again. This class should be 5 units class in stead of 3. Just too much and learned almost none for a person who was in cleantech industry like me.

I would recommend it if you are interested in the climate tech space. It was a ton of work and stressful, but I am definitely glad I did it. The middle of the class was a grind when you didn't know what market you could present, but looking back, it was all worth it. It was great to have people outside of Haas on my team to get to know them and get their insights on the technology.
Absolutely would recommend to non- Haas students. So much learned this semester and one of the most rewarding classes taken at Berkeley

I would recommend the course with the caveat that it is highly catered toward pitching and showman ship and less so toward detailed tech review, market entry strategy, and many of the fundamentals necessary to equip the next generation of climate tech founders and funders. Pitching is super important, but this style is much more "big room/TED Talk" style, which is rare, so it's good to get that rep, but maybe not worth 80%+ of the course work going into perfecting. I think the course could also benefit tremendously from bringing in a third professor, or part-time advisor, preferably someone younger and from a different background in the climate tech space (female, under represented demographic group, etc.). This person would ideally be actively involved in the climate tech VC world (as an investor) or as an entrepreneur and could bring current perspectives to class. That would make a HUGE difference and help adapt what is a great, but at times dated, course into the critical new world of climate tech.

Yes I would definitely recommend, with the caveat that there are no guarantees of which team you will get but there's a substantial amount of growth and learning that takes place depending on what you make of the program.

The experience of this class is highly dependent on your team and your company. If you're interested in clean tech and would find the projects alone intellectually stimulating, I recommend taking the class. However, don't bother if you aren't 100% in. Starting off with the technology in this course makes it extremely difficult for people with a non- technical background to get caught up to speed and engage in the project. There are intentionally individuals that are supposed to serve as a bridge between technical and business people, but if those individuals aren't a good bridge and are too technical, the experience is brutal.

Yes, but with caution. It is an interesting class but be fully aware that your experience will completely depend on two things 1. Your entrepreneur and the technology that you are working with and 2. Your team. If either one is not aligned with your learning objectives from this class you are going to have a bad time. That being said, it is an interesting class and worth the experience especially if you have an entrepreneurial sprit.

This is a good course, but it could be better. It is focused too much on the pitching/symposium aspect, and not enough effort is spent on the market research side of things. If you are interested In becoming an entrepreneur or working at a smaller company, this is great! However, if you want to work at a larger company, this may not be the best use of your time.

Yes, as it justifies its reputation as more than a 3.0 credit course, both in terms of time needing to be put in and learnings taken out, and value from the overall experience of being put into a cleantech startup's shoes and seeing the market discovery and go to market strategies get crafted from the ground up. Could have used more material and focus on that G2M backend, but overall the class gave a great experiential opportunity to practice the key life cycle steps for scaling up pre/seed-size cleantech startups. The Investor/VC roundtable, presentation atmosphere and networking, and other non-instructional elements were just icing on the cake.
Yes. 100%. Because of the unique nature of C2M, working with real companies with real stakes, the instructors were especially dedicated to our success throughout this course.

If you are interested in the climate tech space as an investor/entrepreneur/operator/strategy role, you must take this course. This course helped gain a great understanding of this space through personal and team research - learn by doing rather than in class. Also, working with cross industrial and cross functional teams on an unsolved challenge that is not easy to solve led to a lot of personal growth.

Yes, I would recommend this class. It was really helpful to see how startups operate and navigate the early, difficult decisions. It is also underscored just how much work is required to do the research necessary to make those decisions. I would definitely recommend this course to students. I think it was a fairly unstructured course my year and so there might not be a lot of additional learning done, but I learn by doing, and as a non-Haas student, I learned a lot about how to approach market discovery, value-based pricing, business models, and the role of presentations in different contexts by working with my classmates. It also felt good to work with real clients. Again, though, I wouldn't come in expecting to learn a whole lot in this class but rather see this class as an opportunity to put project management, communication, and market research skills to the test.

I would recommend this course to another student. However, I think the focus is a bit different than what is listed on the class description. Roughly a month is spent on developing a pitch for the company for the symposium, with dozens of practices sessions and coaching on storytelling. I think being able to give a really well rehearsed pitch is useful, but students should go into this course understanding that that is roughly ~1/3 of the time of the course. Yes

I would recommend this course even if it is a lot of work. There are several instances where we are pushed out of our comfort zones and that was incredibly beneficial to my growth. This is truly a once in a lifetime experience. Yes most definitely, this class is extremely useful and provides a lot of useful experiences for future opportunities. It will be stressful, and will require a not so insignificant amount of work to get the full benefits of the course. I would absolutely recommend this class. It's an amazing springboard for anyone looking to break into cleantech! Two pieces of feedback on the course:
1) Six students is too many for one group. I think five is a better mix -- six just caused too much spinning and resulted in too many cooks in the kitchen.

2) I'd also highly recommend segmenting the course by early stage/ low TRL companies vs. more established. I think it's too difficult in 15 weeks to evaluate an early stage company with a low TRL with the same level of fidelity and detail as teams with more established companies. I'd recommend not including low TRL companies in C2M because to successfully tackle a project like that you need such a high level of industry expertise. You spend most of the time on 'how would you even sell this' vs. quantifying future markets, forecasting revenue etc. I'd also say that because early stage/ low TRL companies require such industry expertise to figure out 'what is this', the team dynamics become heavily skewed towards engineers who simultaneously lack business acumen. There is less of role for business folks, and the team dynamics really suffer.

I would not recommend this class at all. Despite having 3 faculty members leading the class, they did not actually instruct much and I find this a pity as I'm sure we could have learnt a lot from them. The class meets twice a week but the time is not well used: there is little time for team work, but also no real content that is being taught. Most of the classes require each team to give an update, one by one, about where they are in the process and what type of tools they are using (eg, are you tracking interviews on Excel vs. Word?), which becomes extremely repetitive and is not helpful. In addition, it felt like the entire class was designed for the final summit where the audience is a mix of investors and thought leaders in cleantech. I found it a pity that very little emphasis was being put on actually delivering something valuable for the entrepreneurs and startups we are actually working with and on making sure that students learnt, and instead it just felt like it was important to the faculty to save face in front of whoever was invited to the summit. Therefore, I felt that from beginning to end there was a huge misalignments in goals between the students, the entrepreneurs, and the faculty. From a project perspective, the class was way more "technical" than I expected (but unfortunately with nobody really teaching us any technical content), and there was surprisingly very little emphasis on go-to-market strategies and commercialization! That being said, I really liked that the teams were mixed, with students from many different programs, including PhD students. In addition, Bill and Sheeraz were always available, approachable and happy to help out, and I really appreciated their commitment to the class, their deep care for students and their receptivity to feedback!
this sucked - too much work, no guidance, lots of busy work type assignments, huge time committment and 0 payoff. only cool part is the startups themselves, and the other students in the class

Rewarding, especially if you haven't done consulting style before (less valuable if you have). The courseload is very heavy, so plan for this if you decide to take the class. Also, spend a lot of time selecting your company. Summit presentations were very rewarding
This class was a significant learning for my career and an engaging way to work with startups in delivering significant content. A class that you make your own!
Absolutely! By far, one of the best classes I have taken. An awesome learning experience and a fun community to engage with.
Yes. This is a great class. Really helped me develop, especially within the cleantech sphere.
Yes, this course taught me a lot about market research, interviewing, and giving effective presentations.

I would -- as a PhD student, this is one of a few opportunities to take a business class and diverge from the many technical courses we take. I think it was a good experience overall but is highly dependent on your team and the startup you'll eventually work with. I've had the good fortune of working with some incredible business students from whom I've learned a lot. The startup we worked with this year is also really responsive to our feedback and concerns. The instructors do a great job encouraging us to ask them for feedback or help whenever we need it, though I feel like I got more out of working with my team than the instructors' lectures.
I would highly recommend this course to fellow engineering students because it teaches engineers very different knowledge and motivates them to have their own startups.

Yes, if you could truly put the time in that this class deserves. This class is most valuable if everyone in the team in engaging and participating. There were different levels of dedication in the team and I think that dragged us down quite a bit.

I would definitely recommend this instructor and course to another student. I had a great time in this class and it was so useful to my education to have the real-life experience of consulting with a start-up and learning about how products are brought to market.

I have told students that if you have a passion for working in Cleantech you can get a lot of this class if you are willing to put a lot of work into it, however, if you are only casually interested then I would not take this course. Yes. It was a great opportunity to work with passionate entrepreneurs. High degree of freedom is the beauty of the class. You may set your own goal in this class and leverage the activities to achieve your goal. You can broaden your energy network in a very effective way with this class.
The final symposium presentation is a honorable chance to speak in front of energy professionals in the bay area and get your foot in to the community.

This is a LOT of work - but there is substantial value in deeply getting into a problem, working through it, building external connections, and potentially even finding jobs. Don't go in half-heartedly but if you're committed to cleantech it is the class to take.

If you are interested in clean or climate tech or energy, take this course. Your enjoyment of the class will highly depend on the technology you get and your team. I got an OK tech and an excellent team and the course was one of the best I've taken at Haas. If you end up on a team full of typical "haas apathy" (you know what I mean) then this class has the potential to be rough. Overall, this is an excellent learning experience and, for some of you, why you came to Haas, so take the class. It is a lot of work, but if you keep on top of it all semester, it's perfectly manageable. For all of those interested in how startups find their ideal market and design their go-to-market strategy this is a great course. It is a lot of work, so starting early by defining team dynamics and planning the semester with your team in the first week of class is ideal if you want to get the most out of this class.
Yes I would. I learned quite a lot from hands on research, which is the most impactful way of learning for me. The things I learned and connections I made are directly impactful to my future career.
Yes! I learned so much about early-stage climate tech start ups and the climate tech space in general. I am so happy that I took this course!
YES!

Students should have a very clear reason for what they intend to get out of the class, whether that is presentation skill development, deep exposure to a technology, GTM strategy experience, etc. and make sure it is worth the high workload required to do well in the course

Absolutely not. I was so excited about this class, and it was one of the main reasons that brought me to Haas in the first class. I'm very sad to say that this course was the single biggest regret of my Haas experience. It was poorly designed from the start.

This class hinges on having strong client partnerships. Several of the clients did not set their teams up for the success. They came in with different understandings of what they would get out of the course, indicating that the instructors did not prep or debrief them well. It's also very hard to teach uniformly to a class that is working with very different clients at very different stages. If you don't see a client you're SUPER excited about, please don't even think about this course.

The lecture materials were disjointed, and topics didn't flow well from one to another. The instructors attempted to give us group work time during class, but it was usually only in 20 minute blocks amidst other content. This was disruptive and we were unable to get much done in this time. Most of the content ends two thirds into the course, and the end is dedicated to the symposium presentation and report.

The instructors are just okay. Bill and Bill have been doing this forever, but it seems like their hearts just aren't in it anymore. Sheeraz was truly a fantastic instructor and is a great leader in this space.

Much of the course is spent conducting stakeholder interviews and doing market research. I believe that these concepts are better taught and better utilized in other courses and experiences at Haas. Due to the forced deliverables (symposium presentation and 75+ page report) and needlessly uniform teaching style, this class ate up more time than all of my other courses combined. It was a frustrating experience in which I look back and reflect that I have learned very little from it. I wish so badly that I could reset this semester and not take C2M. Please don't make the same mistake I did.

C2M is an incredible experience. Probably life changing. It gave me the opportunity to apply the learnings from my MBA to a real-life scenario. I would highly recommend this for anyone who wants to work in clean tech but I do agree with comments from previous years that it requires A LOT of work. I spent easily 5-6 credits worth of of time on it

sections.goodFor: Students fully committed to cleantech who want an immersive, consulting-style semester with a real startup, cross-program teammates, and access to the C2M alumni and sponsor network; fans call it a capstone, life changing, and one of the best classes at Berkeley.
sections.notFor: Anyone casually interested, short on time, or expecting to be taught: a large contingent across all three terms says there is little actual instruction, the experience hinges entirely on the team and startup you draw, and several openly regret taking it. Also flagged as less relevant if you are not headed to cleantech or marketing roles.
sections.workloadNote: Repeatedly described as the workload of a 5-credit class packed into 3 credits, culminating in a 70+ page market report and a heavily rehearsed public summit presentation.
sections.redFlags: Recurring (10+ comments): little to no teaching; learning is almost entirely self-directed project work. Recurring (8 comments): workload far exceeds 3 credits. Recurring (8 comments): experience depends heavily on your assigned team and startup. Recurring (5 comments): course prioritizes the public summit showcase over student learning and deliverable value to the startups.
sections.quote: Don't go in half-heartedly but if you're committed to cleantech it is the class to take.
comments: No one should take this course until it is completely overhauled. Working with cleantech startups feels like the quintessential Haas project, and in many ways it is, however, there is little to no education being provided in this class. At their worst, AI courses are unpaid internships, and that's what this course is in its current form. Almost 2/3rds of total class time was dedicated to unstructured teamwork, which is unacceptable. If we could be properly taught about how to go about performing the final deliverables before they were due, this would be a decent class, but with so many years to get things right, it's hard to believe there will be any significant change.
Ultimately most of the course is experiential and I learned a lot through the process of the projects assigned and would recommend the course.
Yes, this course is one of the best classes I have taken at UC Berkeley. I learned a lot about the technology commercialization process through this course.

Overall if you are interested in the Cleantech startup space I think that this is a good primer for what it looks like. It puts you in a place where there is a lot of ambiguity and you need to just grind a lot to get to your ultimate goal. I think that most of that work has to happen at an individual and team level, and it is not easy, which can make it easy to complain about the instructors even if it does not necessarily have to do with them. Ultimately I think this is very valuable course and would recommend it.

C2M was a challenging but ultimately rewarding course to enroll in. I got to learn about a very interesting technology, dive into new markets and areas of knowledge, while working with a good team who were all bought in in their own ways. I think if you get the short end of the stick on the team perspective it can be a pretty miserable experience given the volume of work and relative lack of structure in the class.

I would highly recommend taking this class as it's a capstone class where we can practice aspects of finance, marketing, econ, data, sale and last but certainly not least, public speaking. I wish more Executive MBA (EMBA) would be aware of this class as it's a great opportunity to work directly with founders. EMBA also bring a different perspective as well as access to a more robust network that will come hand during the industry interviews.
If you want to learn about clean tech in an immersive experiential way, AND have plenty of time (i.e. few other time commitments) then it's a great experience
It depends. Your experience will depend heavely on the team you are assigned to and the entrepreneur you are assigned to.

Besides this, the class itself in terms of content was not particularly attractive to me. The content was not well structured and the feedback you get during the process of preparing the final presentation and paper are not necesarrily appropiate or helpfull.

On the other hand, you get a real consulting kind-off experience and learn a bit about how startups work. But for the most part, your are on your own with your team and the entrepreneur without too much detailed guidance.

This course is challenging not just because of the subject matter, the workload, or the deliverables, but because of the scattered instruction, poorly designed class meetings, and irrelevant interim deliverables.

Yes - beware that while this is 3 credits, expect to put in work akin to a 5 credit class. It really feels like a badge of honor to have for anyone looking to make their career in climate tech but certainly not a walk in the park and there are certainly easier applied innovation courses to take if you're not all in on climate tech.

For a fellow science-focused student I don't know if I would recommend it. This was a good overall experience, but the summit made me feel like most presentations could have been written a few weeks ago with minimal research. It becomes a game of giving the best "show" and not showcasing research. The final presentation that called TEM tea and had a planted question from a friend to start off the discussion made me feel sick to my stomach.

I cannot recommend this course in its current form. It is an ungodly amount of work which may or may not have any influence for the companies we work with. The professors do not maximize our class time or really teach us much valuable content. They do not provide enough guidance throughout the semester or add much value to the projects at all. This class has added a tremendous amount of stress to my life. I was warned that it would be stressful, but thought that if I approached the course proactively and diligently, I would be able to avoid the horror stories I had heard from past students. I was wrong. Given the current format, the stress is unavoidable.

I would only say that I hope this course changes. It has so much potential, but unfortunately falls short. A hard maybe. The course is well run and an intense learning experience. Students need to understand that this is at its core a marketing course. If students are going into other fields outside cleantech or marketing, this course may be less relevant. Weigh this against C2Ms significant time commitment. However, if going into cleantech, I feel like this course is a must take if for the network of C2M alum and sponsors alone. Learnings are largely based on the specific team and technology you will be working on so choose wisely!

Without significant upgrades, I would have a difficult time recommending this course to a fellow student. With that being said, it is an awesome opportunity to dive deep into a clean tech-focused market. I learned A TON about the market my team was focused on (critical minerals), but wish there had been far more teachings on Go-To-Market strategy, project scoping, and other project management skills.

I would absolutely recommend this course to a fellow student. I feel that I gained a lot of really valuable experience, and that it was very much worth the effort. I feel that I am a better-rounded student now.
If you are interested in Climate Tech, this is a course that you have to take.

Mixed feelings.... depends a lot on the expectations students have. Hopefully students get a very real understanding of the class before enrolling. Maybe having panels with alumni could be helpful before round 1 bidding.
Not sure; I have mixed feelings about the course. We worked very hard, but there was little guidance or class lectures that made me learn from them.

I would not. I think there are easier and more educational ways to fulfill this learning and the applied innovation requirement. I think that there was just not a lot of learnings in class and that the experiences vary so widely by the project that I would pick a different course for a sure thing. If you need a project, there are other classes. If you want to learn this stuff, right now it is better to chat with faculty rather than sit through this whole class and project. I would absolutely not recommend this course unless one of the startups is exactly the type of company you are interested in. You will learn very little from the instructors about cleantech, start ups, business strategy, etc. The priority of the course is not student learning but putting on a summit that connects the instructors and the broader cleantech community. The most direct learning you'll do is I guess around how to present a powerpoint at a summit - not exactly what I signed up for.
The course is very poorly organized. The uses of BCourses was so confusing and the expectations around assignments and final deliverables was constantly shifting at the last minute.

I was also pretty unimpressed by the quality of the startups. Furthermore, because the priority of this course is not actually student learning but the final summit which is basically a pitch competition you don't actually get authentic engagement from the startups. Instead the startups are more or less pitching to you the whole time because they want to win the money more than they are interested in your learning. Remember that the financial awards presented at the summit go to the start ups not to to you so they want your free labor to make them look is as good as possible! On top of that, it is a ton of work. The market report and summit presentation is a huge lift but you will not be learning new tools to execute on it. Instead, you are asked to bring whatever skills you already have to perform free labor. Yes, if the student is a non-Business School student and if is particularly interested in getting a sense of how climate technology and business intersects. I would definitely mention that even the class connects you and your team with a startup, there will be a lot of business knowledge that students are supposed to know beforehand. Probably not really hard to get those knowledge over the semester, but definitely something to keep in mind.
Yes if they're really interested in diving deeper into climate tech companies and working with start-up for commercialization. It is a lot of work so it depends on the students willingness to commit!

Definitely recommend IF you are interested in Cleantech. But it requires a lot of work outside of the class Working on this course absolutely destroyed my fall semester, and as much as I'd like to say I learned a lot about clean tech and go to market, I didn't really learn about either of those things. The course is basically one giant consulting interview with an added bonuses of working with 4-5 other people (at least 2 of whom probably don't actually care about this class) and a 70+ page paper on the end. Do market sizing on 20 markets, select some of them, interview random people so that there's an air of legitimacy to the whole thing, then send the final result over to a startup that might appreciate it or might literally never look at it.

No, I don't recommend it. Like many incoming students passionate about cleantech, I was really excited about this class but ultimately I regret taking it. Previous students tried to warn us but I chose not to heed their feedback and even bid all my points to take this class; after the first few weeks it became apparent I made the wrong decision. The class was not worthwhile at all, in fact it made my semester difficult. We did not get much lecture content or learn much and were expected to basically teach ourselves while at the same time do work for the clients on such short and immense time pressure. Essentially we were paying our tuition to do free consulting work, except it isn't free we're paying to work for these startups.
Not really.
yes.It is very practical for work
Yes
Yes if you have the right assumptions going into the class. This a good course to get a basic sense of what leading people involves but not to do any deep dive into any subject.

sections.goodFor: Students who need it for the AI Certificate; a few say the topic matters and the last two sessions were the strongest.

sections.workloadNote: Not discussed in hours; the graded work students cite is quizzes, which several say tested concepts not covered in class and rewarded memorizing slides.
sections.gradingBasis: Quizzes (called very difficult and slide-memorization based); attendance appears not to count.
sections.redFlags: Four rotating instructors made it disjointed (5+); title/description misleading - little business content (4+); quizzes covered untaught material (3); one says Thomas Lee is pedantic and confrontational with students.

comments: As it stands right now, I cannot. I hope this becomes the class it should be (and a part of core), but clearly it was hastily put together and expectations the faculty had for the class were very different than what we had as students. If we want a technical AI class, we can go to a different school - we are here for a business class and this was not it. Additionally, the first two quizzes were mostly on concepts that were not even discussed (at least in detail) in class. No, not at all. And this is the only class at Haas where I'd say that.

The name "Business AI Foundations" is a misnomer. We never really got into the practical business applications of AI in any meaningful way. The course covered AI at a surface level from a technical perspective, but I didn't leave with any greater practical knowledge of how to actually use it. I think I got more value messing around on my computer during lectures than I did from the lectures themselves. Three of the four instructors I'd be interested in taking again, just in different classes.

So I'm left wondering what the point was. If this had been called just "AI Foundations," it was too surface level to earn the title. The business portion felt almost entirely absent. And the fact that it's required for the AI Certificate and costs a real chunk of points makes that worse, not better. The curriculum needs to change and the instructor team needs to be managed pretty dramatically before this is worth taking. Knowing what I know now, I wouldn't take it.

You have to take this for the certificate but if you don't need the certificate, you can probably get a similar amount of value out of just talking to other students, keeping up with the news, and taking Data Mining

Yes, this is an important class. Four instructors in such a short period was not idea. But in the future, one or two professors would be idea. Overall, this is an important class and i encourage everyone to take it to understand the AI impact and landscape in business.
Not as it currently stands - I recognize that the administration is revising the course to be more pertinent to stuent desires and to what the market is asking for, however.
The course give insights into the world of AI in bits and pieces, but it failed to bring it together, particularly difficult to see its business alignment.

This course has potential, but it's disappointing in its current form. The course spent a lot of time on technical topics that were too complex for non-technical people to understand, and not complex enough to add value for technical people. The rotating professors seemed cool in theory but made the class feel disjointed. If the curriculum was overhauled and focused more on practical business applications of AI and problems that businesses are encountering, it would be much more worth it.

If this course were more refined, I would recommend it - but in its current state, I would not. There is a lot of potential, and I believe the professors could be excellent, but the class needs stronger continuity across instructors, content, and the evolution of each lecture, as well as clearer connections to real-world business applications. The learning objectives were often unclear, and the quizzes did not meaningfully reinforce learning... they felt more like memorization of lecture slides than true understanding. As a result, I'm leaving the course unsure of what I actually learned. Given how rapidly AI is evolving, this is an incredibly important moment to offer a course like this at Haas, and it feels like the class didn't fully harness that opportunity.

It's a really great way to get real-world experience in the impact VC space and connect with many investors, startup founders and accelerators. Be prepared for a significant amount of time outside of class to juggle intro calls and due diligence work but it's definitely worth it! Maybe - it depends on the student. I would say that overall I learned a lot from working with my team but I don't feel like I learned specific strategies on how to be a better investor.

Take the class if you are interested in exploring early stage seed stage investing. Your mentor matters a lot and so does your sector area (assigned team). It's good practice in sourcing deals and due diligence. I did not like the structure of other students deciding if you present in front of judges (seems like there is some bias there). Yes, Overall the class went well. However, I think that this course needs to assume a much lower base knowledge of students and explain some fundamentals of investing and sourcing. 90% of time and effort was spent on sourcing which was a tiny part of instrcution and support.

This course and the teaching staff is amazing! 10/10 recommend, however, EXPECT A TON OF WORK. Learnings are directly proportional to time put in, but you can't really do the appropriate amount of work to be successful and keep it to a reasonable 2 credit course load.

I would recommend this course to people who are interested in early stage VC investing, but this course is much more experiential (there's less structure/guidance on how to do valuations/due-diligences). I would only take it once you have taken a well-taught course on venture finance.

This course gives you real experience of trying to source and invest in an attractive impact startup. It is very self directed, so you'll need to be comfortable in ambiguous and challenging situations. Only the basics are handed to you in this class, but its a great opportunity to learn and bring together learnings from many courses.

I would definitely recommend this class to anyone who is interested in VC. It was helpful to go out in the field and source and diligence investments. This class is a ton of work, especially toward the end, and it's only worthwhile if you put in the effort. It was a great opportunity to learn from experts in the field, however, most of the learning happens on your own and you will only get out what you put in. However, the professors are there to support you and provide a ton of their time through office hours to help you along the way.
It was definitely a great learning opportunity

I would recommend, with the caveat "you get what you put in". How much or little time, effort, commitment and energy you put into the class is what you will get out of it. If you want to experience what is its like to source and pitch early stage impact oriented start ups, this class is for you. However, it is up to you and your team to really commit time and effort to make the most out of the opportunities the course provides. The real learning is in the experience of finding / sourcing the company.

Highly recommend! It's super time intensive and one of the hardest sprints I've ever done, so be ready for the time commitment, but it was such a great applied learning experience (hopefully it'll get the AI designation in the future). I loved talking to founders, VCs and deciding what company to pitch. It was super helpful and aligned with my internship search in climate tech VC, too, because it gave me a great reason to be in touch with all of the VCs and accelerators I wanted to get connected with!

Overall, the course was a good introduction to impact investing. I think if the course had a bit more structure and provided more direction, it would be an even better learning experience. The instructors in the course can be a bit harsh and direct, but I think they're just trying to help everyone succeed.

HIF was pitched as an exciting "day in the life of an impact investor" where you could make an actual $50K investment if you win - the course has so much potential but ultimately fell flat this year. They tried expanding and grew too big, brought in new faculty to replace Adair who didn't properly structure and organize the class, and despite good intentions across the board, left most people feeling disillusioned. You'll get the following for sure: an interesting team of classmates to work with, an overview of what impact investing is, and an introduction to the VC deal sourcing process. You won't get: a thorough understanding of venture fundamentals, a structured course with real learning objectives, or too much of a relationship with the faculty. Experience probably varies pretty widely. They're trying but it seems like they just jumped into things and didn't thoughtfully plan for how things would unfold. That said, VC offerings are limited, especially for first-year FTMBAs. It's a worthwhile course, but they really have a ton of room for improvement before it becomes anything people would rave about as a "must take"

Personally, I got a lot of out HIF as it's directly related to my career goals. It allows you to begin to think like an impact VC and begin to build a solid VC/startup network. It's very important to get on a good team and one that's relevant for your future career as you will be spending a lot of time doing research on that sector. This class is a LOT of work (often more than all my other classes combined) in a very short time. I would only recommend this course if it aligns with your career interests, because so much of it is self taught and time consuming. This class did not provide the technical guidance I was looking for, so you have to find that yourself (e.g., how to value a company, how to create a pro-forma, how to conduct due diligence). Since it's a relatively new course, it may change considerably over the next year, so reach out to the professor/GSI to learn more about the expected time, course material, etc.

At least in its current format, HIF is a class that asks for a ton from you without necessarily promising much in return. SO much of your experience in this class depends on your teammates and mentor. I was one of two people on my team who were very engaged, and we ended up shouldering much of the work. Because there were so few classroom sessions in the beginning of the semester where we learned how to source, diligence, and pitch companies, teams get pushed out of the nest pretty quickly and have to figure things out for themselves. Luckily, our team had an amazing mentor who was an industry expert that we were able to meet with weekly. I heard other teams weren't as lucky with their mentors. This class does provide an amazing platform to get out of the classroom and talk to real founders and companies. In that way, you do learn a lot about how the real world of impact investing works. But it's very trial and error — although the professors made themselves available through weekly office hours, there was very little hand- holding. I think this class is a rewarding one, and is a must-take if you're considering a career in impact investing. But it could be structured better.
I would recommend as an experiential learning opportunity in sourcing early-stage deals, but not as a way to learn core tools of finance.

Yes overall. it was a rich (and very messy) learning experience but I did learn a lot. The course could use a lot more structure and re-working to make it a richer learning experience, but overall HIF is a great way to get hands dirty on the work of impact investing or even VC.

If you want to get the most out of this class, I would highly recommend taking VC/PE or New Venture Finance prior. The class is very light on actual skill building and the majority of the time spent is on deal sourcing and diligence. The class touches very lightly upon venture math, how to evaluate companies, or even how to develop and justify an investment thesis.

I would absolutely recommend this class if you want experience in deal sourcing. 90% of the class will be spent talking with founders and venture firms which is great exposure not only for the class but for your career. On top of this, it was helpful to dive deep into a startup's deal room, talk with the CEO about their strategy, and really think about the potential impact of the company. Overall a very hands-on class with a lot of work done by each team on a weekly basis, but a very useful class if you're looking to dive into this industry area.

There is also a substantial opportunity to build a network in this space. The instructors are very knowledgable about VC and helpful for both your learning and your professional network.

NO, not in its current state. The course needs a LOT of work to be a valuable experience for all students participating in it. The course lacks even small things like a BCourses page or any centralized information portal. The lack of structure and guidance, especially at the start of the course, makes the experience very dependent on the assigned mentor, which we have no control over. Although it's meant to replicate the early stage investing process, we are still here to learn how it works, not simply be thrown into it with little to no context or guidance. Finally, the structure of the fund itself - being constrained by a short investment horizon, having to follow-on on an existing deal, and not knowing as we're sourcing that we will in fact be able to make the investment - makes the whole process very unsatisfactory, especially if you have to pass on a great startup just because their fundraise is planned for a month later than our timeline cutoff. Could this course be valuable if some big changes were made to it, yes. Is it valuable right now, unfortunately not.

It's a good opportunity to work with a team and get to know startups in a sector you're interested in, but the structure of the course and the lack of helpful instruction or encouragement from the teaching team leave a lot of potential on the table. I would recommend taking the course if you want credit for exploring a sector you would already want to on your own time, but I would make sure you don't allocate too much time to the class or expect to learn much about VC.

I wanted it for the resume builder of actually searching & evaluating startups (which it kind of accomplished, but only 1 team from the class will get to actually 'deploy capital' to their startup), but it did not teach the process very well. There were only 4 lecture days, which gave great overview of the VC investing process, but then our teams were left to our own devices for the reset of the semester to figure out how to source (yes, there were office hours with the profs where we asked questions, but more structure would have been greatly appreciated). A lot of the work can be thrown into the last month of class out of necessity to just get it done (but quality of the work and our learnings would have been better if had more structure throughout). With the current structure, our experience in this course was very dependent on your assigned team; any team who happened to have someone with VC experience had a

great advantage, and since we did not get to pick teams and it is a mix of FT & EWMBA, it was hard to coordinate schedules. In short, there are other classes about VC at Haas that would teach the concepts better, but if this is the only one that can fit your schedule and you don't mind flailing with your team a bit, then this class is okay. Totally recommend it to anyone curious about VC or willing to use the course as a productive use of academic time to learn about a startup industry or get a job. I networked with founders, VCs, and learned a lot about climate tech, which was one of my target recruiting industries at the end of my second year.

This course taught a lot of practical application of the core, but avoid LeBlanc if possible – grading seems arbitrary, no matter how hard you try you?ll be wrong, and the structure of grading is ambiguous. He knows his stuff and respects when you defend your position, but lack of organization and the intimidation factor on those predisposed to step back leads to a pretty echo chambered conversation.

While a strategy course feels valuable, this approach to it does not. I'd rather have a McKinsey consultant come in and teach us their strategy framework and approach, rather than hear all LeBlanc's case analysis. Additionally, I have the following concerns:

LeBlanc needs to really consider what he says in class in regards to his off–hand comments and jokes. While it may have been acceptable decades ago, now his comments and jokes about homeless people, veterans, and other disadvantaged groups are uncomfortable, and in my opinion, unacceptable. It is brash and is not a demonstration of "confidence without attitude" or "beyond yourself" – there is a lot of attitude. Additionally, the way LeBlanc engages with students in class discussion can feel brash, condescending, and arbitrary. It does not create an inclusive learning environment, as people feel afraid to speak up for fear of being verbally attacked. For example, in the final presentations, LeBlanc left students feeling undermined. While challenging ideas and asking questions is a typical part of a presentation, LeBlanc's approach, rather than leading with curiosity and interest, undermined students' ideas and left them feeling undermined or frustrated by his mid–presentation attacks.

Another concern is that there was no rubric for grading of assignments. When questioned about how to succeed in the assignments and what he was looking for, LeBlanc said he was looking for students to arrive at his conclusions – which were, of course, a matter of opinion. This made grading decisions feel arbitrary.

I think strategy as a course is important to include in the MBA core curriculum, however, in the state its being taught in today, there is little value because the learnings are very unclear. If revamped to include more frameworks that would help students execute on assignments or think critically about business decisions, I would recommend it, but it needs a lot of work as is.

Absolutely not recommended. This class was the single biggest waste of my time. DDP was not a great class, but I still preferred that to whatever this course was. This class cheapens the Haas brand and makes me reconsider advising potential students to come to Haas.

Toby Stuart who hopefully remains one of the lecturers for the course is a great industry leader and makes you think.
I would not recommend, better off taking an LLM course. I am not sure what they were trying to do making us take this course.

Yes. This class should be a core class, right after Data and Decisions. It is crucial for today's market that every MBA students masterizes these concepts and is able to "talk AI" and understand the technology in a proper way Interesting course to get exposure to the nuts and bolts of AI and how it will affect workplaces and society from several different perceptives.
Yes, The course is useful and brings clarity about AI in the business world

I would recommend this class because I still got unique insights into what's happening in the space and readings I would not go looking for own my own, but not all the professors were equally good (Toby Stuart was great; Jonathan Kolstad was good; and Anastasia Fedyk was not as great; we haven't had the fourth professor at the time of this submission so can't speak to them) but the learning experience fluctuated a lot depending on who was teaching. If Toby is teaching his own class on this subject, I would probably just take that.

No, but I think this class can only get better (hopefully it will). Some general comments about how to improve the class (it didn't feel appropriate to write it down only for one faculty): stop relying on the "this is the first time we teach the class so things will go wrong" and actively try to prevent that from happening (Question the status quo, anyone?); if you ask us to answer the pre class questions before 11 pm, make sure to open them with enough time to answer (most of the times I would try to answer them on Saturday (closed), Sunday 11am (closed), Sunday 5pm (still closed), and then by 9pm it was open but it closed at 11pm), and several times they didn't even open the questions so you would be checking all the time until finally giving up; communicate with other faculty on a regular basis (e.g., it happened twice that the printed quizzes were not enough for the students); and in general, the class should be called AI foundations and not Business AI foundations, as there was little to no connection to the business side (eg., it explained how AI works when translating words into 0s and 1s, then doing some calculations for the error, distance, etc when it could have been explained much simpler and why this is relevant); if the class will continue to have this technical focus, then there is plenty of overlap with the Intro to coding class
It was ok- I hope they update it to be reflective of the feedback in terms of balancing how much time was spent on the content the students found most interesting
If you need the AI certificate sure. I'd like to see an iteration of this class with less professors. 4 in one half semester was way too much.

I think this course could be good but this year was not well coordinated and prepare given it was the first edition. Also, is important it is taught from a business/ corporate lenses, not so focus on research and academia but rather what kind of problems, challenges and decisions we are gonna have to face in the corporate world (even if we don't have a technical role) and what do we need to make them efficiently. I would think of the course as a guide for a student who is put in charge of defining the AI strategy of a company, what kind of tools they implement and how these are integrated, what factors to take into account, how do you train employees, what workflows should be redefined, etc. I would recommend this class because I learned a lot about how businesses are currently thinking about AI and what AI strategy should look like.

This course will give you a strong and broad understanding of AI fundamentals from the theory perspective, which is great. There is little content on its application, though, nor really content on policy/ how to handle it/ etc. There is also no hands-on learning with AI. So if you take this class, be well aware that what you get out is theory and understanding (which is a helpful thing, no doubt), not practical application.

Hopefully, from an organization perspective, this class will improve because it was a hot mess this semester. There were 4 professors who each taught a few weeks of class separately. This was great from a knowledge and perspective breadth POV. However, they never seemed to actually talk to each other or have a handover when switching to then next professor, which made the class disjointed as they didn't seem to know what was covered, where we were at, when quizes where, if past deck material was actually posted, etc.. Furthermore, they didn't seem to manage or update bCourses regularly, causing confusion, and there was no real GSI in tow to help keep up with this either. First year course with a number of different professors so it tended to be disaggregated. Solid material and deep dive into AI.

MOST IMPORTANTLY, the lecturer admitted that students with extensive presentation experience would not learn much from this class, and that they should spend their class time helping other students learn. Despite this admission, 30% of your grade is attendance and participation –– and you lose points for being on your laptop! In general, I'm flabbergasted that Haas mandates its MBA students take this class. It's an offensive waste of time and needs to be completely overhauled for it to add any shred of value to the MBA program.

This is by FAR the worst course I have taken at Haas and an enormous waste of time for me, my classmates, and the university. While the idea of "data driven presentations" is a worthwhile topic for academic and

professional exploration, this course needs to be COMPLETELY redone in order to do this important topic justice. As it stands, I (along with the vast majority of my classmates) gained ZERO from this course because it was disorganized, redundant, and taught at a 7th grade level. It is extraordinarily discouraging that, in a place where we are supposed to be learning how to be effective business leaders and take bold, meaningful action when problems exist, that our feedback (and that from the 2023 class) has been met with either gross negligence or conscious inaction on the part of the academic and program offices. Fundamentally, few of us got anything out of this class. It was a lot of time lost and that sucks for the amount I am paying. I am upset about this, and this is another reason why I struggle to recommend the Haas program to others. I don't know how to make this class great, but I know that all the things I got from it personally could be condensed into one 2–hour class at most. I felt that answers to questions were sincere but not very useful often. Each topic felt like it was being taught to someone with no prior presentation experience. I think "I don't know" would have been a fairer answer in many questions or getting into more specific case studies. I would have also liked to see more references to academic literature a la leading people! This is a great way to ensure that we get lessons that are non–obvious. Why am I taking this course at Haas for 70+k when I could get it all from my local library for free?! Most of the time in class was so basic or so non–specific it could not have been more useless. Repetition for public speaking was the lens of business communication class, so we didn't need that here. Smaller exercises with more reps would have been better than larger projects, but in general we didn?t feel any project was particularly useful.

It is worth asking why this class is part of the core. I cannot imagine that employers are telling Haas that we are deficient in this area. We cannot test out and that is a problem for a class that is so basic that I cannot fathom its utility for most of us, especially our consultant peers. Some students may need help here. I personally would have taken a seminar or audited a class of this type to learn the best practices that we got here, but this class was maximally inefficient. I don't want improv practice here or a class that is just fun, I need that in classes dedicated to useful topics. I don't understand the purpose of this course or why I was forced to take it.

There was little personal growth possible in this course, and it is further undermining my faith that the academics office is acting in student interest. Genuinely, why is this topic even needed. I know no peer that felt that they learned a lot. I just don?t get it. The caliber of students present here in Haas is far more advanced than this. Either the people who decided we need this class don?t know that or are incapable of understanding the difference in level that these students play at. What was the point.

I would not recommend this instructor / course to a fellow student. Many of our other classes at Haas require us to create presentations. To create those presentations we worked with other classmates. This class is a disaster. I would like a refund on my tuition reflecting the time and credits spent. Future students reading this, if this core class is still taught this way, we have failed collectively to push for change.

The course would be better suited for students pursuing a masters or PhD in statistics rather than for business students who will be matriculating into jobs where we won't use R or really be the ones designing studies. This is by FAR the worst course I have taken at Haas and an enormous waste of time for me, my classmates, and the university. While the idea of "data driven presentations" is a worthwhile topic for academic and

professional exploration, this course needs to be COMPLETELY redone in order to do this important topic justice. As it stands, I (along with the vast majority of my classmates) gained ZERO from this course because it was disorganized, redundant, and taught at a 7th grade level. It is extraordinarily discouraging that, in a place where we are supposed to be learning how to be effective business leaders and take bold, meaningful action when problems exist, that our feedback (and that from the 2023 class) has been met with either gross negligence or conscious inaction on the part of the academic and program offices. I am upset about this, and this is another reason why I struggle to recommend the Haas program to others. I don't know how to make this class great, but I know that all the things I got from it personally could be condensed into one 2–hour class at most. I felt that answers to questions were sincere but not very useful often. Each topic felt like it was being taught to someone with no prior presentation experience. I think "I don't know" would have been a fairer answer in many questions or getting into more specific case studies. I would have also liked to see more references to academic literature a la leading people! This is a great way to ensure that we get lessons that are non–obvious. Why am I taking this course at Haas for 70+k when I could get it all from my local library for free?! Most of the time in class was so basic or so non–specific it could not have been more useless. Repetition for public speaking was the lens of business communication class, so we didn't need that here. Smaller exercises with more reps would have been better than larger projects, but in general we didn?t feel any project was particularly useful.

It is worth asking why this class is part of the core. I cannot imagine that employers are telling Haas that we are deficient in this area. We cannot test out and that is a problem for a class that is so basic that I cannot fathom its utility for most of us, especially our consultant peers. Some students may need help here. I personally would have taken a seminar or audited a class of this type to learn the best practices that we got here, but this class was maximally inefficient. I don't want improv practice here or a class that is just fun, I need that in classes dedicated to useful topics. I don't understand the purpose of this course or why I was forced to take it.

There was little personal growth possible in this course, and it is further undermining my faith that the academics office is acting in student interest. Genuinely, why is this topic even needed. I know no peer that felt that they learned a lot. I just don?t get it. The caliber of students present here in Haas is far more advanced than this. Either the people who decided we need this class don?t know that or are incapable of understanding the difference in level that these students play at. What was the point.

sections.quote: This is a great introductory course on how to finance new ventures through a variety of vehicles (VC, Angels, Search Funds, etc.). Really a fantastic and manageable class.

I would recommend Maura as an instructor because she is engaging, experienced and her passion for teaching others comes through in every aspect of the NVF class. The information she teaches is so relevant and deep and it is provided in a way that is incredibly helpful for someone like me who wants to start a company and raise venture funds in the next few years. She focuses on key information (like, you should plan to raise 2x the amount of capital and assume it will take you 2x longer than you anticipate) and also shares incredibly engaging stories from her real world experience during each class.

I would totally recommend this instructor and course to a fellow student. The class resulted in substantial learning not only through traditional methods (readings, slides), but also through great speakers that shared their insights. If you are an entrepreneur trying to understand how to sustain your business, this is a valuable course. Likewise, if you're an investor (or an aspiring one), this course provides exposure to the broader financing environment outside of your specialty. If you're pretty experienced in either of these, though, this may not be the class to get the latest techniques — it definitely hits the highlights. This course can also serve as an intro to venture funding as well for the uninitiated. At times, I felt like the course could be shorter — but the bulk of the benefit comes from hearing from the guest speakers.
